The picture is flawless. DirecTV has a very detailed picture on many of the cable channels (National Geographic, A&E, etc.), but my local channels on DirecTV are not quite as good as they are directly off the air.

My only complaint is the inherent heat output of the plasma display. If you have marginal air conditioning, you will not like the noticeable heat being put into the room. It will be a plus in the winter time.

Delivery by Pilot was on-time. The TV was ordered on a Friday evening and it was delivered the next Thursday within the window given by Pilot. Although the box was clearly marked with two labels that the TV was to be handled by two people, Pilot showed up with one person. He unloaded the box from the truck and dragged it into my house. He and I had to lift my 76 lb old DLP TV off the component cabinet and then lift the new 100 lb TV onto it. I am 74 years old with back problems and I did not appreciate Pilot showing up with one person.

That bad taste was quickly replaced by the enjoyment of watching the 560. It is a BIG screen and dominates the corner of my room, but is just the right size for me, viewing from about 12 to 14 feet away. It makes for an awesome viewing experience! I don't think one can go wrong buying this TV.

The TV/dongle was located on the second floor directly over the first-floor location of my Linksys Wireless WRT610N dual-band router.

First, I could not get the dongle to recognize either the G or N network. After trying various TV positions in the room with no success for about 30 minutes, I moved the TV downstairs about a foot away from the router. The dongle then picked up the G network, but not the N. I connected to the G network, but as soon as I went to the on-screen menu to connect to any site, I got disconnected. I could go back to the menu and immediately re-connect, but I would always get disconnected as soon as I tried to connect to Netflix, Youtube, or any of the sites available in the LG menu. I spent about another 30-60 minutes trying to troubleshoot, then gave up.

I have a moderate amount of networking knowledge, but I am by no means an expert, so it is possible that I could have done something to solve the problem; however, it was not worth the hassle, so I returned this item. Maybe the right combination of equipment and circumstances would make this work, but I would not recommend it to anyone who isn't willing and able to do a lot of tweaking.

title: good alarm
text: The alarm works well. The installation took a few hours one weekend. I wouldn't recommend a diy install if you aren't too familiar with electrical wiring. The wire harness was plenty long and the ECU was small enough to be able to tuck into some open space on my Honda Shadow. Like other reviewers, I too was fooled by the description of the engine shut down feature. The feature is integrated into the ECU, however the wiring associated with that feature requires an optional relay (the grey wire in the center of the schematic). After looking at the wiring diagram, this makes sense as the ECU connects on top of the existing bike wiring and doesn't actually require any bike rewireing. One other minor issue is that for the alarm with the remote start feature, there is no provision to bypass the kill switch. The key ignition is bypassed during remote starting, but if the red kill switch on the handle bars is not in run, then the bike won't start. This means that when I park, i have to kill the bike and then place the kill switch back to run if I intend to use the remote start feature later. Not a big deal but if I forget, then I basically have to go out to the bike to flip that switch which defeats the remote start's purpose. On a positive note, the alarm is sensitive enough that I set it off just by flipping the kill switch back to run after parking. The remote works from a long distance too. I live in a third floor apartment and can start it even when it's parked around the corner, out of view. Other than those two issues, it's an inexpensive deterrent to thieves and helps keep stupid apartment kids from messing with my bike or saddle bags. It's a great but for the price.

title: this antenna may be fine for an attic installation
text: I didn't actually install this antenna.  The construction was far too light for my area (60+ MPH winds are typical).  A far as the construction, this antenna may be fine for an attic installation, but I think would fail quickly if mounted outside due to weather.  The down lead is quite thin, and I think the cable loss would easily negate the amplification.  After I looked at this antenna as a technician of over 40 years, I would not recommend this antenna.  Homework as to what you need is important.  Don't pay too much attention as to mileage, as this isn't an accurate metric (the way different companies measure mileage make this meaningless), so much  as the color scale established by the FCC.  Check out antennaweb.org for a fair representation of what you need. Keep in mind that you should choose an antenna based on the weakest channel you wish to receive.  With the 20+ year old antenna I'm presently using, I'm receiving 135 digital channels, 3 analog.  I know the antenna I'm using is corroded, and held together with duct tape, and I'd like to replace it, but do your homework

title: GREAT Auto Focus Camera
text:
I purchased a $400 Canon auto-focus, image-stabilizer camera about 2 1/2 years ago and hated it from "Day One." My husband claimed it was "operator error," until he tried changing every setting to see if he could get it to take decent pictures. We finally gave up and bought a new camera about one month ago: the Nikon S8000 from amazon.com. I couldn't be happier. The pictures are awesome with or without the telephoto. Unlike my Canon, the Nikon takes nice pictures in low light situations, or when shooting into the sun (with flash turned "on.") The controls are very intuitive and I like the "scene" feature to tell the camera if you are taking a portrait, landscape, night portrait, indoor shot, beach/snow, sunset, dusk/dawn, night landscape, close-up (such as a picture of a flower), etc. The only negatives I have found are the placement of the flash (as noted by previous reviewers); it's in an awkward place where some people would normally place their left index finger to hold on to the top of the camera. I also find that the LCD screen is very hard to see in bright (outdoor) light, even when adjusted to the brightest setting it can be. However, I can live with a few minor inconviences as this camera takes just awesome pictures! I have always loved Nikon cameras and wished my husband had NEVER talked me into the Canon. After two+ years, I am finally ENJOYING photography again!

UPDATE -- JULY 21, 2010: I just returned from an Alaskan cruise and am still in love with this camera. My pictures are incredible and the various scene selectors were very helpful. I would encourage anyone purchasing this camera to also buy a second battery (and keep a fully charged second battery on hand at all times). When you receive the low battery indicator, you only have about one or two more photos you can shoot, so there's not a lot of warning that your battery is low. I charged up both of my batteries every night while on the cruise (took 500 pictures in seven days) so I was always ready for a full day of sightseeing and picture taking.

title: One of the must have lenses for the Sony A7 series bodies.
text:
I recently switched my DSLR kit over to all Canon 1D series bodies. The biggest downside of this is that the DSLRs are no longer anywhere near convenient for travel photography. For a while, I was using the Canon 16-35 F/4 IS on my A7R with an adapter, but that's not really an optimal solution in the long run so I picked up a copy of this lens for a recent vacation. First let me start off by saying that this lens is not quite up to the amazingly high standard set by Canon's latest 16-35 F/4 IS, especially at the long end, but the gap between the two is not enormous.

The Good:

- Excellent performance at the wide end, almost as good as the Canon everywhere except the extreme corners. Nobody will be anything but thrilled with how sharp this lens performs at 16mm.
- Fantastic build quality. The lens is all metal and feels extremely solid and smooth, well done Sony.
- Excellent control of flare. You can shoot directly into the sun and not experience any flare. Good luck doing that with a Nikon 14-24.

The Mediocre:

- The AF with this lens on the A7R is not very fast. I also found it seems to miss more often than the 35 2.8 and 55 1.8, but I thinks that more of an A7R issue than a problem with the lens.
- The OSS is there but it's not terribly effective at the wide end. I'd give it somewhere between 1-2 stops effectiveness at 16mm, as compared to the Canon versions which is easily at 3 stops.
- The price of this lens is noticeably higher than the competition while performing a bit worse.

The Bad:

- The image sharpness at 35mm is fairly poor, even stopped down to f/8. For travel photography this doesn't matter, but I wouldn't expect to make giant prints based on images taken with this lens at 35mm.

Overall, despite some minor flaws (most notably performance at 35mm) this lens is pretty much a must have for anybody shooting a Sony A7 series body. The weakness at 35mm can be pretty easily overcome by adding either the FE 35 2.8 to your kit or even the FE 24-70. Highly recommended.

title: Bad product, beware of false 5-star ratings
text:
Edit: it looks like this company is posting false reviews with the verified purchase tag on the end. That's pretty shady. The comments still don't match the product. The main reason I know that these "verified purchase" reviews are fake is because I've seen, touched, and used these headphones. Holy crap, no. No way someone gives these 5-stars. These shady companies are doing whatever they can to trick people into buying their poorly made garbage. Don't buy these. They're just bad. Seriously bad.
Also, if you click on the profiles of any of the 5-star "verified" reviews, you will see that they all leave 5 star ratings for other cheap, Chinese earbuds. Who buys this many headphones? 4, 5 pairs a month? Who buys 3 different phone cases (for different phones) in the span of a month? Why are all these people buying so many cables? It's because they're fake accounts, leaving fake reviews for all these cheap Chinese products. I wish Amazon would slam these sellers, seriously.

(original review)
So I'm thinking that I am probably the first review for this product that wasn't posted as a bot. They are all 5-star ratings, none of them are verified Amazon purchasers. And even if they were, I would still think that they were bots because these earbuds are simply terrible, completely undeserving of a 5-star rating.

The sound is okay, good enough for a $10 pair of earbuds. The sound isn't going to blow your mind or anything, but it is fine when they work.

The tips that it comes with are not great. They aren't comfortable and feel like cheap rubber (which they are).
The cable is weird, tangles easily and does not feel sturdy at all.

The main bad thing, however, is that these arrived at my door with a dead spot on the 3.5mm jack right out of the box. If you jangle the cable at the jack 1 or 2 mm to the side you get a complete loss of all bass, and about half of the treble volume goes right out the window. And occasionally the sound cuts out completely.

The volume slider works, however it's just a volume control for the earbuds themselves, they do not change the volume your phone puts out at all. So you basically have two volume controls, which is weird and annoying. The cord is also loud when it bumps up against anything. Definitely could not be used for joggers. You couldn't use it for jogging anyways because the buds would fall out of your ears within 20 steps.

So my message to anyone looking at this review, all the other reviews are fake. I'm guessing they pull reviews off of another product (a good one) and then use bots to plaster the page with these copied reviews.

If you ever see a product with a ton of reviews and none of them are verified Amazon purchases, don't buy it. If you ever see anything with more than 100 reviews, all of them 5-stars, then it's a scam. There is no way to get more than 100 people to rate something 5-stars, with no deviation at all, no matter how good the product is. Sorry, it just isn't gonna happen. I don't think Amazon is going to crack down on this kind of garbage because I don't think they actually care that much. So it is on you, the buyer to watch out, and not have your time wasted like I did. Look out for reviews. If it looks to good to be true, it is.

This product is cheap Chinese trash. Don't buy it. The other reviews are fake, don't let them trick you like they tricked me. Luckily Amazon's return policy is great. But I would have liked not to waste my time on this stupid product in the first place.

title: Doesn't seem ready for prime time
text:
I am specifically reviewing the B004-DP2UA2-K 2-port switch (the Ultra High Definition one with USB2 and the little switcher dongle).

I had really high hopes for to use this KVM switch for a daisy-chained dual monitor setup, but I had too many problems with it, so I decided to return it.

My setup consists of a Windows 7 PC, a Macbook Pro Retina, and a Dell U2415 monitor.

These were the issues I ran into:

1. When my Macbook is attached to the KVM switch, it's closed (I do not use its internal screen). It whenever I would switch away from it, it appears it thought the external screen was disconnected and would rearrange the windows and go to sleep. This made it unusable to switch back and forth between the different computers with any kind of flow: you always have to login again and the windows would be messed up.
2. It appears Windows or my video card could not display anything on the screen if it was not in control when it started up. So, basically, if I booted the Windows PC while I was using my Mac, it wouldn't ever show video.
3. I had keyboard and mouse emulation on, but my Windows PC hardly ever recognized the keyboard and mouse, so I had no way to log in after bootup. Occasionally it did work, but I could detect no pattern to it.

I have been using an IOGear DVI KVM switch for years, and never had any of these issues (unfortunately that can't handle dual monitors).

Pluses:
* Support for multiple daisy-chained monitors (Multi-Stream Transport)
* Has a physical switcher dongle
* All cables are detachable, so you can swap in your own shorter cables if you want.

title: Maybe I Received a Defective Pair- NOT for iPhone use
text:
I excitedly opened the packaging I admit my expectations were high. I thoroughly enjoy my Ultimate Ears 600vi and though I don't use them much because of size I do like the sound of my UE TripleFi 10's. I recently bought a pair of Bose SE215’s, which sounds terrific. Actually they sound awesome. Maybe a little light on the bass but very enjoyable. Now admittedly my source is an iPhone 6 or iPad Air.
These Sennheiser headphones sounded like crap to me. The bass drowned out the mids and the overall sound was like a cheap set of headphones.

I read all the audiophile reviews and I know a flat sound is the standard but they also said these were extraordinary on the Head fi reviews. I couldn't believe it. I understand ear buds and sound is subjective but to be so far off the mark is unusual for me. The louder I made it them more indistinguishable the source was drowned with boom, not just bass. I thought I enjoy a bassey sound, as I also was not thrilled with the Etymotic HF2 and the Klipsch X10 as I found them as way too flat. I do enjoy a nice bass line but this sounded like junk.

Excuse the layman's terms for my experience but I love ear buds and I get the most use out of my Bose Quietcomfort 20i with active noise cancellation. That's my in bed pair. I use The UE's on my train commute and the Shure when the train is very noisy or I just want to change up. The Bose is a flatter sound than My UEs or Shure but I strongly advise you listen to the Sennheiser and don't just buy based on the price drop, as I wouldn't keep these for $57 let alone $257.

Maybe I just received a defective pair!?!

Update: I purchased a pair of sure SE215 and I liked them so much I tried the SE425 even and though they are flat on the bass line without some third party equalizer, they didn't sound as good to me as the cheaper SE215. But when I put on a third party equalizer and upped the bass line, I understood why these were called reference ear buds and flat. They sounded great.

There are so many positive reviews for the IE80 they must have some quality I am not missing. All I will now confirm is the pair I received which did not appear counterfeit, had "embossed logo" and sounded poor. Muddy bass and definitely not along the line of a reference ear-bud.

They were unusable for me. Your mileage may vary.

title: LinkS Gold Plated Display Port to HDMI Cable Adapter - Slow Delivery
text:
I purchased 3 of these units for use with wall mounted displays in meeting rooms. These units were shipped from overseas and there were very significant delays in shipping and delivery. The vendor changed the expected delivery date several times. It took more than 8 weeks to receive these items that were supposed to be delivered in 3 days, or less. Be aware of that if you want the items quickly.

Pros:
- The units do work on full size Display Ports.
- The units handle both audio 5.1 sound and 1080p video without problems.
- The price was competitive.

Cons:
- Poor delivery time.
- The cable connecting the Male Display Port end to the Female HDMI end is small diameter and feels flimsy. Unlike other DP to HDMI adapters I have from COBOC which were the same price.
- Will not work with 4K video streams. Be aware of this if you are planning on Upgrading your system.

These Display Port to HDMI adapters are good for HDMI 1.2 and 1.4 but do not work with the new HDMI standards. That is only important if you have a new 4K HDTV, new HDMI 2.0 cables and a 4K compatible video source to use them. Since this is not common, these adapters should work for 95+% of the applications. I had no problems with them on any of the client PC's or Servers I attached them to.

My biggest concern is for the lifespan of these adapters. If you are just putting them on a single device and not constantly attaching and detaching them or moving around the cable, these devices will probably suit you fine. If you use them in a mobile environment where you are moving the cable or attaching them to the display port and removing it constantly (Example: you have a wall mounted display in a meeting room which employees use for presentations and their PC's have Display Ports but no HDMI ports), there could be problems with the adapters going bad. I have not had one fail yet but, I have only had the units for less than a month.

If you are planning on using these adapters for a home environment where they do not get moved much, they will most likely meet your needs.

title: I don't recommend
text:
So first thing first, I am leaving the review for both the BeQuiet Dark Rock Pro 4 and BeQuiet Silent Wings 3 at the same time, so you can see the context of my review.

I want to start by addressing that I am a sound engineer, and a person with an ear that most just don't have. I have difference in mini-decibel range (10th of a decibel), I am a recording engineer, with a psychology understanding of the brain, and I have built computers for a while now. I have tried more fans you can imagine, but actually listened to them besides of using them as well.

Here is what I can tell you for both of Dark Rock Pro 4 and BeQuiet Silent Wings:
They produce frequences below the level of human ear hearing, and above hearing range of normal human being.

We can hear from 20hz to 20,000 hz, but not everyone, some start hearing from 45 hz, and only hear up to 14,000 hz. Hearing is very important, but the way the brain works is even more important in this review.

The BeQuiet fans in Dark Rock Pro 4 are Silent Wing 3 fans, with 135 mm variation fan specific only to BeQuiet coolers. Those motors/bearing in the fan produce frequencies around 6hz and above 19,000 hz.

Why does it matter? Well, 5 hz is frequency of the brain, if the sound produced is around that frequency it affect the brain, and it can actually make the person very angry (without knowing) or make them sick, physically or mentally. Frequencies above 17 hz are very damaging to the ear drum, they make your ears hurt, and you will feel a dull pain in your eardrums. Reason why, is the follicles in the ear drum are damaged in the process, and the pain is of hair follicles dying. Hair follicles in our ears act as nerves that transfer fluctuation of sound as perceivable sound that is transferred directly to brain, and then decoded into a set of known memories within our database of the brain. The problem with high frequencies is that they damage the ears, make you go deaf eventually, and erode your ear canal follicles in the process. Here is a key issue on top of it, frequencies above 17khz are very seldom heard by a human ear, around 18,000 hz-19,000 khz is where the dangerous zone trully begins, you cannot hear those frequencies (most people) but you are killing your hearing, but your brain is subjected by the sound and goes "insane" after a while. To subject a person to a 19,000-20,000 khz will cause a person to go insane, as will producing 5 hz - 8 hz, that range is very dangerous as well.

I studied science behind it, so I understand it, but I am not paranoid about it.

After sitting for 2 hours next to 3 fans of Silent Wings 3, I started getting annoyed, and I could not figure it out at first. I started hearing my fridge more, I suddenly started hearing air conditioners around my house (that I never noticed), and those sounds started hurting my brain and ears.

I am a logical person, so I started to check outside and inside for any kind of malfunction. What I realized that the frequency of the fans heightened the perception of sounds around, but NOT in a good way. I isolated the issue to the 3 fans first. I removed them, and my pain in the ears and irratation has subsided by about 80%. I returned the fans back to Amazon, but was greeted with the same issue in 4-5 hours of sitting at my computer. My moods are very stable, and they are not fluctuating up and down by the way.

I realized that the fans in the Dark Rock Pro 4 are causing the same issue, but to a lesser degree. Due to them being less rpm, but the frequency is the same, just to a lesser degree.

After removing the cooler, I realized it was not loudness of the fans, but the frequency it produced. I ABSOLUTELY would recommend to STAY AWAY from these fans for health reasons.

That is of course if you belive me, I have nothing to gain by it, but wanted to warn people.

Also I don't blame BeQuiet, as I am sure they are not aware of this, but maybe you will see that email and do a revision, because I care for people in this situation.
I will be sending them a separate email as well.

Other reasons for return: I am returning Dark Rock Pro 4 for several reasons, this is the main issue. Second issue is that cooling is very unstable. That part is more trivial now. It cannot compete with Corsair H105 that I had, and to me temps are jumping up and down. Tightening the bolts a bit less on the cpu, untill you hit the pressure is enough. Otherwise it will push the thermal paste all over, and thin it out too much where is more physical contact with the cooler, but no thermal paste to speak of now.

I would stay away from this cooler because of the fans first of all, and also, you cannot switch the fans to something else. It uses mounting mechanism that is specific to BeQuiet cooler. I would stay away altogether from it, because of those frequency issues, and unstable cooling performance. The fins are too closely stacked together, and fans cannot push substantial air through the fins to cool it. Fan is too low of rpm, and you cannot replace the fans with off-brand ones like Noctua.

Also, the cooler scuffs from tiniest contact of mounting brackets, chips the paint so easy...you will likely be pissed after a while. Fins bend so easy too, it's crazy fragile, and black paint just flakes off the fins, and from the mounting brackets.

Quality is poor in my opinion, but I saw some success with it in HIGHLY ventilated case, but you have to be realistic too. I have Cooler Master Geminii S524 cooler, with 4 heatpipes total, and Dark Rock Pro 4 has 14 (7 on each side), my old Cooler Master has a downward fan and never pushes above 72 Celcius on full Noctua fan profile, with Dark Rock Pro 4 I have seen 68-70 on full RPM load. What?

Geminii S524 was $35 by the way. Good engineering vs not so good. BUT...I will give the cooler 3 stars, because it's not garbage, but it's poorly designed, and not optimized for overclocking stability. I run Intel i7 4790k at 4.8 ghz, but you are telling me that Geminii with 4 heatpipes handles the cpu just as good but with only 1 Noctua fan vs BeQuiet 2 fans?

Results may vary, but I know what I am talking about, and I have to say...if you want great performance, perhaps go with water cooling AIO, or Noctua's high end air coolers.

Hopefully it explains it all, even when it comes to cooling with it. Cooler is fragile, fins, paint, and installation is semi-difficult if you have motherboard out of the case, but if it's in the case mounted....my goodness...may the peace be with you, my friends...it will drive you nuts trying to put those bolts into the bracket.

Unless you have 4 arms and patience of a god.

title: Superb entry level player
text:
I recently developed a strong interest in listening to records and began collecting. My experiences with records had not been very good. While people claimed they could sound better than CDs, I had only listened to records on second-hand players (don't get me wrong, second-hand is great!) or dodgy Crosley players. The sound was no better than if you were playing them through a Pepsi can. Then, at the record store that I frequent for used records, I decided to take "Tenderness" by General Public for a spin. The sound was warm, bubbly and clear as crystal! They were playing on an Audio-Technica LP 120, which after research I realized I didn't have the funds for. Yet I found this model, one step down, and after receiving it and playing records I am extremely pleased.

I am just a "part time enthusiast" and have only very little knowledge of things like cartridges, styli, preamps, etc. Because of my limited space I am using the preamp setting which is extremely nice for those who simply want to start listening and not have to buy further components. I also just have one dinky speaker which, admittedly, can churn out a great deal of noise and bass, and it sounds great. But I could imagine it would be even more awesome on a better set-up. I think my listening experience depends greatly on the cleanliness of the record (which is why I just bought the cleaner also made by Audio-Technica). I do occasionally "dip" the stylus into a chunk of Magic Eraser to clean it (google this for more info) between plays just so that I can get build up off of it.

The clear case has beveled edges and overall the effect is modern but very minimalist, which is what I like. The setting for the record size is a little awkward looking on the bottom right inside. The arm moves smoothly. I do agree with a previous reviewer that the buttons on the front could have been a little stronger but they work. The cords that come with the turntable made it easy for me to quickly set up the player. The only scary part was putting the belt on, but it was less involved than I thought, and watching a demonstration video on YT really helped make sure I didn't twist it by accident.

I bought this model over the USB version because I read another review which said the sound quality on the USB version is not as good. Also, there is no real need for a USB. Simply plug in the line into your microphone and make sure Audacity (downloadable for free) is set to receive from line-in.

Overall, I couldn't have been happier. I just like listening to my records finally. If I could add anything, it would be a 78 setting as I also love older music. But perhaps that's for the upgrade :)

title: Great features that work about 50% of the time
text:
I was genuinely excited to get this item. It took a little time to install, as this is my first non-factory car stereo. Finally got everything hooked up correctly after 90 minutes or so.

ISSUES:
1. Non-responsive buttons - The buttons on the face of the stereo system have to be mashed pretty forcefully for the system to recognize they've been pushed. This is incredibly frustrating if you don't have the screen up.This isn't an issue with the touch screen. The touch screen is very responsive, even if there's a 1-2 second delay after you push a button on it.

2. Power issues - I had about a day and a half of perfect use from this system, messing around with all the features driving to and from work. Then, over the weekend, I had some friends in my car as we were driving out to dinner. As soon as I turned the system on, the screen lit up with a "No Signal" notice. The touch screen opened automatically, and would not close unless I turned off the car. None of the features except "AUX" mode worked, and even then the sound was reduced to being barely audible. I figured out the next morning that the "No Signal" display only appeared when I turned my headlights on, which essentially means it would only work during the day time. However, I realized that if I dimmed the interior lights on my odometer, the system would function properly even with headlights on. This is inconvenient, but worth it if I have a fully functional stereo.

3. USB Connector Doesn't Work - There is a chord running from the back of the stereo that has a USB connector. The first time I plugged in my iPhone, it switched from "charging" to "not charging" so fast I thought it was having a seizure. It wouldn't connect long enough to do anything. The next time I tried it, nothing happened. Again, the USB port is not essential to me, so I can overlook this.

4. Weak radio signal - Self explanatory. I'm 90 miles out from a station in a major city that I picked up very clearly with my factory stereo. Nothing but static with this new system.

5. THE LAST STRAW - Touch Screen Committed Suicide - I tried to plug my phone into the USB one last time to see if it could get a charge. As soon as I did, the touch screen went black and became unresponsive. I powered off the stereo, but screen was still unresponsive. I restarted my car, but the screen was still unresponsive. The buttons on the face of the stereo became unresponsive. The only way to control anything is with the remote. This piece of crap won't even give me my DVD back. The display says it's trying to open, but absolutely nothing happens. There is not a button on the remote to eject a disc, and there doesn't seem to be a reset button either.

I've had this system a week. There have been WAY too many functionality problems in that time. Cross your fingers when you order this that you don't get a defective system like I did. About to call and give someone hell about why the majority of the things don't work on this. NOT WORTH THE MONEY.

title: Better CPU than advertised, "Sesame" branded memory installed wrong, failed, ancient hard drive
text:
UPDATE 2: The seller told me they would not honor their warranty because they were located in Canada and Hawaii was not part of the United States. Whatever. Amazon customer service intervened and although the seller wouldn't budge, Amazon did fix the failed memory problem. I've been using the computer daily for 2 years since.

UPDATE: One of the "Sesame" memory modules failed. Waiting to hear back from seller on how this is going to get fixed. Computer won't even start with defective module installed.

Since listings can can change but the reviews stay the same, this review is specifically for:

Dell Optiplex 7010 Business Desktop Computer (Intel Quad Core i5-3470 3.2GHz, 16GB RAM, 2TB HDD

The actual CPU installed is a 3550 which is an upgrade to the advertised processor. The HDD has 57,000 hours on it which is the equivalent of running continuously 24 hours a day 7 days a week for over 6.5 years. If you use your computer 2 hours per day you would have to use it for 78 years to accumulate as much usage on the hard drive. I'm not saying 57,000 hours on a HDD is excessive I'm just putting this into perspective that this is not a "new" HD nor is it particularly speedy. This isn't an issue for me because I'm using an SDD in the machine and it runs very fast with it.

The memory was installed incorrectly- in single channel mode. It works in this manner just far below expectations. I removed one of the memory sticks and put it in the next slot over to make the memory dual mode and it benched twice as fast. I've never heard of "Sesame" memory before and can find little about it on the internet. But I posted a shot of the specs as well. Cheap memory is usually the culprit in any computer problem so it's something to keep an eye on. If anybody knows anything about sesame memory feel free to post as a followup comment.

Unit arrived looking and smelling new inside and out.

title: Great lens for the price, but not great for action in anything but noonday sun due to aperture.
text:
Pros:
-Relatively inexpensive telephoto with a good range of focal lengths
-very, very light, and reasonably small
-great image quality if you can get enough light
-great stabilization to stop MY movement/wiggle at slow shutter speeds.

Cons:
- f/8 aperture at 400mm is just too small to get fast shutter speeds in anything but bright sun
- overall small aperture seems to reduce accuracy and speed of AF on tricky subjects
- the great IS won't stop the subject's motion (not really the lenses fault, just not how IS works), so f/8 and the resulting shutter speeds cause issues when shooting sports/action

I have very mixed feelings about this lens. On one hand, it is great for the price, the Image Stabilization is awesome, and it is much smaller and lighter than other similar lenses, like the much, much more expensive EF 100-400 F4-5.6.

The downside is the small aperture, narrowing to f/8 at the full 400mm, and you really need to stop down one or two notches from there if you want maximum sharpness. As such, you end up running pretty high ISOs if you want to keep the shutter speed high to stop action, and the noise resulting from the higher ISOs starts to rob sharpness.

This issue isn't too bad on a sunny, cloudless day--but be prepared to drop shutter speed and crank up the ISO in less than perfect conditions. Forget shooting anything moving indoors, or in the morning/evening.

I found this out when I was trying to photograph the action at a local airshow--it was a somewhat cloudy day, and I just couldn't get enough light to run anything but wide-open, with ISO 1000+ to get even 1/500 shutter--resulting in blurry AND noisy pictures unless everything came out just right. On top of that, it seemed like it was missing focus a lot, probably due to the small aperture. My camera focuses just fine on fast movement with other lenses.

Don't get me wrong, this lens is awesome for landscape, portrait, anything where you can get everything to hold still, and you can even shoot action on a very bright, sunny day. But if you want laser-sharp photos of things moving fast in anything but perfect light, be prepared to pony up the cash for an EF adapter and an L-series lens, or use a faster, shorter lens and hope you have enough resolution to crop in.

I'm not sure what niche this lens is supposed to fill. For a beginner who is trying to save some money, the RF 24-240 is a better all-rounder, or the Tamron 18-400 if you want a one-lens-for-everything. For the enthusiast or semi-pro, the 24-240 is still better at the low end of the range, and anyone seriously trying to shoot telephoto in imperfect light would be much better served by one of the large-aperture 70-200 L-series lenses or the EF 100-400.

Ultimately, I sold this lens and spent about twice as much on a used EF 100-400mm F4-5.6 L IS II, which is superior in every way, besides weight and size.

title: Not as fabulous as expected; for the cost maybe look elsewhere
text:
I work in a very loud metal fabrication shop, but I used to produce audio. I use the most sound-isolating earbuds and the best over-ear hearing protection I can find. When my ears started ringing anyway, I needed to up my hearing protection and decided not to worry about cost.

These Bose earbuds get great reviews for both sound and noise canceling. They also cost close to $300, so my expectations were very high. My experience was mixed.

Sound
At first I was very happy with the sound. I heard things I didn't remember hearing before in recordings I've listened to many times. Then I realized that, since I wanted to hear that great sound, I had the volume turned up. When I turned the volume down to my normal level, what I can listen to safely for an entire day, that effect died. The sound was similar to what I was used to with my old Etymotic Research HF4 earbuds, at about a quarter the cost.

So I went back to those lower middle range ER earbuds and turned up the volume. I actually liked those better than the Bose. Like any good earbud, the HF4s put me in a large space with musicians clearly spaced all around me. I went back and forth. It could be I like a more direct sound, but the Bose earbuds sounded a bit weak.

An additional data point: After the Bose earbuds, I also tried an odd thing called the Nura Loop. It wasn’t for me, but when I followed all the instructions, the sound was incredible. Better than anything I’ve heard before. Unfortunately, its noise cancellation did not match the Bose earbuds.

Noise Cancelation
In my research, I learned a lot. Noise canceling works well for low and midrange sound. Turn on the Bose noise canceling and the world goes away. But when the pitch of noise gets higher than voices, the amount getting through increases. A lot. If you ride planes and trains, noise canceling is world-changing: constant rumbles go away but louder voices, alarms, etc., get through. You're not completely out of unaware of the world around you. If you're working with power tools though, a lot of the noise around you is high-pitched. It’s nice that I don’t hear big machines, but the grinder in my hands comes through clearly.

Bose eartips are silicone with one flange, the little cup that seals against your ear canal. This is common among hi-fi earbuds I’ve seen. For a room, or—with noise cancelation—a plane, this is fine. But in an industrial environment, it’s useless. The excellent Bose noise cancelation doesn’t have a chance against the 140+ dB of >6000 Hz hammering into your ears.

The Nura Loop didn’t even make it into the metal shop. Since Bose noise cancelation is better, there was no point. I returned it.

Etymotic Research doesn't sell noise canceling equipment. They focus on sound isolation--blocking out other sound--so you can hear what you want to at low volume. I hoped that noise canceling would be even better than blocking noise. Turns out not. Good silicone eartips with three flanges keep out more sound than anything I’ve found, even the best foam eartips.

I also tried various types of earplugs. As far as I can tell, the ER silicone eartips beat any other in-ear sound isolation.

Conclusion
$500+ later, I’m back to Etymotic Research. I bought a new pair of ER3SE earbuds to replace the HR4s that were falling apart after 3+ years of hard use. When I can find them, I’m getting a pair of the noise-canceling headphones helicopter pilots use. Those plus the ER earbuds with three flange eartips may actually make listening to Elliot Smith and Chopin possible while cutting through fire escape grating with an angle grinder. THAT is the content I’m here for.

title: K10D -> K7D meh...Consider the k20d
text:
Though I feel that the k7 is an adequate replacement for the k10d I had, I think it's a mostly mediocre product and value given that the k20d can be had for half the price.

There are a few features that I think make the k7d better than the k20d:

Better autofocus.
Better auto WB.
100% view finder.
Electronic leveling.
Beautiful LCD screen.
Faster FPS
Cool retro pentax neck-strap mounts.

No one will fess up to whether or not the k7d is supposed to replace the k20d. Maybe that's because it's at best a lateral hop. The image quality on the k7 is the same or worse than the k20d. On High ISO images, the k7d fares worse with noise than the k20d in most situations. Of the four people I know who have shot pentax, only 1 of them liked the new grip and body size. I don't particularly like the grip myself but some may find it as an improvement given it's got a smaller overall body size. Button placement is off at times and the left justified lcd on the back is brutal. Your thumb is always on the LCD and the left side buttons are a lot less accessible.

Biggest cons for me:
Left Justified LCD screen
Image quality and noise. It's not terrible, but lets face it, it's an issue.
Selective AF point selection is now more or less a menu option instead of direct camera interface.
Pentax did away with tethering.

I have higher expectations than most. Don't take my review too harshly. The Pentax k7 is a decent camera when comparing value of the K7 vs Nikon or Canon per dollar. Unfortunately, the biggest competitor to the K7 is the k20d which frankly is half the cost and offers most of the same features I want in a digital camera.

Given that the $600 extra dollars I paid I view as an early adopter tax, I'm keeping the k7 and selling the k10d. But you should really think about the fact that you can almost buy a k20d + DA* 16-50 for the same price as the k7.

title: Nice product for the price if you need this sort of application
text:
Being newly released I took the plunge and bought this without much information about it. I've had it for about 24 hours now and am happy with the purchase. I'm using this monitor with a current gen MacBook Air. I've found the following:

- Color is a bit muted, comes around a bit after the monitor has been on for an hour or so
- A breeze to configure on OS X Lion
- Sometimes the Display Link connection gets a bit "busy" and movies displayed on screen will get a little bit choppy. This seems to occur when I have a bunch of windows open at the same time, and does not appear to be affected by system load. [I'm just using the default DisplayLink driver on the AOC disk and haven't experimented with anything else yet.]
- Very nice to be able to just plug into a USB and have a 2nd screen on my MacBook
- Very light and "portable." I'll be able to take to longer-term jobs and use as a 2nd monitor without having to lug something large and heavy along. 22" is not exactly portable in the true sense of the word though, the thing is very thin and light, but it's still 22" across.

To summarize: A great product if you're in the market for something like this. If you're just in the market for a monitor, there's a number of better options out there, as this is truly a niche product in my opinion.

This actually reminds me the time when Bill Gates was performing a demonstration of plug and play on Windows 95 with a USB scanner and once he plugged the device he got a blue screen of death.

I have not plans on buying the computer books I already have on PDF format from the Kindle store. So my last word to you kindle developers is to please release an update that fixes PDF books not showing pictures in some of them and to correct the auto scaling features, oh and one more thing switching from portrait to landscape and vice versa takes way too long when reading PDF books.

title: Slight upgrade, storage issue is MADDENING
text:
I bought this bc I my Fire Stick 4K was glitchy and constantly running out of storage. I figured I’d spent a couple of bucks and get something with snappier performance. I also installed an Eero Pro 6 wifi system and was excited about better results.

I was very pleased at first. The interface seemed more responsive, less lag, and setup was a breeze.

About a month in, and I feel like I’m using the same device as before. It’s absolutely maddening to be in the middle of a show or movie and have it stop, because the device is out of storage. Well, no crap…Amazon loads this thing to the gills with junk proprietary apps! I don’t need Alexa Shopping, Amazon Kids, Amazon Live Shopping (I don’t even know what that does), Amazon Music, Amazon Photos, AppStore, FireTV Player, GameCircle, IMDb TV, Screensaver, or Silk Browser. I don’t even use Silk or IMBd, and they’re the largest apps stored internally on this device after Netflix.

The only other apps I have on this are Disney+, Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Peacock TV and a news app. I actually had more apps on my LAST device and had less storage issues. I routinely erase data and cache on this device and still run into storage issues.

Also, I have seen zero speed upgrade on the Wifi 6 connection, so I feel hoodwinked there. Still random streaming issues, shows and movies take 10-15 seconds to buffer into HD, and the system in general runs like it’s bogged down.

Not sure what to do at this point except maybe switch over to Apple TV. I’m not a Roku guy. If there’s not some easy fix to this soon, be it firmware or an easy way to expand storage, I’ll be dropping Fire TV. If I do that, I’ll get rid of my 6-7 other Alexa devices and just go into Apple HomeKit. It’s not worth the aggravation.

Oh, you know what else really grinds my gears about this stupid thing? Every time it self-updates, it reorders the apps. Meaning, the apps you put in the easy access area of the menu, your preferred top 5, are jumbled around and you have to reorder them again. Because Amazon wands to shove IMBd TV and Amazon Photos down our throats.

Actually, I think I’m just going to order an Apple TV device now.

title: Wait To Buy From Amazon Until They Ship Newer Manufacturing Dates
text:
I ordered direct from Amazon. My order was placed on 2/13/2016. The expected ship date when I placed my order was 3/11/2016. I was willing to wait it out with the expectation that I would receive a new model built in January or later. However, on 2/21/2916, I received a delivery estimate update of 2/24/2916. I was thrilled!!!

That elation lasted only up until the package arrived. The outside of the box was dented, and the tape sealing the box closed had visual wear marks, suggesting this unit had previously been opened. I unpacked the monitor and checked out the serial sticker on the bottom to see it was manufactured in November 2015. At the time, I did not have my new computer yet, so I couldn't test out the monitor.

Fast forward to 3/9/2016, I receive my new computer, and hook up the monitor to it. This reveals that all of the quality issues reported in the other reviews prior to January manufacture dates are in my monitor, with one notable exception. Other reviews state that when overclocking, there would be visual scan lines or other issues causing it to be unbearable to watch. I did not experience that as my monitor physically could not be overclocked! It just wouldn't allow it to happen!!!

Just like the other reported quality issues with this monitor, I had a horrendous orange glow coming out of the corners that extended almost to the very middle of the screen.... The orange glow from each corner almost met in the middle.

I initiated the return process today. However, the estimated delivery of a replacement monitor is 4/15/2016 - 4/25/2016. I am extremely unhappy about this, as that will be TWO FULL MONTHS from the date at which I originally placed this order. And who knows what I receive then.... Another previously returned monitor??? So once UPS picks up my defective monitor, I'm not going to be able to use my brand new computer until mid to late April due to having no monitor.

This is an extremely upset customer, and I recommend anyone who wants this monitor to purchase from anyone else besides Amazon if you can find it at a price that is not ridiculously marked up, as it seems Amazon does not mind sending you a monitor that was previously returned and then make you wait another month for a replacement.

E: I've submitted numerous updates, but they don't seem to be going through... Let's see if this one does. I cancelled the replacement through Amazon, while still returning my defective monitor for a refund. I then purchased from another seller that advertised a manufacture date of February 2016. That monitor arrived well before the expected arrival date, and I am now using it. I am pleased to say that I now have the monitor I imagined this would be when I ordered it. This one overclocks to 100Hz without any issue (2 x GTX 980ti). Also, glad to report no dead pixels. There is minimal backlight bleed... an expected amount for an LCD monitor, and it is only in the left side of the screen, no backlight bleed on the right. With how large the viewing angle is, I haven't noticed it unless I'm looking for it.

So, in the end, I love it! However, I'm still deducting 1 star due to the quality issues that plagued the initial batch of monitors and caused me an unnecessary headache. I still recommend buying from another retailer than Amazon until they start shipping monitors made in January 2016 or later.

title: Magsafe is Apple at its most wasteful and greedy
text:
Upgrading to an iPhone 13 Pro from an iPhone XS had me pretty starry eyed at first - catching up on three years worth of new features was an exciting prospect. I was especially excited about Magsafe accessories, but Apple’s offerings are so disappointing that it makes me wish I had held out for a Pixel 6.

Let’s go over the details of the case first, in case you want to know what the experience is like: it’s exactly like putting on a normal case. The rims cause friction, which is good! You don’t want this thing falling off. But it’s definitely not the effortless snap-into-place you might have expected from Apple’s marketing.

And taking it off is much harder than a normal case. The magnets are *strong*. Again, that’s good, but completely contrary to Apple’s marketing. I was expecting effortless case swapping, but had to wrench this thing off with so much force that I was afraid I would cause a permanent bend to the leather.

The case itself is fine. It is worth $40 tops. The buttons are plasticky and the thin leather is unlikely to survive a fall without tearing. The rims provide so little protection that it’s a 50/50 chance a fall impact will have dire repercussions. I’m ashamed to admit that part of my decision to go Official Apple was the idea of swapping case colors on the fly, which has gone out the window with how exasperating the removal process is.

But hot-swapping cases isn’t the main reason anyone wants to buy *this* Official Magsafe Case. You want to take advantage of the shiny new charging ecosystem Apple has promised. Unfortunately, it’s such a joke that I wish I had gone with Android or, better yet, kept my XS.

If you want to use that Magsafe Charging Puck, here’s what you need:
• This case (or a similarly expensive one that includes the magnets needed to take advantage of the increased power) - $60
• The puck - $40
• A USB-C charging brick - $20~

No, you can’t use your USB-A brick from two iPhones ago. Apple decided that, after leading into “no free wall charger” under the guise of environmental advocacy, they’re just going to make you buy a new one and throw out your old one anyway. Their USB-C brick is $20. Generic is $10. Make your choice. It’s going to be over $100 for Magsafe either way.

To add insult to injury, the puck might be the worst designed charger I’ve ever used. The magnets are so strong you have to use two hands to snap it off, removing the “effortless” gimmick of wireless charging. You have to move it around a bit to make it fully snap into position, removing the “just pop it on” illusion Apple’s marketing presents. The cord is a pathetic three feet long, which means you can’t use it comfortably while charging if you’re sitting on the couch or laying in bed. The cord is hardwired to the puck, so you can’t add a longer cable. It’s completely inferior (and three times more expensive) than a generic case and a 10 foot Lightning cable.

But what about the *ecosystem*? My first glimmer of hope: Magsafe could be a godsend for car convenience. Guess what: there are *no* official Magsafe car chargers. Your options are either a Magsafe *mount* (which snaps your phone into place so you can connect your normal Lightning car cable for the low low price of $40) or a $35 mount *for the $40 Magsafe puck* which allows you to suspend the overpriced disc from your air conditioner. Oh, and you’ll doubtlessly need a $20ish USB-C car adapter too. That’s about $100 USD for the “seamless” experience of being able to use Magsafe in your car instead of sliding it in and out of a plastic mount.

How about charging on the go? Well, Apple no longer sells their fantastic battery cases - you have to shell out for their $100 Magsafe battery pack which *cannot fully charge an iPhone*. These battery packs are unwieldly and swivel uncomfortably while you hold your phone. Sure, competitors sell magnetic battery packs for half the price with more capacity, but even then they’re not half as convenient as my old iPhone XS battery case. Unofficial magnet batteries also aren’t Magsafe Sanctioned, so they charge at half speed.

So if you want to use Magsafe charging at home, and on the go, *and* have a Magsafe battery for backup, you’re looking at about $300 in extra costs on top of the price of an iPhone 12 or 13. Sure, you could use generics for a lot of this stuff, but only Magsafe Official Products will wirelessly charge your phone at a reasonable speed. (And there’s no other way to get those endorphins from having Official Apple Whiz-Bang Animations when snapping on their overpriced battery, of course.) Even at this premium, the experience pales in comparison to the convenience of what you may already own.

Every step of the way, Apple has designed the Magsafe standard for maximum profit and minimum convenience to customers. And all of this is fixable! Bring back the battery case. Open up the Magsafe ecosystem. They could even let us ***switch out the cord*** on the puck. But no. Apple’s strategy is unbelievably disappointing, and bodes poorly for my personal future choice in phones. Go with a cheaper case, keep using your normal accessories. The seamless wireless future is a long way off.

title: Fire tablets aren't what they used to be....good quality and user friendly.
text:
Update: Actually, I already wrote an update about 10 days ago. Amazon has not approved it. It was a bad review of the product and the product service. I live out of the country and they said they wanted to help but....they wouldn't even call or message me. My Fire barely works. They said they'd give me 15% off a new one. NO THANKS! The quality just keeps getting worse. It's screwing with me right now so I'm signing off. Just don't expect too much from this product or Amazon.

Previous review

Ah, the good old days. When I got my first Kindle in 2014? I was very pleased with how user friendly it was. If I put my music on it - there it was under Music. If I put my books on it - yup, they were right there under Books. Now, Amazon seems so afraid that you're not going to buy everything from them that they make it super hard just to find what you've put on much less read it or listen to it. And now, when I recently had to purchase a new one, the storage size has shrunken even more... 16gb... I don't think so. Nope it's 10.52gb that you end up with. I guess if I could actually use all the extra crap that they loaded it down with, that would be one thing - but, I can't because I live out in the sticks and Alexa is nowhere to be seen.

I just can't see why, other than greed, that they'd take a user friendly, reliable product and turn it into...... this. My screen is constantly glitchy, the light goes in and out, it has trouble finding my place in my books, hell the volume isn't even as loud as it was on my old one. Yes, the price is reasonable, but; I'd rather pay a buck or two more and have the quality back. I gave my original Fire to my husband to use and it still works perfectly (with no updates).

Updating to let you all know how this was handled.
Amazon contacted me to see if they could help. I gave them my number. I live in Mexico. After a couple of emails they still could not, apparently, figure out how to call Mexico. Amazon. Really? Then they said it wasn't under warranty. Yes, I knew that. I asked if we could live chat or messenger. They did not respond. They just told me to go through the "contact us". Nothing. title: Keyboard Awesome?  NO IT SUCKS!
text:
OK, overall I'm very happy with my new laptop. Instead of going with the 128GB SSD variation I added my own Samsung 850 EVO - 500GB - M.2 SATA III Internal SSD (MZ-N5E500BW) (insert link here...the review stripped it out even though I also git it on Amazon)
...and I'm glad I did because for the money I got 4x the SSD size and I feel Win10 has plenty of room to breathe.

The one thing that I think is atrocious and really lets it down is the keyboard. THe touch and feel are just fine. It's very decent quality, keystroke action etc. However unless you look very closely you may not notice that ASUS doesn't have a dedicated POWER button on this laptop, so some ABSOLUTE NITWIT decided to steal the [END] key you normally have on your 101 key keyboard and use that for a laptop power button.

As a result, this keyboard has no END key. Perhaps you out there do not use that particular key. If so, then read not further. However, I use it a LOT (I used to). I also use my numeric keypad a lot, so while I can convert my numberic keypad over into edit mode to provide me with an alternate arrows and home and end (along with page up/dn), than I can't use it for numbers.

The other thing it means, is you must be careful not to let your finger stray to the top/right of the keyboard without being careful because if you brush that PWR key, you have just initiated SHUTDOWN right in the middle of answering your email etc.

SO, whoever the clever idiot is that decided to scrap that [END] key and replace it with a Power function...thanks and no thanks and next time, if you are so proud of your clever engineering why don't you point it out in your advertisement, marketing guides and specifications so your buyers have a chance to go on with eyes wide open.

Another thing this keyboard lets you down is that it is not illuminated during power up so that if you are running the computer in the dark you can't use the back light to enter your Windows Password because it will not come on until after you login. Another FAIL.

OH, and two more fails regarding keyboard. You can not tell when the CAPLOCK, NUMLOCK and SCROLL LOCK are engaged. There is no apparent status lamp, and the computer also does not give you a audible BEEP when you hit these keys like so many other brands do. rEALLY? wE DON'T HAVE A CAPSLOCK STATUS? OOPS, SORRY FOR THE ALL CAPS, i HIT MY cAPSlOCK KEY AND DIDN'T NOTICE UNTIL NOW.

Finally, the front leading edge of the laptop is quite harsh. If you spend much time typing, you will find a significantly painful line across both of your wrists where the laptop edge is digging into your forearm while you rest your arms on the surface.

Considering how eye catching this keyboard is, and how proud of the red backlight ASUS seems to be, they have two very glaring fails in this keyboard as far as I'm concerned. Also this is a huge laptop at 17", there is no need to squeeze in these keys into a tiny space, spread them out and don't remove keys that some people might miss.

One last time, yes, I love the laptop. I love how easy it is to open up and upgrade the disk/ram/SSD. Price/Performance/Value it blows away the competition in my opinion. It's very fast especially once I got the system disk over to a SSD...wow, talk about fast bootup times! However, the keyboard is just a huge disappointment and since it's one of the two primary input devices you will be touching the entire time you are using the computer it really deserves more attention from the designers. All the reviews I read go on about the red backlight, I don't remember any of them warning me the [END] key was missing. Oh, they all go on about fingerprints....who cares about fingerprints? functionality misses are more important to mention...Pfft.

title: AWESOME sturdy tripod/monopod!  I use with DSLR, camcorder, Zoom audio recorder and video projector!
text:
I am an amateur photographer/videographer/recording engineering (what can I say, I have a lot of hobbies) and the first tripod I ever bought was a cheap Amazon basics one. What I liked about it were the price and how lightweight it is. Beyond that, however, you definitely get what you pay for. A strong breeze will blow it over, it is rather short and not very heavy duty.

After shooting a dinner dance event recently, I found myself wishing I had a taller, sturdier tripod with the monopod option that I could carry around. This tripod seemed to have everything I was looking for and indeed I am VERY happy with it so far! I have now used it with my Canon DSLR, my Sony Vixia video camera, my AAXA P4 Pico projector and my Zoom H4N digital audio recorder and it has been awesome! Really my only complaint so far is that it's about 2 and a half pounds heavier than my cheaper and smaller tripod, but it isn't fair to compare the two because the cheap one is a 50", doesn't have the monopod and is...well, cheap. I included one side by side comparison photo for reference. I looked at other 70" tripod/monopod combos and they all weigh about the same, so this isn't something I will dock stars for. I weighed the tripod on my kitchen scale (which I know is very accurate) and it put this tripod at 3.84 pounds even though it's advertised to weigh 3.63. Not a huge discrepancy, but still, when you're hauling around a bunch of gear, especially traveling with it, every ounce counts. The monopod by itself only weighs a pound which is awesome! I found the height specs to be as advertised (70" fully extended). Just for your info, the monopod fully extended is about 64" and the whole thing folded up is 2ft long.

This tripod really couldn't be easier to use. Sometimes equipment like this requires a PhD to operate but I didn't even have to look at the instructions to figure out how to liberate and extend the monopod and put it back (which only takes seconds)! It comes with a nice travel case that has a little room to spare for cables or other gear which is nice. I also love that this tripod has a hook underneath. I use it to hold my camera case for easy access to my lenses, batteries, SD cards etc. The tripod itself also comes with a very nice, sturdy handle built it for ease in carrying it around without the case which I appreciate. Best of all, this tripod is SO STURDY!!! It feels very durable and well made with quality materials, unlike the cheap little Amazon Basics one. For the price I feel like I got a really good value in this tripod. It does everything I want it to do quickly, easily and is very strong and reliable! What more could you ask for?

I can highly recommend this tripod for amateur and professional photographers and videographers alike! As I mentioned I have also used it successfully with my Zoom recorder and projector as well, but this tripod is probably overkill for those if that's all you need it for. Hope this helps!

title: I've dropped hundreds in buying the base station and a flex and I can tell you that I am extremely disappointed at the what that I got for it
text:
I do not suggest buying any Canary device based on the cost and quality of the product when compared to other equivalent products, the fact that IT WILL NOT DETER THEFT, but most importantly due to the fact that they want to deceive and price gouge you!

I've dropped hundreds in buying the base station and a flex and I can tell you that I am extremely disappointed at the what that I got for it. I could have spent much less money and got a system that does Much more. And now they are forcing me to pay $150 to purchase the things they advertised on the box or be left with 10 sec video recorders. In short for the hundreds of dollars you will need to spend to make this thing work I could have got a full fledged security system from ADT or other security service.

Don't assume this will be a DIY security system where you get videos of people robbing you, then you turn on an alarm and then they get scared and stop robbing you. The delay in the functionality of the system is ridiculous. I bought the flex to keep watch of boxes from UPS. First the I couldn't get the flex to work because the wifi range is so crappy there was nowhere outside the house that got connection. I finally found a spot where it worked near a window, because apparently it will not communicate through stucco walls very good. But once it was set up to my shugrin I found out that the delay was so bad the camera would not even see the UPS man dropping off the box. A video of a box just appearing would happen or no video at all. So how is it supposed to catch a thief?

Look yes they did the bait and switch on the features and subscription, but the real problem here is that the damn thing don't do anything. The siren sucks, the wifi sucks, and the delay sucks. All that equals UNRELIABLE.

Pros
-Looks nice

Cons
- wifi antenna range is limited.
-Only 10 sec videos (unless you pay $15/month)
-No 2 way talk as advertised (unless you pay $15/month)
10 sec delay of video starting to record. This is a deal breaker for me. Note this includes the base station too.
-No recording video or detect motion while your at home (unless you pay $15/month). Note:. You can set your device to Away mode while your at home to make it work, but that is tedious and frustrating.

The lesson I have learned after buying the base station and flex:
-Canary is not a security device, it is a webcam. It will not prevent a break in and it will not give you enough time to react to any break in.
- if you don't want to pay the $15/month (like me) you will get a over priced webcam that only takes 10 sec videos that are delayed 10 seconds.

Learn from my mistakes and get a real security system. In the long run you will probably pay less than this paperweight.

title: Sturdy construction makes the Acer Spin 11 a great value
text:
To start with a caveat: I do not personally consider ANY Chromebook to be a viable "desktop replacement." I acknowledge that plenty of grown adults *do* work full-time in Chrome OS, which I admire, but I think those dedicated few are probably willing to shell out a lot more on a Chromebook than I am. To ME, however, the idea of spending $500+ on a cloud-based netbook is audacious to the point of silliness.

I've waffled a lot between preferring either the Chromebook or the iPad Mini for travel. But I'd be really upset if I ever lost my iPad... whereas a lost or stolen Chromebook is pretty survivable. I'd hate to lose one, but I'd feel that my data is safe. I know losing a ~us$400 device is still major, but it just wouldn't carry the same life-and-death meaning, y'know?

Anyway. This review is long, so let me begin with its salient takeaways:

Pros:
- The build quality cannot be beat. Sturdy construction makes this Chromebook a great value.
- Decent performance for the size and expense.
- Terrific keyboard, very comfortable for long-stint typing (although I did put a silicon cover on mine, and I do feel that this has made a difference)
- "Handsomely benign"
- Not an ASUS
- Free stylus
- It's a Chromebook!

Cons:
- Bulky and rather heavy, not at all a tablet replacement (although tent mode does work well)
- Grainy screen and tinny speakers will be a dealbreaker for some.
- Lower battery life than Acer claims -- 8 hours or fewer, I'd say. Not bad, not exemplary either
- The mousepad is... functional, but not good.
- It's a Chromebook.

When I first started looking for a new "portable machine," I knew I wanted a small computer to serve as a reasonably-priced "go-between" (I switch a lot between a Mac and a PC for work, and I also travel a fair amount).

I quickly realized that "performance" was, weirdly, not going to be the highest criterion on my priority list -- if it were, I'd just bring my MacBook Pro with me to Europe, right?

What I wanted was something small. Secure. And rugged! A TANK! And with a Gorilla Glass screen, ideally! If a small, inexpensive computer IS meant to be tossed into a backpack, it should be sturdy and tough! A lot of tech reviewers praise other Chromebooks' superficial resemblances to MacBooks, which I personally find baffling. Aluminum unibodies are prone to dents and scuffs!

I realized I was probably going to be looking seriously at, not an "adult" Chromebook, but a Chromebook designed for kids and students.

And the Acer Chromebook Spin 11 IS, in fact, intended for kids. But please don't be deterred if you're older -- there is nothing childish about wanting a laptop that won't break in your luggage.

It's called "Spin" because it's a four-position convertible laptop. I actually really enjoyed my last ultrabook, the Lenovo Yoga 2 Pro, only because I could leave my laptop in either "stand mode" or "tent mode" and use my own mechanical keyboard. The exact same is true of the Acer Spin: I can set up a cozy little workspace in a hotel with my external bluetooth Filco keyboard. Ahh, so homey.

Except... I *like* this thing's keyboard? Elsewhere I've seen it called "mushy"; *I* would say that it just isn't as weird and clicky and "chicklet" as some contemporary keyboards. Even though the machine is a petite 11" or so, the keyboard is very comfortably sized, not noticeably cramped at all. I've been typing on my Acer Spin for six hours now -- really!! -- and although I wouldn't go so far as to call the keyboard a "pleasure to use," it's certainly more than acceptable according to my high standards. I WILL say, however, I slightly prefer typing with a silicon keyboard cover on top. (The Spin's keys' "travel distance" is actually very short and shallow, so maybe I like using a silicon cover because it gives the illusion of a longer travel distance.)

The touch mousepad is... not great. It's almost bad. Two-finger "right-clicking" is kind of a chore. It isn't quite as bad as the mousepad on my Predator gaming laptop, though, which is also made by Acer. (Who is designing these terrible touchpads? Is it just one guy??)

For that matter, the Acer Spin 11 won't win any audio/visual awards. The screen is dimmer and lower-res than you might hope, and sound is tinny and pretty quiet. It isn't a very exciting machine. It struggles to run certain sideloaded game ROMs, for instance.

And the entire machine is plasticky. For its size, it's heavy and pretty beefy. It's too thick to really use as a tablet (although I HAVE used it to read an eBook in portrait mode). A lot of people won't like the design overall.

I personally think that, aesthetically, it's appealingly sporty, like a running shoe. It reminds me of "survivalism" -- you know, army knives and "tactical" breath mints and all that. You could definitely take this laptop and go camp in a yurt.

It's still just a Chromebook, though, so the associated perks and limitations apply. Chrome power-users know that they can also install and run Linux, access Windows and Mac machines remotely, et al. (I consider Chromebooks' reliance on cloud-based storage a huge negative, but Android support has changed this somewhat.)

Thanks to Google Play support, the Acer Spin 11 does run Android apps. I regularly leave the Android versions of BlueMail, Telegram, 1password, and iA Writer all open and running simultaneously. (I'm writing this in iA Writer right now! Through Dropbox, it synchronizes my drafts with my PC, MacBook, and iOS devices.)

But what really makes Chromebooks great is the fact that, ultimately, they offer a stripped-down work environment, free from distraction. The fewer apps and tabs you leave open, the better the machine functions, which in turn imbues a certain monastic "practical minimalism" in the user. Generally Chromebooks are snappy... but a Chromebook ill-used will be sluggish instead.

The Acer Spin 11 definitely zips along far better than Chromebooks that come at a lower price point, which are the Chromebooks I have previously used. I can enthusiastically confirm that this particular model of the Acer Spin can simultaneously run four other Android apps and a handful of "live" browser tabs -- in addition to Netflix Android simultaneously playing an episode of the Joel McHale Show -- without running into any hangs or lags.

I encountered performance difficulties only when I briefly disabled a Chrome browser extension called uBlock Origin. The ads on the website I was visiting slowed my machine to a halt, and I finally had to reboot my machine (for the first time in two months!). I also use a plugin called "The Great Suspender," which "sleeps" on open browser tabs that haven't been looked-at in a while. Both add-ons have drastically improved performance in a machine that might otherwise fall short.

At this price point the available eleven-inch Chromebooks are slim pickins, unfortunately. You've got Acer, you've got Dell, you've got the more-expensive Samsung. The top-rated frontrunner, if you read a lot of tech reviews, is definitely one of the 11.6" ASUS machines.

I've had two ASUS computers previously -- a netbook and a Chromebook -- and both fell apart. It was like plate tectonics, where the different planes of the chassis slowly shifted out of place. After a couple years with the netbook, it got to a point where, if I were typing and I paused to rest my right palm on the space for palms, the machine would suddenly shut off, losing whatever I was working on.

Still, the ASUS Flip is probably the top-rated Chromebook in this price point, so I remained open to it. But when I read user reviews suggesting the build quality was not great... ugh, call it confirmation bias, but it sounded like a familiar tune. So I wrote the ASUS off and kept searching.

The Acer Spin 11 is definitely a polarizing machine. I've noticed that professional tech reviewers give it glowing, middling, AND low reviews, depending on what they're looking for.

Ultimately it all comes down to how you intend to use the machine. It isn't a desktop replacement -- I've read that the Acer Spin 11 can huff and puff during certain benchmark tests -- and it's too large and cumbersome to function as a true tablet replacement.

But I think it's a great... Chromebook.

Philosophically I think a practical Chromebook should never be stunningly beautiful, or able to run everything you throw at it, or even necessarily sound great or whatever. Sure, there are Chromebooks that can outperform this one, and there are Chromebooks that look like "grown-up" machines, with backlit keyboards and aluminum unibodies and all that. This machine, in comparison, isn't glamorous.

But I can't help but feel that, in this category, no Chromebook will ever really measure up. You have to manage your expectations instead.

Although it would be impossible to ever mistake it for a Google Pixel computer, the stalwart Acer Spin 11 is a handsomely benign device, and a wonderful little work machine. I would wholeheartedly recommend it to "road warriors" as a secondary laptop, to students who require a go-anywhere note-taking essay-writing machine, and to kiddos whose parents want them to have a safe, secure "grown-up" computer that can also stand up to some roughhousing.

title: Great radio in a small package.
text:
This is a very nice CB in a small package. It installed under the dash and did not get in the way. Do not be misled by the compact size and low price. The final output power of the Uniden Pro520xl is four watts, the maximum allowed by the FCC for CB radios. All CB radios are rated at a maximum four watts, including the larger more expensive models. With the larger more expensive radios you only get more features, such as analog meters and fancy lights that you cannot see while driving anyway. The trade off is that the larger radios are much more difficult to install in late model cars, SUVs and trucks.
The pro 520xl features subdued modern styling and does not look like a left over from the 1970s. The controls are conviently located and easy to use while driving. A draw back, however, was the short microphone cord that took some getting used to. If you buy this or any other CB radio, do not use a "cel-phone" style glass mounted antenna. The glue on antennas look good but are very poor performers without exception. If you must use a glass mounted antenna, do not key up the microphone. The high SWR and electrical inefficiency may very well damage your new radio.
The Uniden Pro520xl, hooked up to a properly installed three foot Firestick II antenna had a 1.5:1 SWR on channels 1, 20 and 40 right out of the box. If you want to find out just how useful a CB radio can be on vacation or during the morning commute, purchase the Pro520xl.
