title: Outstanding binoculars!
text:
I purchased these for use on an Alaskan cruise where the weather is notoriously damp (rain, fog), so being waterproof was a must. I considered the Bushnell H2O for about $40 cheaper, but since I was extremely happy with my small 10x25 Nikon binoculars I decided to spring for these. Boy am I glad I did. First, be aware that these are fairly heavy, especially if you are used to the more compact models. They seem to be at least twice as heavy as the three sets of compact binoculars I have, including Nikon, Pentax and Alpen. Part of this is certainly because of the much larger objective lens and rubberized shell needed for waterproofing, but the Action EX Extreme's use a completely metal internal structure that also adds weight (but makes them much more durable). The binoculars come with a very nice, wide neck strap, individual cups for the objective lenses, and a double cup for the eye pieces. Each of these parts also has a slot on the side so you can hang them from your strap when not in use. Nice touch. The case is also large and sturdy, unlike the canvas-like case you often get with cheaper binoculars (like the Alpens I have)

Now to performance. I'm fairly certain these binoculars use porro prisms and not roof prisms as stated in the description. You can generally tell by the offset of the eyepiece and the objective lens. The eye relief on these binoculars is more than adequate, and while I had a larger field of view without my glasses, they worked perfectly fine with them. The binoculars were extremely easy to focus, and with the 40mm objective lens let in lots of light and provide a greater than 400ft field of view at 1000m. Everything fit snugly and workmanship on the product appears to be very high. The eye cups all fit well, and there is very low risk of them just falling off. The focus wheel is firm but moves smoothly. Just perfect in my mind. I absolutely would not hesitate to buy these again or recommend them to anyone. Right now I have 4 sets of "good" binoculars and several cheap ones that I wouldn't mind being dropped overboard (decent for a 10yo though). Unless I'm traveling super light/small, these are going to be my "go to" binoculars. I like them that much.

title: Survived Hiking in Alaska - Love it!
text:
I love this camera case. L-O-V-E it! I just returned from trips to Alaska and Canada and it performed beautifully. I knew I was going to be hiking in rugged terrain and sightseeing in an elegant city and wanted a camera case that was appropriate for both environments without being bulky. This case was perfect and I received several compliments.

I read conflicting reviews on whether you could use the camera with the case attached, and in my experience you absolutely can. I simply unsnapped the button on the bottom right of the camera, flipped the back panel and molded front forward, then spun the case on the still-snapped (bottom left) button in order to get the case out of the way for shots. Easy-peasy. Then I could quickly spin/refit/snap it when I continued my hike. There were a few occasions where I wasn't as concerned with the safety of the camera and I just left the case stashed in my shoulder bag, but the unsnapping method was quick and easy and not an aggravation; I just made sure I practiced several times before the trip so I got the mechanics of it down pat. The hard molded leather made the camera feel really secure.

Highly recommend this case! I got the light brown color.

title: Great Purchase!
text:
I'm very happy with my Google Pixel 7 256gb purchase. I have had it now for about 3 months and I couldn't be more content with my purchase. I was dead set on getting the Iphone 14 but decided last minute to get the Pixel 7 because it was more economical and still had the features I was looking for. Not to mention the fact that in getting the Pixel, I was able to then use the other money I had set aside to get a GoPro Hero 11 creator addition, more accessories, and cases for both my phone and GoPro for the price I would have paid for the iphone and an otterbox alone.

The interface is easy to use, and I like the android platform more than I thought I would. My previous phone was an Iphone and I was worried that I would loose the easy to use platform that I had become accustomed to.

The cons - The fingerprint reader at times doesn't recognize my fingerprint. I mostly attribute this to the fact that I work in a restaurant and after touching hot things for an extended period of time, my belief is that my fingerprint is just damaged enough to where the device has a harder time reading it, and the technology itself for reading fingerprints is a little outdated. The other thing I have noticed is that when I go from being on wifi to out and about, some times my device has a hard time connecting to my 5g smoothly which will make my IG or Pandora not want to work. When I have this issue, a quick restart seems to do the trick.

With the cons in mind, I still think that the google phone is an excellent option and I am very glad I purchased it. I likely will stick with google phones in the future unless something else catches my eye enough to make me want to switch.

title: Great Rig With Impressive Quality for the Price!

I was able to put the rig together easily and I like how customizable the parts are. The shoulder rest is fairly comfortable, though I would recommend a counter weight. The handles also feel very secure, and don't move around. Another plus for me is the tripod mount on the bottom, it's nice being able to put the whole rig on a tripod, and it saves me a lot of time not having to take the camera off the rig.

Edit 2.23.2016
One issue I did have was with a DSLR that I mounted. There is no way to move the camera left or right on the rig independent of the light box (only forward and back), this is not a problem for cameras like the BMCC with the lens in the center, but for my DSLR (Nikon D5200), the lens is not centered, and the light box was unusable. The follow focus still worked the same though. I am keeping the rating at 4 stars, because it does not really effect how I use the rig that much.

title: Great camera for the price
text: I really, really like this camera.  For the majority of the pictures I take, birds and other wildlife, it is a big improvement over my Canon XTi.  It has greater reach over my XTi with a 70-300 lens plus a 1.4x teleconverter.  I am also enjoying playing with some of the in-camera filters.  I used some of them recently when shooting fall foliage and many beautiful sunsets, and got some great results.  I also appreciate the fact that Canon resisted the urge to cram more pixels into a camera with such a small sensor, although they did put more on the SX60, which is why I bought a used SX50 instead.  So, despite all of the great things about this camera, it isn't perfect.  I am forEVER hitting the camera self-timer and menu buttons by accident.  The self-timer thing is an easy enough fix, but I have accidentally changed some settings more than a few times, and that's a little harder to fix.  Also, the manual focus option seems to be very, very limited.  The auto-focus searches and searches in low light situations, and I haven't had much luck trying to use the manual focus.  There is also a lot of noise with pictures taken in low light.  If Canon makes an SX70, I really hope they can nudge the aperture down to 2.8 or 3.1, while leaving the megapixels alone.  I know that it would make the camera heavier, but it would still be much lighter than a DSLR, and would be worth the trade-off, in my opinion.  In a dream world, a larger sensor, without a drastic increase in cost and weight would be awesome too, as it would no doubt lessen the noise in some pictures.  All, in all, I would recommend this camera to anyone who needs some reach, but can't afford a DSLR with a very long telephoto lens.  I included a few photos, just to give an idea of what this camera can do.

I have only owned a few scanners and this is my first digital trunking scanner but so far I am very happy. Quick summary:

Final point...more and more agencies are going full encrypted. Just factor that in before you spend $650 here. I knew what I was getting into and ended up receiving more public safety traffic than I expected. I know that will decrease over time.

title: Solid sound and wireless connectivity; responsive tech support
text:
Giving a tentative four stars to the Enclave! May bump to 5 if my interactions with their tech support turn into action items.

Pros:
1. The wireless speaker connectivity was instant and perfect, and has not failed once yet
2. No noticeable latency, despite the wireless connection method
3. Sound is nice and clear
4. Really easy to set up, pretty much plug-n-play
5. Mobile app works okay (and is better than the remote for controlling the system)
6. Good experiences with tech support so far

Cons:
1. Wish it connected via Wifi & had a web-control interface/API and not Bluetooth connection for remote control (as an AV automation engineer, I like IP control, because I can program for that!)
2. Remote is a little on the cheap side, but it gets the job done -- the app is better in every way (except using Bluetooth to connect)
3. Some minor hiccups, mostly caused by my (Sony Bravia) TV
4. Wish the DC power supplies fit more nicely into a power strip, they're just a lil bit bulky

Tips:
1. When switching to Aux/ARC and using TV to control volume, it typically defaults to muted -- raise the volume up by one or two notches to get it started, and then adjust up/down as needed
2. On a Sony Bravia TV, ARC shuts off when you switch to the HDMI/ARC input, so just make sure to not be on it when you want to Chromecast or use other TV apps (if you want to turn ARC back on, you have to switch to another input on the Enclave and then switch back to Aux/ARC). If you have a smart TV and use the apps, use the ARC input for controlling the Enclave only (as recommended in the quick-start guide they provide) and plug everything else into your TV's inputs

title: More than decent for techno!
text:
Very good headphones, lots of fun, lots of bass on a budget.

So I bought the refurbished ones for $100 shipped, they look just like new, one of the ear pads was crooked but I had to slowly twist it.

People most likely break these headphones because they don't handle them with care. They're fairly big and not built very tough, so when you grab them off your had you have to be careful and use both your hands. You can't yank them around and expect the plastic to hold up, they aren't $400 DJ headphones.

Pros:
-Excellent wireless execution by SONY, definitely have never been disappointed by this company in my life
-Good sound, Sony has never done me wrong. Not too rich but very clear, could use better highs and more spacious mids, idk how to put it but there isn't a lot of depth in the sound
-Sound awesome with bass boost off
-Sound awesome with bass boost on but you will sacrifice mids and highs, the bass boost isn't anything out of this world, for a less experienced listener they are "WHOA THESE ARE SICK" type material
--I let all my friends try them vs the MDR1000x (which are very good noise cancelling and sound amazing btw) and they all loved em, these headphones offer that wow factor with the bass for not that much money
-Very comfortable
-Noise isolating
-Aesthetically pleasing
-Work with my bluetooth usb dongle on my PC, so easy to pair and the play/seek buttons work well

Cons:
-Can't use while charging
-MUST USE PROVIDED AUDIO CABLE if you want to do wired, otherwise they don't work
-I hear bad things about its capabilities as a headset, again these are headphones for music, if you want a wireless headset probably look elsewhere or answer your phone like a normal person
-Certain lack of clarity with bass boost on, easy to pick up if you've owned better headphones, but for the price these are amazing.

The headphones are enjoyable, I bought the extended warranty in case they snap like I see the other reviews, but I'm just pretty sure people don't understand the full scope of how to handle things, maybe they don't understand how manufacturing works and how hard it is to take all aspects into account and give you an indestructible and good sounding and long battery and this and that all in one package, engineering is pretty tough. Handle these precious electronic devices with care people, they're not bulletproof. They're pretty much magic wrapped in plastic, take it easy when you move them on, off, and around your head. Everything breaks if you handle it like a 5 year old child.

Overall very happy with my purcahse and I would recommend these to anyone who listens to electronic music. I listen to techno, some may know how bass heavy this music actually is, and these sound amazing.

When you buy them listen to the following song to test out what they can really do: Astral- Tale of Us

Enjoy!

title: Great speaker for the modern world;  they prefer better than casual amp...
text:
I struggled with my decision to keep these and retire my huge Boston Acoustics A150’s, but I think I will end up keeping both. I had the B6’s but returned them because they were too directional in their highs, and plainly sounded to me like the small speakers they were. These are different in all the right ways. Moving the tweeters more to the front and putting the port on the front were great changes, and the upgraded connectors are a plus as well. They have an airy quality that the B6’s lacked, IMO. I have 100 and 125 wpc amps and neither one has trouble driving these to a satisfactory volume. These speakers sound great at low volumes as well. They don’t require a subwoofer for most music but it helps to have one to really get those below 40hz lows out there. I might’ve been tempted to get the Ufi’s if not for countless reviews advising 200+ wpc amps. These do need a break-in period so the more you play them, the better they sound.
Update 07/05/2018:
I returned these not because they were unsatisfactory, but I got a good deal on the Uni-Fi UB5's and wanted to try an "upgrade", as is were, and also they were not sounding noticeably better than my Boston Acoustics A150's from way back when (much bigger speaker, better efficiency, 10 inch woofer). With both the 2.0 B6's and the UB5's I notice a lack of comparable bass between the two amps I have, and I've not seen any hard-and-fast rule about what an amp needs to run these properly and what won't, except for general agreement that you need more than the casual wattage rating and the ability to drive 4 ohms, guessing that if you can't get/find an answer about how your amp drives 4 ohms, then it's not going to be adequate, because that's a selling point that companies will promote if they can. I'm not going to spend $2000+ for another amp, not happening. So far (still breaking in the UB5's), my general impression is, if you're not hearing amazing, surprising bass out of these speakers with your current amp, the amp's the problem, not the speakers. If either of these were my only speaker, I wouldn't be dissatisfied with either because they both sound good with my amps, but the ability to compare is what keeps me from going "WOW"

title: Great case.  Using it for pfSense.  Airflow could be improved.
text:
Pros:
- It is tiny! It is about as small as is possible with the component compatibility it has.
- It is rugged. For the $55 I paid for this I was expecting it to feel more like other cheap stamped cases I’ve used. However, this thing has a military-grade feel, especially the front panel.
- The top of the case lifts off to add/remove components. It comes with 3 screws: 2 philips heads and 1 thumb screw. The way this panel slots in makes the philips screws optional, so it allows you to decide if you want something tool-less or more tamper-proof.
- Uses a proper server power supply form factor (very hard to find in non-rack mount cases)
- Space for an expansion card (very hard to find in this size case)
- Available mounting accessories. You can buy wall-mount of vesa mounting parts for about $10 which allow this case to be put almost anywhere.

Cons
- Airflow. The front 80mm fan in the front has a very restricted inlet, the design of the front panel blocks most of the available air. This would be an easy design change, and I find the decision to obstruct the only usable intake to be very confusing.
- Airflow again. The side 60mm fan conflicts with the PCIe slot. The product page says you could put a thin (10mm) fan here but even that would block the PCIe slot. If you’re not using the PCIe slot then you could easily fit a standard thickness fan.
- Cooler height. My build uses an Intel Pentium G4560 which comes with the smallest intel stock cooler. Even that cooler was about 5mm too tall and would conflict with an expansion card. I ended up using a Noctua NH-L9i which is just 37mm tall and you really couldn’t go any taller with an expansion card installed.
- Drive Mount. In my build I decided to use an m.2 drive, which I’m very glad I did since the drive mount on the top panel interferes with the front 80mm fan. This means that if you want to mount a 2.5” hdd/ssd you can’t mount a front fan, which makes the case useless. Also since, there are no ventilation holes on the underside of the case, I wouldn’t want an itx motherboard with an rear m.2 slot (as many do) and would only pair this case with an itx board with a top m.2 slot.
- Doesn’t come with rubber feet, which are required to not damage any surface you set it onto.
- You will need a PCIe riser cable (not included) in order to use the expansion slot.

What would make it 5 stars:
All it would take to make this 5 stars would be to put 2x 80mm fan mounts on the front of the case with a more open inlet (bonus if there was a filter), add more ventilation holes on the back, and move the top drive mount 10mm further back. Those are all tiny changes, but would make this case infinitely better.

I’ve still given it four stars because it is so nicely built and because there are no other cases that really compete with this one.

title: Great mount with some caveats...
text:
I purchased this monitor mount to hold 3 identical Dell 27" (U2719) monitors. Setup instructions were very clear, and written with a little humor to make the reading a little more enjoyable. The mount is very solid with these Dell monitors, which are fairly light at 14lbs each. Overall I'm happy with the mount, but there are a few caveats to know about before you buy...
#1: Monitor height is very difficult to adjust once the monitors are mounted.
The curved horizontal beam mounts to the vertical tube via a pipe clamp, so any vertical adjustment with monitors mounted would require access behind the monitors and 3 people (one on each end and one to loosen/tighten the clamp). You'll need to get the vertical height set correctly before mounting the monitors, so better make sure you test fit. I used the basic monitor stand that came with the monitors to set the height on the desk, then I measured the height at the top of the VESA mount and used this measurement to set the height of the curved horizontal beam. If you ever plan on rotating displays 90 degrees, make sure you give enough room for this!

#2: There is no fine adjustment to get all the monitors aligned vertically with each other.
When I first set this up, I was getting about 1/4" offset in the leftmost monitor as compared to the other two. I swapped left and right monitors to see if the issue was the monitor or the mount, the offset remained so the issue is with the mount. After a lot of loosening & retightening of the VESA mounts, as well as the pipe clamp mount, as well as using a laser level to check heights as I made tweaks, I got the left & right monitors aligned, with the center monitor a little higher (see pictures). I found most of the issue was with the slop in the pipe clamp mount to the vertical tube. If you plan to use this mount for gaming, and you need all 3 monitors aligned with zero offset, this isn't the mount for you. If you can live with a little offset between monitors, then this will do the job. Ideally, given typical manufacturing tolerances as well as the large tolerances with the pipe clamp mount, there should be some way of fine vertical adjustment at each monitor. Ideally, redesign the mount to get rid of the pipe clamp mount and use a slide compression sleeve to lock the perpendicularity between the curved horizontal beam and the vertical tube.

All that said, setting spacing between monitors and tilt/rotation of each monitor is a tool-free breeze with the knobs (see pictures). Just make sure you can live with the caveats!

title: GREAT lil' turntable for aspiring vinyl collectors & music lovers on a budget!!
text:
I purchased this turntable because it seemed to have pretty favorable reviews&since im on a pretty tight budget&wanted to "upgrade"a bit from my Ion duodeck I had been using for years as my vinyl collection rapidly continued to grow&I began to truly enjoy the"vinyl experience",ive been embracing since a child,yet didnt have nearly the budget some of these "holier than thou""audiophiles"that review on forums&sites like this seem to have...

I received the turntable quickly but the 1st one I received gave off a strong electronic humming sound as soon as the motor started.Thanks to Amazons great return policy, I returned it and was PROMPTLY sent a replacement. The new one still had a slight hum through the speakers when set at a high volume once the motor started, but it seemed tolerable for the price. the sound is much better than my old ion duodeck that i loved for quite a bit so I was happy with that. It has very loud clean open sounds,BUT it does lack a bit of bass response,luckily I have powered speakers though with a bass enhancer which made it a little better. And also the tone adjustment knob tends to help with that aswell.

One thing I did notice though was it seems the needle/stylus wore out quite quickly,maybe from improper handling or the quality of it. I looked into replacements and most I found werent specifically for this turntable(buyer beware)so i was reluctant to purchase one from those buyers on ebay,etc but remembered another reviewer on here mentioned that Spectra(the actual manufacturer of this turntable)offers replacement needles for only 5 dollars! So I went ahead, called their customer service&ordered two and was quite delighted by the quick shipment of them. I replaced the needle(which can tend to be a bit difficult but just be patient&careful)and was surprised at the improvement of sound once I played a record again! It was now more crisp,open and clear, and Kate Bushs high pitched vocals sounded much more delightful and clear. So i would suggest saving money&time by ordering needle/stylus replacements directly from the manufacturer by calling the customer service# within the turntables manual for even more enjoyment. Also the tonearm did tend to skip a bit on some records but MOSTLY on very BASS driven(electronic/hiphop) albums which at times causes the needle to vibrate even more&due to this turntables inexpensive mostly plastic construction thats somewhat expectant. I simply taped a nickel to the far back top end of the cartridge&it played splendidly.

In closing I must say I did enjoy this turntable during the short time(nearly 2 months)I've owned it YET i MUST say.....only purchase this turntable if 1.you cant afford a better one but love listening to records(like me). 2.are just starting with vinyl&need something to test the waters before growing a pricey collection. 3.just like listening to a few records you own casually. Its a GREAT turntable for all those 3 reasons!!!
BUT if you CAN afford a better turntable I would HIGHLY suggest spending 50bucks more and purchasing a audio technica turntable! Or perhaps you'll be fortunate,like I recently was,and WIN a audio technica one at auction for under 50 bucks that actually works! Yes I acquired a (gently)used audio technica turntable and compared to this jensen(which will now become my backup turntable)...the sound and handling IS quite incredible. I was splendidly pleased. But if you arent quite as lucky to find one that works at a price you can afford i would go with this turntable until you can!! and DONT be deterred by those "audiophiles"out there who are able to spend upward to thousands of dollars on turntables&somehow expects everyone else to be able to aswell. Music is to be enjoyed&loved so enjoy it however you can on whatever budget you can ie:this turntable :)
so in summary...
PROS:
PRICE, decent sound quality,size,flexibility, Spectra/Jensen customer service needle replacement &its great for a starter or casual listening turntable until you can upgrade to better!

CONS:
noisy little motor,motor humming sound through speakers, low bass response

Happy vinyl listening people! :)

title: Cool, useful and stylish. Hardware leaves a lot to be desired...
text:
I've been using the Vivoactive HR everyday for about 8 months. Here are some pros and cons from my time with it so far:

Pros:
1. Very long battery life. The battery easily lasts two weeks without a charge despite constant use.
2. Heart rate is consistent. The heart rate monitor seems very consistent and the on-screen heart rate tracker comes in handy.
3. Screen continuously on and readable. The screen is always on and displays the time in considerably large numbers. The watch uses a color dot-matrix screen which means it can be read in any environment, including the bright sun. There is also a built-in backlight for reading the watch in the dark. The backlight comes on automatically when you tap the screen and stays on long enough for you to read the screen.
4. Interface easy to use. The interface is very easy to use since you can navigate from screen-to-screen with just the swipe of a finger. From the watch screen you can flip through different screen such as notifications, weather, heart rate, daily exercise, etc.
5. Stylish. The watch goes with almost any outfit you wear. It is sporty which is good for workouts and exercise, casual for everyday, and sleek for more formal environments like work.
6. Multitudes of different exercise routines. You can select just about any exercise routine and it will keep track of your workout consistently. Anything from indoor/outdoor walks to running to skiing to swimming.

Cons:
1. Phone sync is a bit slow. The watch can sync automatically to post your exercise information onto the Garmin Connect app you can install on your phone. Sometimes the sync will not go through and you have to sync manually, which can take a couple of minutes to refresh.
2. Arm imprint. The watch is a bit on the thicker side and the heart rate monitor protrudes slightly from the bottom of the watch. Therefore there is usually a sizable square imprint on your arm when you take the watch off.
3. GPS eats through battery. When you have the GPS turned on during workout mode, your battery life will significantly drop. The GPS easily uses quadruple the amount of battery as the watch uses when just idle.
4. Interface slow. The interface on the phone is easy to use and full of information, but the interface can be a bit slow and laggy, especially when flipping through the different screens. The non-multitouch touchscreen is not very precise and can sometimes take multiple attempts to tap and select something.
5. Stairs climbed flat out inaccurate. The steps and calories burned are very consistent. Unfortunately the sensor that monitors your flights of stairs climbed is completely inaccurate. I walk up exactly three flights of steps to get to my office every day yet the watch will post anywhere from zero to fifteen flights climbed on any given day. Any effort to improve the flights climbed reading simply defeats the purpose of the watch.

title: Great flash before it crapped out after 5 months.
text:
I've owned this flash for 5 months now. I owned multiple Yonguo flashes in the past (YN560, YN560-II). I decided to upgrade to the YN568EXII because I wanted the high speed synch and rear curtain synch features.

Likes:
- Highspeed Synch seemed to work very well. I used it often outdoors with my kids.
- The rear curtain synch also worked well and I was able to get some fun photos with the feature that I couldn't get with the more basic models (i.e. YN560-II or YN560)
- When the flash worked it was easy and great to use
- For the features it's an affordable flash

Dislikes:
- Well, in the last few weeks of operation my flash would randomly start making a grinding sound with the motor. I wouldn't be touching the flash or the camera and the motor would just start to move and then stop. After a few more days it started to move and not stop until I shut it down. One time the flash wouldn't even shutdown as the motor was grinding and I had to take out the batteries. I just noticed today that now the flash won't zoom. So I can't move the flash out of the 24mm setting. Fortunately that's the setting I use most. I'm really bummed that the flash broke after just 5 months of use.
- For $186 I expected the flash to last more than 5 months. Thus, the 2 star rating. If it gave me at least a year I'd probably give it 3-4 stars.

Notes:
- The only thing to note is that using high speed synch will drain batteries faster but that is an issue for all flashes. I got higher capacity rechargeable batteries just for this flash. If you don't need to use high speed synch I would recommend keeping it off.
- I primarily shoot all manual so I didn't use ETTL too much but the few times I did it seemed to do a decent job. I felt that sometimes I had to knock down the strength -1/3 or -2/3 stop. Sometimes my wife will want to take some pictures so I set the camera to auto and flash to ETTL mode.
- I used this with multiple Yongnuo RF-603c radio frequency remote triggers with no problems.

I hope this helps. Happy shooting.

Update 12/7/14 - I dropped the flash on the concrete from eye level because I didn't tighten the flash properly. Now the flash will occasionally zoom properly again, weird. It sometimes goes back to making the grinding noise when I bend the flash but it's not consistent. The rear-synch and high speed synch still seems to work though. I still use the flash but not if I need reliability because it doesn't trigger as reliably as my YN560-II.

title: Fact: The voltage is adjustable and 14.4 is no problem. NOISY FAN.
text:
I've only unpacked it and tested it under low loads, but here are some facts that no one seems to get straight. The voltage IS adjustable, the case is clearly marked with a trimpot at the left side of the power connections. Mine came set to 12.12V, and with a little patient tweaking, because the trimpot is not very fine, I was able to set it to the 14.40 that I want, which is "car alternator" full voltage. (By a calibrated voltmeter.) The trimpot wants a 5-pointed (star shaped) adjustment tool but a small screwdriver and patience will work it. It also goes well under 12 volts, I didn't check how far below 11 it would go.

Came with some signs it might be a return or repack, some plastic film caught under screws, some bangs and scrapes on the metal. But at this early date, it looks like it will do what it is supposed to and more. Now, If I only could find a simple metal enclosure for it, because even with the terminal cover, that leaves the AC input lines too close to being exposed.

UPDATE: 12.2017
I've been running a 10a 12(14)v load, and that's 120watts at full power. I'm running about half power, and the fan still kicks in frequently. Even at idle, with minimal power. Noisy fan. This might be good self protection, but it makes this an industrial supply, not suitable for use in attended areas, etc. No good for HOME computers, radios, kitchen or bedroom strip lights. Industrial.
The lack of a power switch or place to install one is also a problem, since you won't easily find one to add in a 3 wire supply cord.
Well, it was inexpensive. I'll find someplace else to use it.

After setup on my first time trying it, I caught Jupiter on the periphery of viewing, the moon, dead center, and Venus dead center. I found all of these in well under a minute aiming. Now my viewing time can exceed the time I spend aiming. I am very pleased with this purchase.

Let me pass along three observations.

(1) Celestron is CHEAP, CHEAP, CHEAP and not just because this is made in China with plastic parts. The unit requires screws, either two 8-32 x 1/4 or two 10-24 x 1/4. The instructions tell you so. ... but after spending $17.50, the screws were not included. Cheap.

(2) The instructions tell you to align at night by finding a bright star or planet. If I could do that, I would not need this add-on accessory. Duh. I did the alignment during the day aiming at a distant telephone pole. Of course, the pole could not be seen initially. By moving the scope up and down using fine adjustment, I found the telephone wires. Then moving left-right, I followed the wires until I was focused on the telephone pole. I then aligned on where a horizontal and vertical part of the telephone pole intersected.

(3) I had to drill mounting holes in the scope. If you find you need to do that, do the drilling such that shards from drilling do no fall towards the main mirror.

title: You get what you pay for.
text:
I got mine used on Amazon for $35 shipped. Maybe it was returned for being bad. You decide if you want to pay $60 new and see what percentage are good.

The 10mm eyepiece, which has a K on it supposedly for Kelner, looks to be a Huygen, with a 30° apparent field of view. Huygens are not terrible. At low power, they are more than wide enough to fit the moon, and find it in this case. Their resolution at their edges drops off much more than Kelner's and especially Plossl's.

The finder has a baffle right behind the objective, which reduces the aperture to 16mm. The finder's eyepiece seems to be a Huygen. Very narrow field of view. Edit: I discovered the lens cover unscrews off, and you can push the baffle back to halfway, where it should be, then screw it all back together. So that part is fixed now.

The focuser tube points to the side of the secondary but is loose enough you can wedge it to center by inserting a tooth pick. I think it is missing two slider pads. Folded paper might also do the trick. I think some clear tapes might have more friction than others.

The secondary mirror is not aimed at the center of the primary, so you do need to know how to adjust the 3 screws to get it aimed. I opened the tube to center dot the primary. I also have a cheshire collimation eyepiece with crosshairs. It was not too hard to adjust, though it ran out of range. Maybe the focuser being off is what made me think the secondary needed more adjustment.

The primary does not have adjustment screws per se, but you can losen the 3 attachment screws and wiggle it enough and then tighten them back down. f4 is not very forgiving on any misalignment.

The base is good. I may have got my money's worth just because of the base, which I can use in another scope. It is not tall enough to use without a table, unless little kids like to get down on the ground, which many do.

I focused on myself in the mirror from the other side of the room. The resolution is noticeably off. I can see more detail in my $30 7x monocular. The Cometron can focus even closer, so that is not the issue. The issue is I did not get the mirrors aligned enough, which has a big penalty at f4. I have to insert two focuser pads before I can align them better.

I really wish I could recommend you a better scope. I've looked through many, and you will encounter trade offs, such as cost and weight. More power means harder to aim. Many say the $110 Orion SkyScanner is much better. It is a 100mm aperture table dob, also f4, but maybe better aligned from the factory. Many cheap refractors have wobbly mounts. I doubt a 6 year old could easily more around my Celestron Powerseeker 114mm, which has great optics for only $70 shipped. I had to make a few modifications to it to have any real fun.

Many people recommend binoculars for newbies. They are inexpensive and small and let you learn the sky with a wide view. However, they do not zoom in on planets. In a light polluted city, you will prefer the magnification of a telescope for the moon. A mounted scope scan share views between people, whereas binoculars show different views to different people who don't know where it was aimed last.

For the low price, you get what you pay for.

title: Does it all, if you put in the time.
text:
I bought the DS411+ from Amazon a few weeks back and added 4 WD Caviar Black 1TB drives. The setup process is relatively easy, but it takes some time. The documentation is very good but it will be harder for someone who is not technically savvy.

Pros -
- Great transfer speeds
- Feature rich - You can host your own websites, email server, photo server, music server, media streamer and much more. These features are more common with a server than a NAS, hence why this system costs more than the basic NAS units.
- Quiet operation
- Great documentation
- Streaming 1080P video, audio, and photos to my PS3 is simple and the quality is amazing.
- iPhone apps work very well, even remotely.

Cons -
- The only problem I had was related to my complex home network. This Synology machine should be on the same subnetwork as your main router and streaming destinations.(ie. - if you have two+ routers in your system) If not then it makes it impossible to stream content.

This machine is solid and I'm thrilled with the features as well as the data security and access I now have.

title: Kindle break-down and replacement
text:
From the moment my Kindle arrived, I was in heaven! I've been a user of eBooks since the first one that unfortunately became unusable because the company went out of business and the book pages were no longer maintained. I tried Sony's eBook with indifferent results. So it was with no little trepidation that I paid my money and bought my Kindle.

From the first, it lived up to its promises. I could download material in minutes and I could have a newspaper delivered every morning. I was a very happy camper. I packed for a one-month trip outside of Kindle's delivery area (France and Canada) and bought several new books to occupy me on planes and quiet moments on my trip.

Then disaster struck! My Kindle's face looked like a broken mirror and the books were of no use to me (the actual machine was not broken, only the image). I emailed for help and was given several suggestions but nothing helped. So I was told just to wait and a new Kindle would be sent to me (but not in Canada - they could not, for some reason, do that) and a return shipping label was given to me by email.

The book arrived while I was still in Canada but it is a perfect operational Kindle and the return process worked fine. Amazon lived up to its promise and that is all I can ask - I'm old enough to know that things break down here and there, even things you love and can't live without (see how Kindle has installed itself in my life?) but the new one did arrive timely and the return was seamless and I'm in business again.

title: Nice idea with a few limitations
text:
I have an M1-chip powered 2021 MacBook Pro that spends most of it's time in a dock connected to an external keyboard and monitor and I wanted a good-quality external camera that wouldn't require taking my Mac from the dock. The Lumina seemed one of the higher-quality and more compact choices, so I started there.

The camera itself is a rugged but tiny metal device about 3" long and 1" tall. It can be used on a small tripod or clamped to the top of a monitor with the included clamp. On the front is the lens, a pair of microphones and a small LED light that serves to generate front-lighting and to show when the camera is in operation. On the back, there's a USB-C connector for wiring it to your PC or Mac. Once connected, I found no difference in operation between using one of the Thunderbolt 4 ports on my MacBook, or going through an external USB dock.

I used the included mount to clamp the Lumina to the top of one of my desktop monitors. One quirky thing is that instead of just making this a simple thumbscrew of some sort, Lumina opted for a design that requires a hex key to tighten. In my case, the hex key was nowhere to be found in the package, but thankfully I have a set of my own. Once mounted, I found the tiny camera a bit sensitive to motion - it pretty much just rests atop my monitor...there's no "clamping" force to keep it in place. One problem I had was that the included USB cable was too short - at 30", there's no way it reaches from a perch on top of a large monitor all the way to a PC docked nearby.

Lumina includes a magnetic shutter that can be used to block the lens, ensuring privacy. The idea is good, but I find that the magnet isn't strong enough when the shutter is slid away from the lens...it stays put in the closed position, but when open, it's prone to falling off the camera. An internal shutter might have been a better choice.

I found the built-in microphones to be adequate overall, although I tend to use a Blue Yeti desktop microphone rather than the built-in ones most of the time. Because the Lumina microphones sit further away from me, I find they're a bit more likely to pick up background noise than my Blue Yeti. Still, the sound quality from the Lumina is more than adequate for things like videoconferencing, especially if you're in a quiet room.

The camera is 4K-capable and overall, I'd say that the lens and sensor generate a reasonably good image under good lighting conditions. Like many cameras, in dim light, picture quality degrades somewhat, but few of us want to use a webcam in the dark. I do find that if you have a lot of backlighting, the software struggles a bit with exposure, but thankfully, you can manually set exposure levels yourself.

Once plugged in, you can use the camera in "raw" mode from pretty much any application. I tested with all the popular web conferencing solutions (Zoom, Teams, WebEx, GoToMeeting, etc) and none of them had any issues at all with the Lumina camera. I also used Camtasia and a few other apps that support the video capture and they worked fine as well. I also tried the Lumina on a Windows 11 PC with similar good results. I give Lumina high marks for compatibility - I find that on my M1 MacBook, some apps - notably Microsoft Teams - don't play well with many cameras I've tried...the Lumina is the hands-down winner in this regard.

Note that in the "raw" mode, you don't get any of the video manipulation features Lumina talks about (that's part of the "Pro" mode using Lumina's software) and the wide angle lens means you need to get pretty close to the camera to have a reasonably sized image. It works great for groups, but you'll probably get a lot of background in the scene for individual use unless the app you're using provides some sort of cropping.

As for the included Lumina Pro software, I must say that I found the installation and configuration process the weakest part of the entire Lumina experience. Once you download the software, you're forced to register for an account and obtain a license key by email before you can proceed. To get the license key, you need the serial number of your device, and it's not stamped on the camera itself or on the packaging...the only way you can get it seems to be from within the Lumina installer. For some reason, the software didn't detect my camera properly, so there was no way I could get the serial number without rebooting my MacBook. Even after that, the approach is a messy "we'll email your license key, then you need to cut/paste or type it in".

Once you manage to get Lumina's software installed and configured, you'll see the option of "Lumina Pro" in the list of cameras connected to your computer, and if you choose this option, you get all of the features Lumina advertises. To me, the most significant feature is subject tracking, a feature that (digitally) zooms in on you, then keeps you centered in the frame, even as you move around. The motion is smooth and similar to what you might get if there were a human camera operator tracking you. Of course, the Lumina isn't a true PTZ (Pan, Tilt, Zoom) camera, so there are limits to how far it can track you.

I have a few gripes with the Lumina Pro software. For one thing, I was a bit disappointed in the Lumina's implementation of their background blur feature. Even configured for the maximum possible blur, I felt it left too much detail. Also, the Lumina software doesn't have the option for custom background images - for that, you need to rely on the video software you're using, or else use the camera in raw mode through something like Krisp. The good news is that many apps have this feature, but for those that don't, it would have been nice to see it in the Lumina software.

I did have the opportunity to communicate with Lumina's customer service team, and I found them easy to deal with and responsive. That's rare in today's world among consumer-grade products and Lumina deserves a hand for trying to be responsive to customers.

Bottom line is that the Lumina hardware platform seems about as good as any of the options out there. I'd say the Lumina Pro software is the weak point, but the camera works fine without and there are other options for most needs. Lumina seems to be a young company, and hopefully they'll continue to improve on their software - if they do, this will definitely be a five-star product that competes with anything else out there in this price range.

title: Definitely worth an audition
text:
Depending on who you are, these headphones might be all you ever need--or possibly not. I'm returning mine.
The short version: These sound truly incredible for certain kinds of music--but not all--and they're too uncomfortable for me. If I didn't have comfort issues, I would definitely keep them.

The full story:

My listening habits and setup: mostly listening to pop and rock music, but also classical, techno, metal. Very occasionally jazz. (side note: I am also a cellist and singer. I have an ear.) All of my audio is on flac, CD quality or better when possible. Setup is SPDIF optical out of my computer motherboard, to a Schiit Modi 3 DAC and Schiit Magni 3+ headphone amp ($100 each). I listen in a quiet space, very nice for open-backed headphones. I also own a Sennheiser HD 598 for comparison. I have also auditioned 3 or 4 others from Grado and one Beyerdynamic.

What's good about HiFiMan:
--They easily produce clinically accurate timing. They're always right there, never losing composure. There's no sense that they're "trying." Very definite audible difference in this regard, compared to the HD 598.
--If you like to listen loud, these will rock your brains out, without any sign of distortion or effort. Frankly, they're dangerous in this regard. I had so much fun with them the first night, I went to bed (late) with ringing in my ears. You could easily do some damage--these headphones don't give you any sense of needing to turn them back down.
--Very detailed sound.
--No tonal coloration added that I could hear.
--My first try with them on classical music was a hi-def recording of Vivaldi's Four Seasons. I got continual chills of excitement. My body responded like I was in a concert hall. These are the best headphones I have ever heard for classical music, hands down.
--caution: if you don't own a headphone amp and DAC, then you're not going to have the experience that I did here. A headphone jack on an old receiver will do, but it'll probably give you flabby bass. Many people have reported that phones just don't cut it. I didn't even try.

HiFiMan complaints:
--discomfort. My ears are too big. They press on my lobes and rest on the tops. I feel an internal struggle between wanting to hear them and wanting to get them off. Maybe you have smaller ears than mine--if so, then you should buy them now.
--On pop music from the last couple decades, the drums and the vocals hang back, in a detrimental way. My Sennheisers produce a better sense of separation than the HiFiMan. Especially on tracks with a quiet intro, the Sennheiser sound gives me chills when the singer comes in, like they're right next to me. On the HiFiMan, the singer is back next to the band.
--The HiFiMan is a meatier sound than the Sennheiser, which I would consider a good thing overall. It's spread thicker, while the Sennheiser takes the same sound and spreads it wider, but thinner. However, for much of the music I listen to, I prefer this more open sound, even if it means sacrificing some meat.
--The clinical accuracy of the HiFiMan is also a weakness in many cases of pop music. To be sure, my Sennheisers lose some timing and just sound sloppier on many tracks--but I actually like this. It feels like the Sennheisers are letting loose and having more fun, while the HiFiMan gives me an impression of discipline and restraint. When I'm listening to Smashing Pumpkins or even Coldplay tracks, restraint isn't the feeling I'm going for. I want unrestrained passion.

This is perhaps a standard difference between planars and dynamics. Many people will say that planars are just flat out better, but in this case, I feel that my Sennheiser dynamic headphones are more... well... dynamic. Again, for classical and jazz, go for the discipline. You don't want sloppiness in that case.

In fact, at this price, if the HiFiMan is comfortable on your head, then you should just keep these--even if you need to own a second or third pair of something else. They make a truly incredible pair for classical, jazz, loudness, or just for times when you want their sound over the dynamic sound. If they didn't bother my ears so much, I would do exactly that. With my comfort issues, I'm going to return them and go for an upgrade to the Sennheiser 600 line instead.

title: Dead after only FOUR uses
text:
I bought this because I trusted SanDisk to make a reliable product. This is one of the most expensive USB flash drives sold, so I expected it to last a long time.

Amazon won't allow an exchange, return or refund because it had been more than 30 days. I won't send it to SanDisk for replacement because they won't honor their "Lifetime Warranty" unless the product is physically undamaged. Since I can't access the drive to format it, I can't make sure my files are gone unless I physically break the drive. I will no be not sending my files to SanDisk so their "Lifetime Warranty" is useless.

If you do buy this, I strongly recommend testing it thoroughly as soon as you get it; because otherwise Amazon won't help you and if there's anything important on the drive you won't want to send it back to SanDisk.

title: Great, but slow to react
text:
I bought the camera for our townhouse, installed it on the south wall with the majority of sunlight to ensure I don’t ever need to charge it.

The positive:
-picture and audio is great, seamless and not choppy. To be clear my router is very close inside the house so I’m assuming it’s getting full strength signal.
- installation was easy, I did it myself but I also consider myself handy.
- charging is amazing, I have been using it for 30 days in the winter (living in the Northeast corridor) and the battery is now at 96% which is amazing.
- no fees or bulky servers to deal with. Not fully sure if I’m gonna run out of internal memory yet.

Cons:
- it’s slow to react, your “events” have a couple of seconds in the beginning not captured so at times you see someone who dropped the package and leaving or a car already halfway through.
- I live in a fairly private area so I don’t get random captures aside from rabbits and when it rains heavily. I would imagine it would be worse if you are facing higher traffic areas.

All in all, for the price and convenience it’s worth the purchase, I’m happy with it, minus the delay in capturing content.

title: Outstanding upgrade from my HD 1080P viewing experience!
text:
I put quite a bit of research into this before making the decision to buy the LG 60UH6150 4K Ultra HD television. I sold my existing Samsung 50" HD (1080P) television, so that I could upgrade to 4K. The Samsung was a great buy, but this New LG is way better.

I did pick up 10 more inches of screen real estate, and do notice the difference in size, which may be attributed in part to the extremely thin bezel on the LG. Comparing HD from my Samsung to the 4K with this LG is absolutely noticeable and delightful. Blacks, whites and the color palette is much improved. For those of you interested in moving to a 4K television, the noticeable improvement is not so much in sharper resolutions, but more in overall color sharpness and richness. This is a Smart TV, so it comes with several Apps, i.e., Netflix, YouTube, etc., which broadens the viewers options for watchable content. Additionally, this television can be networked to your home either wirelessly or via an Ethernet cable. The LG menu can be overwhelming, but overtime can be adjusted to and for most; you will find that once you have selected your favorable viewing options, and are accustomed to navigating to the Smart TV Apps, you have learned all that you need.

I have a 7.1 home theater setup and understood that once I had invested in a 4K television, I would need to upgrade my surround sound receiver, and upgrade to a 4K Blu-ray player. I purchased the Denon AVR-X2300W surround sound receiver, and the Philips BDP7501 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray player. Each of these components offered 4K signal pass-through, with the ability to up-convert the video signal for programming or media that was not originally produced in the 4K format. The Denon also offered Dolby Atmos, which is amazing for home theater surround sound, and the Philips was a "True" 4K Blu-ray player, not an up-converter. There are lots of 4K Blu-ray up-convert players available, but I did not want to invest in a television that was 4K capable, and then up-convert video signals to it. I did not feel I would be getting the full benefit of the LG 4K television. Also, make sure that as you move into 4K, all of your components tied to your setup support HDR (High Dynamic Range). This is a must, because this option greatly improves the color palette of your video!

Watching 4K Blu-ray videos on the LG television is taking some getting used to. Some movies that I have watched in 4K UltraHD appear to have the "Soap Opera" effect. What I mean is the picture is so clear, the colors are so vibrant, the (in my opinion) movie loses that "Theatrical" type appearance. In other words, it is like watching video in a style typically seen on a sports event, local news cast or soap opera, that is not similar to going to a theater to watch a movie. I would imagine taking the time to calibrate the TV, would allow me to cater the look to a more personal preference. This is not a criticism, rather my best explanation of the clarity, color improvement and resolution that 4K offers over HD. And for me it is taking some getting used to.

All in all, I am happy with the LG 60UH6150 4K Ultra HD television and without hesitation would recommend it as a choice if you are close to making a purchase. It offers so many features, you may find it overwhelming. Picture quality is stellar, and it has made a definite improvement to my viewing experience, along with meeting my expectations very well.

title: Amazing, wish I had bought it sooner. Voice sample inside!
text:
I decided to go ahead and order the Sena SMH10-11. So far I love it. I am pretty happy with it. Here are some of the reasons.

Options galore. What kind of options you say?
1. You can use earbuds with the optional accessory. I haven't thrown down the cash yet, but I am definitely considering it in the future.
2. You can use the boom mic, or the wired mic if you get the SMH10-11. Typically boom mic for modular, wired mic for full face, but up to you.
3. There is an aux input, so you can wire non bluetooth accessories as well. Haven't tried it yet, since I use my phone.
4. You can get the SMH5 for a partner for cheap. The SMH5 runs about $100. The main difference is smaller speakers, less range, less connectivity, and no aux. Perfect for a secondary set or to convince your cheap ass friend to buy so you can communicate while on the road. It does pair with the SMH10.
5. Firmware updates. They just released v4.2 last month or so.

The wired mic is really nice because I really disliked the idea of a boom sticking out of my helmet. Now, they do have the boom where it's a wired boom now, so you can stick it in the helmet so half the boom flex is not sticking out of the helmet which is a nice touch, but I still prefer the wired mic. Much smaller and manageable. However, maybe the sound isn't as good? I haven't compared the two.

I use NRR 33 E-A-R Soft Blast UF Foam Ear Plugs and with these, I have no problem hearing music at 75mph from the speakers. I have also tried having a phone conversation and could hear the other person fine. He could also hear me. I have uploaded a sample conversation we had at 50 mph and 80 mph with the visor up and down. dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/83612395/sena_test_final.mp3

I was pretty amazed.

The jog dial is nice. It makes changing volume and tracks very simple. I have the SMH10 connected to my HTC Evo 4g LTE and use Google Music to stream all my music while I ride.

I have the Shoei RF1100 and was able to route all the wires pretty cleanly behind the cheek pads except for the initial wires coming out of the unit. Those just wrap over the rim of the helmet. I could mod the pads to squeeze it through but I don't mind.

I ride a 2001 Suzuki SV650.

Now I have to convince my riding buddies to go with the Sena lol.

title: Solid 10G router - no drama
text:
I was pretty happy to see TP-Link come out with a 10G WAN/LAN capable router. I paired it with a TP-Link TL-SX1008 8-Port 10G Unmanaged Network Switch, and a Sonnet Tech Solo 10G Ethernet adapter at my laptop.

The TP-Link router was hot swapped for an older, non-10G capable router. There are several access points, so I am not going to comment on the wifi signal from this one unit.

The router then ran to the unmanaged switch, then a 75' cat6a run to the Ethernet adapter. The fiber service to the router typically delivers about 9 to 9.5G of download speed. After the router and through the switch, I get about 9G download, with 4.5G upload. Not sure if the router is limiting the upload or the service provider has throttled the upload speed. Will test that later.

In general, the router performs very well for what I need. Note that the latency is 1-2 ms as well - so gamers rejoice.

In summary, TP-Link has been making very reliable and easy to use products and I have tried many of the SOHO products out there with a lot of frustration and disappointment. I was very happy to see TP-Link release this 10g router so I could max out my ISP's bandwidth and it has proven, so far, to be easy to use, reliable with solid performance.

title: Great for Xbee breadboarding but be careful...
text:
This is a great little adapter board that converts the pins on an Xbee module - which don't fit into a standard breadboard - to the 2.54 mm (0.1") spacing required by a breadboard. This is simply an adapter - no components (like a voltage regulator, etc) on it whatsoever.

There are no instructions so it looks like a simple soldering job and it is however you need to be careful - the 2mm XBee pin headers themselves are built differently than what you are likely used to. The female ends that the XBee plugs into are hollow (as they should be) but are OPEN at the bottom instead of being sealed. This mean when you have the adapter board upside down to solder the male ends of those pins to the PCB board and if you use too much solder it can actually run inside the female part of the pin and prevent an XBee from being completely inserted. I've also read of people having their XBee plugged into the pins while soldering (to keep them square) and not being able to pull their XBee out because its now soldered to the socket! I threw out my first adapter after learning the hard way but my second one went perfect. Best advice - don't be nervous or apprehensive - simply use minimal solder on each pin of the header and it will be fine. Heat the pin and just dab the solder to get a nice solid bead on the top and do not keep driving solder down into the PCB hole because it will end up in that female part of the 2mm pin.

Note this is not an issue with the 2.54mm pins since the they are sealed at the bottom, just the smaller pins for the XBee.

title: Worth The Money 100%  (Smart Tv Setup Below!)
text:
1. Review
Most difficult part was setting it up with my smart tv, and there was really nothing I could find online. It sounds great for the money. If you’re wondering if it’s worth it, it is! The LED’s dance to the sound of whatever’s playing as well which is pretty cool. I’m super pleased with my purchase, I couldn’t have asked for more for the price! One last thing, the range on the remote is about 10 feet lol !
2. Setup (Smart TV)
Hook up all speakers, they’re all labeled with stickers
You’ll need a digital to analog audio converter, I’ll link it at the bottom
Plug in the digital optical to the headphone jack in the converter (this will give better surround sound)
Plug in the red and white RCA to red and white RCA into the aux ports of the amp and into the corresponding ports in the converter.
Plug in Converter and Plug in Speakers
Change source on the display to “Au—“
Turn on your Smart TV and go to Settings > Sound/Audio > Expert Settings/Advanced Settings > Digital Output Audio Format > PCM
!!! Make sure you turn your output setting to PCM, you should also set a 40ms delay if you have the setting as well !!!!
Your speakers should be working now!! P.S. The bluetooth should be easy enough to set up, if not just hold down the stby button for 3 sec then try again.
Digital to Analog Converter - https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07MPF4F68/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_api_i_N89mEbKR4X4BF

title: One-Bag Commuter Laptop Backpack
text:
I needed two bags for work (laptop backpack & lunch cooler bag) so I am really glad that this bag has a built-in cooler and still room left over for my laptop, folders and my daily commute needs.

LUNCH COOLER - There is enough room for four 4-cup Pyrex bowls and an ice-pack! I can have my salad, yogurt, and other dishes in this cooler. Since there are two side mesh pockets for a water bottle or two, I don't have to worry about them taking up room in the cooler section. The cooler's silver insulation section is sturdy and heavy duty. Besides using it as a cooler, I can also use it as a special compartment for my swim thing or shoes to keep them away from the rest of the bag.

SEPARATE LAPTOP POCKET - I love this separate laptop pocket as it not only fits a 17" laptop but also has an extra pocket for a tablet as well as enough room for various folders.

MAIN POCKET - The main pocket can be used as one big pocket or it can be separated into two top and bottom (lunch cooler) pockets. Even with the cooler in use, you can still fit a few textbooks into the top section. Note, this cooler at the bottom / pocket at top design is great if you use lunch containers as they will form a platform to hold up you books and other items on top. However, if you bring sandwich in foil wrap, for example, the items from the top pocket can crush your lunch. There are two mesh pockets inside for a battery (with built-in wire to connect from the outside) and other smaller item.

BACK SECURITY POCKET - This is a back security pocket with zipper that sits right next to my lower back. This is a great pocket to keep my wallet and other valuables.

FRONT & ORGANIZER POCKETS - There is a good-size front pocket for a pair of glasses or frequently needed items. The larger organizer pocket can fit pens and other stationery items.

SIDE MESH POCKETS - These pockets are deep and fit a Nalgene bottle very well. You can put you small umbrella on the other side.

MATERIAL QUALITY - Material is above average and I expect that the bag will last for years with regular usage. Surprisingly, the padding on the backpack straps and around the laptop compartment is somewhat skimpier than expected for such a large bag. It is not a deal breaker though since I do not plan to go hiking with this bag.

SUMMARY - This bag is very roomy and gives you the option of a lunch cooler that can double as a shoe compartment or swimwear bag. When the lunch cooler is not in use, this bag offers much room and many pockets to organize your work gear. Although padding is somewhat less than expected, the many benefits of the bag far outweigh this tiny nit. I highly recommend it!

The only difference is a Kykr sticker on the outside and a Kykr branded microfiber cloth included in the packaging.

The protector itself is fine. It follows the bottom edge nicely, but you can tell from the corners that it wasn't designed with a strong attention to detail. The curve of the corners of the glass don't exactly match the curves of the corner of the display. These are small enough not to bother me at a $15 price point, but at $40 I expected an EXACT match to the curves of the display. Also, the screen is cut to the same dimensions as the screen, meaning you have to line everything up with virtually no tolerance for mistakes, otherwise the screen protector goes off the edge of the display. This makes installation a very difficult thing to do. It would have been nice to receive an alignment tool to help get the installation perfect.

Finally, the biggest gripe I have with this protector is that it doesn't play well with polarized sunglasses. You can see from the picture that the right hand side of the display is strongly discolored when viewed from the driver's seat. Head on it looks fine, which is okay for devices like smartphones and tablets, but for a vehicle it makes a large portion of the display difficult to see.

Overall I think this screen protector is fine, and is probably par for the course. However, I'd recommend buying it from any other seller on Amazon since those are more affordable (and are most likely the same exact product).

title: Nice Complete Kit, a bit pricey for what it is.
text:
First off I want to state that I do really like this clock. It's a really cool display and the kit was a lot of fun to assemble. The directions on Adafruit's website are extremely detailed and precise. The printed circuit board is nicely silkscreened and seems to be of high quality. The display tube is of course beautiful. The acrylic case is very clever and shows the clock off nicely.

Once assembled and working, you can use it as a clock or since it can be re-programmed you can use it as a starting point for various hacks/mods or a programming project.

I would not recommend this for someone with no experience soldering before. Many of the solder pads on the circuit board are close together and without experience I could see it being easy for someone to create a short. If you have a a low to moderate level of experience soldering circuit boards you'll be perfectly fine, just don't make this your first project involving soldering.

Now, why only 3 stars:
If I could give it 3 and a half I would. I was really borderline on giving this 4 stars (again I do really like it)... a lot of what I am going to list as wrong here I would have forgiven on a less expensive product. If it were more around $50 I would easily give it 4 maybe even 5 stars.

Quality Control Issues:
Case Quality Control:
Another reviewer complained abut this as well. Their complaint was about the hole in the side for supporting the tubes nipple. For me that's not an issue, I figure not all tubes are exactly the same and they need to account for that. The bigger problem I have with the case is that some of the screw holes were cut so close to the edge of the acrylic that they actually blew out the side (imagine a c instead of a o). It wasn't visible once assembled but I have to worry about lost strength.

Component Quality Control:
My clock did not work with the components included. Specifically the transistor used to control power to the tube failed. Their instructions do warn that it's very static sensitive, but I took every proper static precaution. Reading in their forum this part seems to be a common point of failure. I was able to get the clock working by by-passing this transistor for now and I've ordered a different model transistor to replace it which was recommended as a more durable alternative. Since it's known that this component frequently fails and a more rugged alternative cost less than 50 cents, why include it in an $85 kit?

Cost:
I was going to give this kit 4 stars based on my purchase price of $85, but when I went to put my review in Amazon I noticed that the price was now almost $120. Since I was borderline on that 4 stars, that convinced me to go with 3. FYI at the time I'm writing this the manufacture does still have them available on their site for the normal price. Anyway, while I appreciate the fact that it comes with a clever laser cut case and good quality pre-printed circuit boards.... if you were to purchase the tube and all of the components on your own you would only be at around $30. However you wouldn't have a nice printed circuit board or perfectly fitting acrylic enclosure to put it in or a support forum of people who have built the exact same clock so that has some value.

Conclusion:
Great Kit that's a lot of fun to put together. Especially for someone who likes unique clocks and electronics projects. I feel it's a bit expensive for what it is. I would expect better QC from a kit in this price range.

title: GREAT camera for the price!!!
text: I purchased this digital camera on Amazon after pricing it at several stores and got a great deal (under $200) with free shipping. I have used this camera at both a concert and a play (Wizard of Oz) and using the STAGE function (no flash), was able to capture some really great pictures.  Am looking forward to visiting the zoo this weekend and getting "up close and personal" with the animals by using the 30x Optical Zoom lens and then running off to Dollywood to capture the beautiful Christmas lights and Christmas parade in Gatlinburg.  I especially like the ease of use and the special "FUN" feature of a four-pose snapshot (like you used to get in those little photo booths along the boardwalk or at Woolworth stores many years ago).  This camera also comes with a view finder (most of the cheaper models only come with the digital LCD screen unless you pay mega-bucks for an SLR-type of digital camera with changeable lenses at $650 - $1000).  I find that using the view finder helps steady the camera and you get much less camera shake (although it is equipped with stabilization).  This camera uses rechargeable AA batteries (or alkaline batteries in a pinch), so it makes the camera a bit heavy for those wanting a thin-wallet size camera, but the 30x zoom and special features are a plus if you're at a concert, zoo, play, or outside sporting event - including NASCAR racing. It also takes video (which I have only used once) and the results were great. Two things that are not furnished are a "paper" instruction manual (you have to download it off the internet) and a memory card.  Be sure to purchase at least a 16x SDHC card to enable you to take plenty of video.  A 32x would be even better.  Again, this is a great camera for the price.  So for less than about $260 - $280 total cost (adding in the purchase of an extra set of AA rechargeable batteries, 16X SDHC memory card or better - and maybe a camera case if you don't already have one) you get a camera that takes great photos (even at long distances).  Buy this camera - you won't be disappointed.

title: It works, its not great, but thats fine by me
text:
[[VIDEOID:efdf560be376318fde362885953f1d47]] First off before I write this review let me just say I did a lot of research on this kind of record player and even a few of my own experiments so i would consider what i found to be pretty credible. I wish someone wrote a review like this for me when I was considering buying it.

#1 Is this a good record player for beginners or people who only want a few records to play for the aesthetic? Absolutely. The sound quality is meh, but I mean what do you expect for $40. It plays the records no problems, and the bluetooth is great for just whenever.

Now here is how you can upgrade your setup with minimal spending. Get an RCA to mini jack cable. Plug that into a speaker you already have or if in my case you have a practice amp cause you play an instrument, get a mini jack to 1/4 converter and plug it into the amp! It works great!

#2 Will this ruin my records?

No. It will not. I made a little scale and using pennies weighed out the tracking force to be around 5g. Now compared to $200 record players that track at 3g this seems like a lot. But be aware, when records were made, they were made to withstand up to 7 or 8g of tracking force cause lots of old players tracked at around 5 or 6g. Now tracking heavier like this will yes, wear them out faster, but it will NOT ruin them! The needle is also a diamond, so the needle is pretty decent actually.

Now you can actually fix the tracking force on this thing. Get a small scale, like the kind to bake with, put your tone arm on it, get some pennies and nickels and start stacking them at the back of the tone are where the counterweight should be. One your tone arm reads at about 3.5-4g. Take those coins, tape them together, and tape them to the back of that tone arm. Maybe even go for around 4-4.5g because in my experience these cheap ones skip very easily.

#3 Is it portable?

Absolutely not. You need to plug it into an outlet, and it could totally break with some throwing around. Also the lid is completely useless.

I took the lid off by unscrewing the screws on the back hinges. The lid is NOT big enough even when open to run 12" vinyls. The edge is right under your record, like millimeters under, and if you have ANY warping, at all it will hit the edge and cause it to skip. This is likely the problem a lot of people have when it skips and just don't know it. Just take the lid off its useless.

#4 Does it skip? Does it sound weird?

No, not at all. I had it skip on me once, and after replaying that section it never did it again. Probably was just my fault since i accidentally tapped the vinyl I was playing when getting it out of the sleeve. Also I tested the wow and flutter using a phone app. Let me tell you that it is BAD, like the wow and flutter is REALLY HIGH. But, even so, I didnt notice ANY sort of distortion in the sound. It might be worse when playing above 33rpm but at least for 33, its fine.

#5 Is it worth the price?

100% as long as you know what your getting. I didn't expect this player to be good or even great. Its okay at best and I'm fine with that cause its $40. If you are looking for a very nice player that delivers great sound quality, dont get this. If you want to really get into vinyl, dont get this. If you want to experience the most you can from your records, dont get this. If you want to just play a couple of records for cheap and have them in your room cause its cool and aesthetic, go ahead, im doin it for that exact reason.

(Also, I purchased an amazon return and found no problems with it. Dont be afraid to purchase a used one for less, you can always return it if it is actually broken, but it will probably work anyway)
