title: You see... I have this silly smile I can not get rid of.... My smile has faded away, read on.
text:
I ordered this tablet, my first Android device, and I was kinda wondering what I would receive...
So far I'm really pleased with this thing!
Being a Palm and iPod Touch user and early adopter of what people call "smart phones", I wasn't sure if I wanted a large-format device. I have friends who are pushing their Apple tablets at me and I'm an iMac user myself... but I just wasn't sure if I needed (read that as wanted) a tablet.
I bought this on "speculation" to see if I could have a little fun and perhaps learn something new.
I'm having the fun part right away and I can see that some learnin' is headed my way here with the Android operating system this tablet uses. Not hard learning, but with the "open-ness" of Android I expect to be finding new stuff to do for a good while.

Out of the box I received a durable-feeling device with a nice large screen. It turned-on first try and responded to the battery charger just like the (little) owner's manual predicted. There is a great deal more going on with this thing than the little booklet speaks of, but the manual is complete enough for anyone to realize all but the nuts and bolts of Android... I believe the manual was not intended to tech Android to a user but to simply expose the buyer to the capabilities of the tablet. The manual is a translation, but a good one with pictures and diagrams. Easy to read and understand.

I haven't done much with it yet, but I have connected to the net using my WPA-2 WiFi "Apple Airport Extreme" and had no problem with the setup. It reminded me of getting a Nintendo DSi connected... it was that easy. I am using MAC address filtering and that posed no problem after putting the tablet's MAC address in my list.
The Localization settings were easy with the only "snag" as yet being the temperature display in the Home screen is in Centigrade and I can't (as yet) figure out how to switch to Fahrenheit. It even "found" my little home town to use as the target city :)
The only other thing I haven't figured yet is if the operating system is consuming part of the 2 gig of memory, leaving only 1 gig free or if the device shipped with only 1 gig of memory.
I think this problem is my lack of familiarity with Android :)
I will attempt to provide a better review as time allows, but for now I'm happy.

One final note, the device is called a "MID" in the Owner's Manual and the following information appears in the "About Device" screen on the device it's self;
Model Number: deb
Firmwear Version: 2.1-update1
Kernel Version: 2.6.32.9 hzhao@emma #1
Build Number: deb-r2.1.1170

There is another tablet listed on Amazon called a "MID" but it does not seem to have a camera or a GPS receiver. This unit's GPS "antenna" is external and I think the little hocky-puck is both an antenna and receiver combined.

Update: (12/26/2010)
Liking the tablet! The hardware is working great, no problems at all, no glitches or silly business from the device or the Android "build" as is installed.
The only things I'm watching are;
- The "Home" button on the front is not indexed exactly right under the front cover. Not a problem but there was a moment where it was trying to get stuck.
- One of the tiny little "plugs" covering the cabinet screws has fallen out. This is no problem at all as there will come a day when I want to take those screws out myself and those plugs are going away on that day. As a side note, this tablet survived a drop from my desk top to the plastic carpet protector under the desk without a glitch.
- The Android "build" has a little trouble when rotating the screen. Two issues so far 1.) When you use Google's Star application, the Horizon is oriented incorrectly and does not correct even when you try the adjustments for screen rotation in Android or in Google's application. Weirdly, the names of planets and stars continue to rotate (to the wrong angle) even if you turn-off all the rotation controls. 2.) When you use the device in the "Landscape" orientation there is a very useful "Back" button in the screen in the top right... when you rotate to "Portrait" orientation that button goes away and you have to use the hardware buttons. Not really a big deal but the behavior of the on-screen "Back" button and the hardware button are not exactly the same in all applications.
- About keyboards, mice, and memory devices. USB supports all these but does not recognize anything else. I am using a Bluetooth "dongle" and my Apple "Magic Mouse" but my HID Bluetooth keyboard and Bluetooth GPS are not recognized. So far I have not found an application that can pair any Bluetooth devices that are not physically incorporated in the device (that's none so far). The Bluetooth dongle I have states it is a wired equivalent of a mouse and keyboard.. but that HID keyboard is not working.

That's all for now. It's worth the $230 to me so far but I'm new at this so I might not have the expectations a more seasoned Android user might have.

Update: (1/7/2011)
The people I got my tablet from are fantastic! I used email to talk to them about getting a registration number for the Android release on my tablet and they were really warm and responsive. It was like they actually liked the product!
I no longer see them listed as sellers but I will look for them the next time I want something from China.
(Beijing Ning Rong Technology Development Co. Ltd)

I Learned some stuff.
- There are a lot of "Widgets" and "Gadgets" that fail when used on a tablet... perhaps it's just this one, but I suspect the large screen is giving them trouble.
- You can use an [[ASIN:B002TLTGM6 Apple Magic Mouse]] and [[ASIN:B002TMRZOQ Apple Wireless Keyboard (Retail Packaging)]] by first pairing them on your desktop machine and then moving the Bluetooth "dongle" to the Flytouch. I use an [[ASIN:B0018O9JIG IOGear USB 2.1 Bluetooth Micro Adapter GBU421]]
- The "Escape" key on the keyboard functions like the "Back" button on the screen.
- F4 seems to first, put the device into "sleep" then shortly it will re-boot.
- F1 acts like the "Menu" button.
Still have not found any applications that provide USB support for other than keyboard, mouse, and memory. I hope the developers of Android see the tablet as a "future" for Android and start providing full support for USB attached peripherals.
The display is really nice indoors. Outdoors it's washed-out but usable.

Price jump. What's this about?!?
I'm a little disturbed that this tablet has jumped in price. I kinda was thinking about a second one for a friend but at this rate, she's probably going to get something else. Too bad, we like this one. :)

Update: (01/19/2011) - Sorry if this is turning into a "blog"...
An update to the Android OS has come out, not a big change like version 2.2 or anything, but it allowed me to see what and how upgrades look like and are done.
It did not go so well. I had to go onto the Internet and find the proper file myself and load it again using a micro SD card. After that everything was back to "normal". I had to find and re-load all the applications I had loaded and every setting had to be re-entered. I later found out that you can back-up these things and save yourself some time. Considering the changes to the Android OS, I will wait for a major update before going with another minor one again... too much hassle for not so much gain.
The tablet is still a winner! I have it running for several hours a day and am even now watching a DVD TV show (converted using "Handbrake" for the Mac). Playback is smooth at 720 x 400 and around 1100 bits per second (m-peg4). See, this thing is making me learn about stuff like Android OS and video data rates :)
Still can't set the Weather widget to Fahrenheit, but otherwise I'm still happy with the purchase.

Update: (06/01/2014) - Amazon still lists this tablet on their site.
Beware of the following issues;
1.) This tablet is no longer supported by the manufacturer. NO UPDATES TO THE OPERATING SYSTEM.
2.) The Amazon Appstore no longer functions correctly on this device. NO MORE APPS CAN BE INSTALLED.
3.) You are lucky if you installed a suite of useful applications because Amazon Appstore and Google Play are unavailable to you with this device. You can "side load" the old Android Market but it is severely "broken" and will likely not even allow you to browse applications.

Good while it lasted! This tablet was my first Android device and it still functions as it did when it was new. A good device left to fallow by an supportive vendor. Beware that if something you buy lasts beyond the 30 or 90 day warrentee period you are likely to be "on your own" from there on out.

title: Overall my favorite secondary mouse with caveats.
text:
I mainly use this mouse as a mobile mouse when working remote, its light, comfortable and thin and the battery lasts months. When I do work in the field, I do schedule to have a lighter data entry work load than I would in the office or from home.

I have this one pictured with my old Surface Arc Mouse and my main mouse, the MX Master 3. My review is from the point of view of comparing my old Surface Arc mouse to this and how I use this as my main secondary mouse.

The size is comparable to the original arc mouse design but is a wider towards the palm to give us a symmetrical shape in contrast to the narrowing of the old mouse, this lets more of your palm rest on the mouse.

The two biggest changes for me with the newer mouse, the haptic feedback while scrolling and separate R/L mouse buttons have been replaced by one button that sense which finger touches first. I'm a fan of haptic feedback so it's just a plus feature for me that i'd like to have but not a deal breaker. I have used a Magic Mouse previous to the Arc mouse so I'm familiar with the sensitivity of a single touch mouse button, so personally I'm used to it, but it is a slight learning curve and mild annoyance.

The new model does have horizontal scrolling which is useful with my application so its a feature add for me.

I did not consider missing features like back buttons, programmable buttons, etc which can be found on larger more feature rich mice like the MX Anywhere series, I would not consider those applicable for my use.

Final take.

It's a basic functional mouse that looks cool. If you need a light weight portable mouse for light use while in the field, at school, or in the home to use with a notebook/tablet, this is the one. There really isn't a decent competitor with price and form factor.

Pros
-Design
-Light, highly portable
-Horizontal scrolling
-6 month battery life

Cons
-lacks features for "power" users
-missing haptic feedback (personal pref)
-missing separate R/L buttons from pervious generation

My impression is that the 1080p picture looks better than the A2's 1080i did, but that might just be wishful thinking. Obviously, as with and HD-DVD player, you'll get a little better ("lossless") audio if you have an HDMI-equipped receiver, but I'm happy to use optical digital cables for now and upgrade in a couple years.

One thing I strongly suggest, though, is that you attach this to the internet using the ethernet port in the back. If you aren't wired for ethernet, consider setting up a wireless bridge (or "gaming adapter"). Updates for the player AND for some of the HDDVD titles (!) are available for automatic download if you're hooked up.

Most of the features are displayed logically and clearly. Navigating around the menus is quick and reasonably intuitive....most of the time.
While navigating a route, the next turn is displayed at the top of the screen and the current road is at the bottom......perfect.
The live traffic works well thru a bluetooth connection to a smartphone once set up. However set-up was not easy (see below)
Voice Command works OK if there is little ambient noise. Out on a highway we had difficulty getting the GPS to understand.

Cons:
The display is glass which results in quite a bit of reflection if not looking at the screen head on.
The traditional suction cup mount is as useless as ever. We opted for a mount inserted in our CD player, which works perfectly, especially since the touch screen requires such a light tap.
The connection between the gps and the mount is a bit difficult to release with 1 hand. Would have preferred a magnetic mount.
The set up of live traffic thru the smartphone was not intuitive at all. It was especially confusing that connection to the Smart Link app showed up as another paired device on the gps. Took me a lot of trial & error to make the Smart Link connection, but then disable the phone (I didn't want phone calls, texts etc coming thru the gps). And if you don't have the Smart Link app running on your phone at the time the gps turns on, you won't get traffic and won't know that you're not connected. (After a while I realized that I can quickly check the Smart Link connection on the gps by looking for the Smart Link symbol at the top of the main gps screen.
Since my wife and I both use the same vehicle with the gps and each have our own phones, I tried to figure out an easy way to switch between phone pairings depending on who was using the car. The gps will automatically pair with the phone it was most recently paired with. That worked great as long as you only have 1 phone. When I paired the gps with both our phones, I expected the gps to connect with the secondary phone if the primary (last used) was out of range. Not happening. I couldn't figure out an easy way to switch phones without going thru several steps to unpair and re-pair the secondary phone; then close the Smart Link app and re-open it. So we'll just use the 1 phone unless we're desperate.
And lastly, driver alerts might be helpful to some, but I found them just plain annoying (notifying me every time there's a curve in the road, school crossing, change in speed limit, etc. At least you can disable the audio alerts, but you can't stop the visual alerts popping up at the top of the screen.

It sounds like a lot of negatives, but as I said initially, this is the best Garmin yet and we're very pleased with it.

I used the Skycaddie SG 3.5 prior to this unit and I found myself paying for maps every year.

This is where the Skycaddie shines. With SkyGolf360, your stats are tailored to your needs.
You can track the distance of your shots, hole by hole.
The garmin provides tracking of your distance but this is computed as an average and you never get to see
your drive distance per hole.
The newer Skycaddie is also touch screen so the Garmin doesn't lose points here, I guess that's where the future is.
The belt clip on my old Skycaddie was a lot sturdier.

You can't go wrong with the G6. I subtracted one star due to the lack of stat keeping.
But you can manually track this information with plenty of free phone apps.

[Update 5/25/2016]
Changing rating from 4 to 5 stars

title: It gets the job done, but prepare for a headache.

Pros:

-Most recommended bang-for-your-buck device amongst archivist/digitizing enthusiasts

Cons:
-Definitely not archival quality. Compresses the files after capture.

-Very sensitive to touch. If you move any of the cabling or change its position, it will stop recording
-When attempting to stitch the files together due to the abrupt cuts, audio is de-synced, thereby having to run it through another software to modify each recording allowing it to play in sync properly when editing. Drastically increases the amount of time needed to properly edit the footage.

Overall: 3/5. Although not archival quality, I'm happy with the overall result and ease of use, but cannot get around the abrupt crashes this toy suffers. Have to constantly monitor this thing hoping it doesn't crash towards the end of a tape.

title: Great protection but...
text:
I'm what might be called a Kindle cover/accessory junkie, so I couldn't resist this one, especially since it seemed to offer great protection for my beloved Kindle, and the price was definitely right. And, in fact, I think this cover does offer superior protection. Of course, it doesn't have soft or thick padding like some of the other covers I have, but I'm taking their word for it that polycarbonate is shatter-proof and very protective. Plus, it has one super feature that I've not found on any other product, and that is the clear polycarbonate covering over the Kindle screen. I don't know what the statistics are for Kindle death, but I'm guessing that if the screen goes, the whole shooting match is over. So that's a very valuable contribution, and the screen cover is non-glaring, crystal clear, fits perfectly (as does the whole thing), and is very easy to read through. (Unfortunately, the rest of the cover, besides the part that covers the screen, is sort of too shiny and glarey. I think it would be very nice if they offered matte, more subtle colors.) Other features that I like are a handy and very functional folding leg on the back that lets you read the Kindle hands-free and cut-outs for the speakers on the back so if you're listening to the audio when there's ambient noise, the volume is not muffled. Of course, there are also cut-outs for all the necessary buttons and apertures.

So why not give this product five stars? Here's why: I just don't much like the way it looks. If you're a twenty-something coolster (is there such a word?), then you'll probably love it. It's sleek, modern, shiny, and purple! It's also compact and functional. So what's not to like? Well, I do LIKE it. I just don't love it. And I think that's because I have some really gorgeous leather covers and some witty, cool other covers, and I appreciate their qualities of beauty and originality. Also, to my surprise, I've actually sort of come to prefer the book-like quality of these other covers. So it's purely a personal preference, and I'm sure not everyone would share it. In addition, I think there are times (like, maybe, travel) when protection becomes the primary consideration, so this cover would still come in very handy. I'd say, even if you have other covers that you love, this one is inexpensive enough that it's worth having just for the extra protection that you may want at certain times.

P.S. I've now had my Kindle 2 in its purple mCover for a couple of days and carried it in my purse. My purse has all the usual stuff: billfold, fabric checkbook cover, glasses case, pill bottle, etc. Nothing metal or sharp. So I'm sad to report that my mCover is now scratched. Its sleek, smooth look is not so sleek and smooth anymore.

title: Great sound quality with a few technical flaws
text:
When I began my search for a soundbar for my tv, it started as many others by looking at Crutchfield and other audio sites. After much research it led me to Q Acoustics and the M4 for its very impressive sound quality and simplicity. I was sold. While the unit sounds great and would get a 5 star for that alone, there are a number of small hiccups that to me drops the overall value.

Pluses:
- The sound quality is great and is as expected based on the reviews.
- The integrated subwoofer is just what I liked. Its got just enough punch for movies but doesn't affect voices too much. Too often I find external subwoofers annoyingly bassy.
- The size is great. I have it on a shelf below the TV which is hanging on a wall and it fills the space perfectly. I would probably look at a thinner unit though if it had to be hung on a wall as it would stick out somewhat far due to the subwoofer enclosure.
- The bluetooth feature to play it remotely is very cool, useful and easy to use.
- Setup was easy (except for the hour I spent trying to figure out why digital audio wasn't working)

Minuses
- The digital optical connection requires a specific setting (that isn't listed in product specs) that doesn't exist on my tv so I was forced to use analog audio cables. To me this was a big compromise.
- Unfortunately the analog audio disables the auto on feature of the unit so I have to manually turn it on every time which is annoying.
- There are no controls for the sound, zero so if you want bass or treble adjustments you are out of luck.
- The bluetooth while easy to use and useful at the same time can be annoying. For example when checking a voicemail with bluetooth on it turns the tv off and switches to bluetooth by priority. So I have to turn bluetooth off on my phone.
- There needs to be more steps between volumes. There are no visual representations any more of what the audio is set to (like a tv that displays bars or numbers). We have it at one volume and its too soft and the next volume increase is too loud. It needs a couple in between steps and this should have been easy to do.
- I would have liked equalization for the price. Some more basic units can regulate the audio between shows and commercials.

So overall a great sounding unit that I wish had a few more capabilities and addressed some product design hiccups.

title: Awesome sound... pity it's so uncomfortable....
text:
This is my first review for an item I bought at amazon, even though I've been a custumer here since 1996. Here's why:

I bought the Sennheiser EH-150 personally depressed, while looking for a decent set of headphones after my $149,95 Sony VibraBass cracked up, which had an awesome sound. I wanted to try something new and decent without spending so much money, and I since have already tried several (more than 10 or 15, each one ++$100) headphone sets, with "Ok I'm pleased" result, I thought I had nothing to lose.

Let me tell you, Sennheiser EH-150 headphone produces the best sound I have ever heard in my life, whether if it's Mp3's, DVD's, iPOD's, whatever, and from what I have read on other reviews of better models from Sennheiser, I am currently thinking in saving up to get any of the 500 or 600 series. I tell you it's worth it, the sound is simply awesome. You actually hear stuff you never heard before or never thought of hearing. Isolates external sounds very impressively. Feels like you can listen to each one of the channels .

Now problem is (and this is why I write the review): Sennheiser designers must still think mankind is Homo erectus or Homo neanderthal, not Homo sapiens sapiens. The headset is small and uncomfortable for normal-sized ears, and believe me I read a lot on other websites, and when I purchased it, I thought "Oh well, maybe these are just people with big ears". Got it wrong. I'm a normal-sized ear human being and these headphones are the best and everything, but after 3 or 4 hours... your ears get really hurt, and you just can't put them back for another 3 hours.

Trust me:

If you have big ears... save and buy the Sennheiser 500 or 600 series. Probably better quality than this ones (I haven't test them but it's logical they should be better, and I would really like to listen), and your ears will fit.

If you have normal-sized ears... save and buy the Sennheiser 500 or 600 series. Probably better quality than this ones (I haven't test them but it's logical they should be better, and I would really like to listen), and your ears will fit.

If you have small ears. Buy this.

3 1/2 Stars, because it's very uncomfortable.

Keyboard skin fits perfectly. I’ve never used one before so I don’t have anything to compare it to, but it seems capable of preventing or minimizing liquid, crumb and dust damage.

Screen protector is a thin piece of sheet plastic that comes with a film on both sides that is (obviously) removed before application. It has a cut-out for the camera lens. It adheres to the screen without adhesive, via static electricity.

CONS: zero.

I’m totally happy with my (inexpensive) laptop protection investment. If you own the brand new 2020 M1 MacBook Air, I recommend this case kit for you!

text:
I purchased this camera three months ago and took it on a cruise vacation shortly after. It was fun to use, but took bad pictures.

The design and interface is great. The menus are easy to navigate and making changes to the settings is quick and very simple. It does take the shots quickly just like I wanted (no anticipating, just shoot exactly when you want it to take). I love the touch screen. It is by far the most fun and enjoyable camera I've ever used, however the output isn't great.

We have a hard time getting good pictures. Landscape pictures in bright daylight are about the only ones that look really good. Indoor ones are always grainy, and live action shots are always blurry unless in full daylight. Do any zooming indoors and forget it. So it seems that the flash just isn't strong enough, and the internal zoom lens isn't the best design. Bummer! We've played with the settings some and certain situations have been able to improve the images, but I like having a camera that can be in auto and shoot great pictures no matter what the situation is (especially when on the go like on vacation). This camera has a smart scene selection mode where it chooses the appropriate scene setting based on its brains, but I think it often chooses wrong. I gave up on that setting and went to regular Auto mode.

title: A smidge TOO slim for commuting.
text:
As a federal contractor, I had to go through security checkpoints on a daily basis. The butterfly X Ray friendly design made that process a little easier, but the slim and compact design is a double edge sword. It fits all the components for the computer efficiently, but other items for the commute would not fit well. No exterior pocket for a water bottle/coffee mug, limited room if you were going to bring lunch or an additional layer if the weather was going to be unpredictable.
The computer sleeve is well padded and good for a slim to medium sized laptop (like a Macbook Air) but had trouble zipping closed on a larger 17" laptop. The second compartment is good for papers or files, third pocket holds mouse, phone, pens and sundries. Fourth pocket fits a 9" tablet, but lacks the felt interior. Fifth pocket is perfect for boarding pass/ passport. However, only the computer compartment is designed to be locked. Sixth compartment on the bottom, I use for power cables.

The construction and material are very durable. I've owned this for 2 years though a fair amount of travel and it shows very little sign of wear. This is great for electronics if you have another bag for other items, but not recommended as an all in one commuter backpack.

title: Small camera - big sensor.
text:
I hate to admit this, but I now own 8 digital cameras (too many) ranging from an Altoids box sized Pentax to a Fuji X100, to two Infrared-converted cameras, to full frame Canon Mark II 5D. Was looking for that ideal combination of a pocketable camera with a decent-sized sensor and some zoom capabilities and the Sony RX100 is in a class by itself that fits the bill. Have now used this camera for several months and am thrilled with the results.
The best things about this camera are it's unique combination of small size, large sensor, and top resolution. No need to carry around a dslr on a daily basis in case I see something worth photographing - which is every day. This guy fits easily in my pants pocket - not possible with the 4/3 cameras with their bigger lens. I have a 27 inch monitor and the images of the Sony appear to be the same resolution and quality as a dslr.
A few other comments:
1. As others may have indicated, the only small flaw (if you even want to call it a flaw) is that the access door to the SD card and battery appears a little flimsy - but I've never had any trouble with it.
2. Some sort of grip or texture on the front might be nice, but I've added a leather Gariz 1/2 case that provides a little better grip without adding much to the bulk.
Having compared and tested the Sony RX 100 to other compact-sized camera - including my slightly larger Olympus XZ-1 here are some final comments: 1. I find myself going to the Sony when I want especially high quality images. 2. I use the Olympus when I want easy access to special effects such as "dramatic tone" or "pop art" or "pin hole."
The higher price of the Sony RX 100 (over $600) is worth it to me - especially if I want enlargements beyond 13 x 19. Otherwise the Olympus XZ-1 is a perfect lower- priced pocket camera with outstanding capabilities as well.

title: Very Happy with the AC1750 Mesh WiFi Extender
text:
Very Happy! Glad to finally have strong signal boost from modem to living room TV.
The total distance from the modem to our TV is approximately 54'. I placed the TP-Link in the living room about 28' from the modem in a different part of our, "L" shaped house. An outdoor heat pump is on the opposite side of the wall and the signal has to passes through to reach the TP-Link plugged in on the other side. The Roku signal on the TV on the far side of the room, another 26' from the TP-Link, has now gone from Poor and Fair to "EXCELLENT".

I was skeptical about buying a signal booster that didn't have at least 4.5 stars. My tech savvy son assured that TP-Link was an excellent brand and not to get hung up on the great reviews posted on all those sights with brandless boosters. He said that as long TP-Link had 4 stars it should be good. He said the company has a US base and was well known for there good products. He recommend the AC1750 WiFi Mesh Extender because he thought it would be the best choice for my situation to give me a really good signal.

I needed to call for tech support to complete the set up. There was no wait time and the tech was knowledgeable & helpful. Set up was simple. The service was available by clicking the link with the product on Amazon and available 24/7.

TP-Link is a global company with an office in Irvine, CA If something goes wrong with the product, they are there to help you...AND, the box says AC1750 has a 2 YEAR WARRANTY!

title: Is it love, or is it just friendship?
text:
I feel like I've been dating my new Kindle HDX 8.9. I'm looking for a long-term relationship-but I am swinging between infatuation for the many things that are terrific, to swinging back to mild disappointment with the things that bother me. A partial list of the very good:

* The fabulous screen (FAB-U-LOUS!)
* The ulta-lightness (it feel like the battery must be missing)
* The great sound
* Sharp sharp sharp text
* The joy of reading Kindle books on it (no rim of purple or blue)
* The smooth, quick operation--no stuttering!
* The really surprisingly decent cameras front and back
* The straight-forward and easy process to add (and view) my photographs and videos to this Kindle (Bravo! nothing hidden or difficult!)
* The placement of the power and sound buttons are perfect for me
* ALL the improvements in the operating system from the previous model listed in previous reviews are spot on. Great job Amazon!

HOWEVER:
* The fit and finish on mine is off. Where the rubberized section meets the shiny plastic on the back is not level, so there's just enough of a sharp ridge of the shiny plastic close to the top corners on both sides to make it uncomfortable to hold. It's where I normally would grasp it, and it's irritating like a bad seam in a shoe or a tag in a shirt that has to be cut out. It makes it feel cheap and I find myself wondering if I could just take a bit of sandpaper & fix it, but one shouldn't need to fix the finish on a tablet.
* The app store (you've already read about it)
* I thought I would not mind the ads on the opening screen, but I find that I dislike them more and more. They tend toward unattractive or childish ads for apps in which I have no interest. Again, this cheapens the experience for me. I really wish for the ability to personalize the screens with my own photographs to take advantage of that beautiful screen.
Tablets are a very personal choice and what may not bother many may rub someone else the wrong way. It's obvious that this little much improved jewel will be love at first sight for some, but I'm beginning to feel that the Kindle HDX 8.9 and I will just be friends. It's more than a 3, but maybe just shy of a 4 for me.

title: Worth the Upgrade from Fenix 3!
text:
this is my third garmin watch as i have graduated from one to the next with latest being the fenix 3. the differences between the two is big enough for me to sink in $600 for this watch. for me, the most important functionalities are battery life on gps, music, and wrist based hr monitoring....but it offers so much more!!! i really like the design of this watch. it is a lot lighter than the fenix and slimmer. fenix was not a watch that i could wear to sleep but this forerunner makes it easy for me. there are so many added features since the fenix 3 that i feel like a kid in a candy store. although not needed, i added my credit card to the watch...so if you want to go on a shopping spree, all you have to do is lift my watch!😂 syncing my airpods 2 was a breeze. have i mentioned that this watch is awesome! the built in heart rate monitor surpasses my expectations. although the wrist type monitors are not as accurate as a chest strap, i am willing to give up that accuracy for something that puts me in the general neighborhood of how my ticker is doing. it certainly does that! as far as the battery life claim of 36hours....i have not had a chance to test that yet but will have a chance toward the end of this year. generally, i can get pretty close to the number that garmin publishes but i do have to turn off almost everything to achieve that number. although i could have continue to charge the watch on the run believe it or not, my mind was too foggy in survival mode of a 100 mile run to want to worry about that. i really like the layout of the user interface on this watch. if you are coming from a garmin watch, it is similar and the learning curve is not too steep. i was able to navigate it within a few hours for the most part. i know someone stated in a review they didn't like the buttons....i love the buttons! they are responsive and get me from me place to another quickly. it is true that not as much pressure is required to do that but that is my preference. the display is very very good. it is crisp and bright. oh....the watch face is very nice. one of the things that i didn't like about the fenix was that i could never get the second hand to move like an analog watch. this one does. as far as fit, it feels so light on my wrist that i noticed it for the first day but now is just there. overall, i love the added functionalities of thhhis watch and will come back to provide a more in depth review once i have a chance to swim, bike and run with it. first impression is that this is a solid well bought out watch with everything i need! highly recommend!

8/10/2019
i have had this watch now for about two weeks. it is awesome. here are some things that i have done with it that i haven't done previously:
- sync my apple airpods and a generic earbuds to the watch. both worked although the apple airpods worked more flawlessly.
- loaded spotify and my music onto the watch. very easy to do.
- the built in hr monitor is awesome! i don't even wear my strap anymore....it gives me a rash so glad to be rid of it!
- i love all the health readings! it is awesome!
- i love the strength app. it actually counts your sets and reps. still has a little bit of work to do but pretty cool.
- i got all my external devices like hr strap, foot pod and power meter connected to the watch
- it uses about 15% per day of battery although i have everything turned on. once i am in race mode i will turn everything off to save on battery
- i bought a couple of extra cables. they charged the watch pretty well.
- i love the voice alerts while running. it gives pace distance and lactate readings
- the watch analog face is pretty good. i especially like the red second hand.. it does eat a little more battery.
- gps is quick to sync!
- the apps and widgets are awesome. well thought out.

that's all i have for now as i am training for 100 miler and hasn't had a chance to swim or bike. i am pretty sure i won't be disappointed there either. will update once i log some distance for those activities.

I can't wait to find more discoveries!

Fyi... Download the Alexa app on your mobile phone. My children can call me from the echo 8 while im at work. Lastly, Ring works well with this device.. You are notified by an alert whule being able to view any visitors at the front door or anywhere else you have a ring camera.

title: Great looking compact case
text:
Let me start out by saying I love this case but I would like to point out everything I can to make sure others know what they they are getting.

PROS
-Sturdy build quality. The metal panels are thick and do not flex and the finish seems very durable without being too flashy or having the fingerprint magnet gloss finish that others have.
-Beautiful. The glass looks amazing and the interior of the case, especially when lit, looks great. Will make it look like you spent hours on cable management.
-Nice compact size without wasting any space for a modern average PC. This could be seen as a negative but there isn't much room to expand past a typical 1 gpu, ATX board and Aio cooler setup. It provides plenty of room for almost any common graphics card.
-Airflow is great. Bottom feet are sturdy and raise the box up enough for adequate airflow underneath, even on carpet. The front cover leaves about a one inch gap top and bottom that provides plenty of air while making the front look great.

CONS
-Terrible thumb screws. The threading on almost every thumb screw is jagged or partially cross threaded and makes tool-less use almost impossible. Its too difficult to remove and replace them by hand. An exception to this is the rubberized screws for the glass, which are very nice and screw in and out smoothly.
-3.5in drive bay section needs work. It has room for 3x 3.5in drives in a standard HDD cage but it is not a toolless design, has no rubber grommets and the cage itself cannot be removed like many other cases. It also requires you to remove the PSU to replace any drives after your initial build. This could be easily fixed by making the cage removable and adding some rubber grommets to the screw holes or making it toolless.
-You must remove the front panel to access the front dust filter. Others say that you can reach this with the panel on but I don't see how. I have skinny long fingers and its difficult for me to reach through the one inch gap to pull this out.
-The power button is loose and wobbles if you touch it or jostle the case. If they made it slightly bigger or added an o-ring it would feel much higher quality.
-The cable management clips in the rear are a nice touch and located in clever spots but are very cheap feeling. If you try and put too many cables through them they won't stay clasped. Perhaps some velcro straps would be better here.
-Included fans do not come with rubber mounting points like a lot of modern fans.
-Included top fan is a 120mm unit in a 140mm fan slot and is unsightly imo.

Overall this is a nice compact case. Probably one of the smallest cases you can get for a full ATX sized system. The interior and exterior are beautiful and the price is very fair for what you get. Its a bit difficult building in the case because of the compact space and the 3.5in drive mount mentioned above but the clever cable routes and clamps in the rear really help. Because of the general design your system will be displayed beautifully when finished.

I would recommend this to an experienced builder or savvy first timer looking for a case that prioritizes aesthetics and size over all else while maintaining decent build quality for a great price.

title: Fantastic Little Machine
text:
Like almost everyone else I really LOVE this machine and have lots of praise. I got the white to minimize the appearance of smudges. I saw the blue in a store and it shows every finger print.

I'm very happy with the 6 cell, battery life is excellent and it's worth the extra weight (which is about 8 more ounces so it weighs just under 3 lbs, still light, but more then the 2.2 lb 3 cell.) This will be a great companion on LONG plane rides. The photos shown above show the 3 cell version, the 6 cell version sticks out about an inch or so more. It's fine and actually provides some balance to the computer when you open the screen.

The wifi works perfectly (in my house, at Starbucks and at McDonalds), so did the wired LAN connection.

Windows XP is a dream, unlike the SLUGGISH and incompatible with everything older then it Vista. Start up and Shut down is fast. The computer stays relatively cool too, so much cooler then all of my other notebooks.

The only negatives... very little minor things...

-The keyboard is a little small, but very managable and the touch pad just takes a little getting used it. The touch pad is actually quite powerful and you can left click (by tapping twice) and even scroll right on it. All the options are detailed under Control Panel. You could always buy a mouse [[ASIN:B000TKHBDK Logitech VX Nano Cordless Laser Mouse for Notebooks (Black)]] or [[ASIN:B00165XQWW Logitech V450 Nano Cordless Mouse- Black]] or [[ASIN:B000RHZJN4 Logitech V220 Cordless Optical Mouse for Notebooks (Black)]]

-There is no Compact Flash reader built in, but it does have readers for almost every other card format built it.

-It doesn't have a CD/DVD reader/writer, but I purchased a Apricorn EZ Writer Dual Layer DVD +/-R/RW Slim Line Combo which works off of USB power and it works great with this machine. Heres a link: [[ASIN:B000MT4JRY Apricorn EZ Writer Dual Layer DVD +/-R/RW Slim Line Combo with LightScribe USB 2.0]]

- It doesn't come with a RESTORE disk, the restore is built into the hard drive... don't know what I'll do if the hard drive ever fails (I actually have an email into Acer support and will update this review when I get a reply.) UPDATE: I emailed Acer, but they responded that they only provide support via telephone 1-800-816-2237... so I called them and they will send me the Restore CD! The restore CDs arrived via FEDEx within a week! Great customer support!

- It doesn't come with a slip case. (The 3 cell version from the store comes with a slip case.) You can easily fix that by purchasing a 9" or 10" DVD player case. [[ASIN:B000YIYS6A XDS-9 Neoprene DVD Player Case (Blue)]] I had an old one on hand (slightly different model) which worked great.

- Screen size is small. It's a little difficult to read the fine print with old eyes, but overall it's VERY usable. If you need to in an office environment, you could hook up a VGA cable to a larger monitor and a USB keyboard to the Aspire One. Great to have that option should you decide to make this your only computer...

I've run MS Office, Corel X4, Adobe Lightroom 2.0 and even Adobe CS3 Photoshop and it works fine, no noticable delay as opposed to my full sized Vista computer. (It can't run Adobe Illustrator or Adobe In Design due to the small screen limitation, but so what! I was just testing to see what would happen and I'm fine with it...)

It's an amazing machine at an amazing price and size. Great portability for traveling or just moving from room to room in your house! Highly recommend it!

title: Not truly 65 mile antenna
text: Although the description refers to this antenna as a "65 miles range" antenna, the product packaging explains the fact that the actual range is a diameter of 65 miles centered at its location. That means it only receives signal from stations within 32.5 miles of its location. In other words, perhaps it would work for a station due north at 32.5 miles AND one 32.5 miles due south. Adding those to distances (32.5 miles + 32.5 miles) gets the stated 65 mile range. That means, as in my case, that a station that is about 40 miles away is outside the range of this antenna. When I replaced my 20 year old antenna with this one, I lost over half of my channels. Realize that actual antenna performance will always depend on a lot of other factors. The distance rating on the antenna SHOULD be a good comparison of relative sensitivity. The description on Amazon should be modified. It is going back to Amazon to try another.

title: Amazing product for the price - I definitely recommend this!
text:
Thank you for reading this, hopefully my feedback will help you.

I work in IT, with over 20 years of experience so whenever I test a new gadget, I take my time with it to make sure that it meets my expectations and solves my problem.

Whenever a friend asks me for advice for a 'good WiFi system', I always point it to EERO, however, EERO systems come with a rather hefty price tag and I had not been able to find a good alternative to them... until I came across MeshForce. Also, my house is rather large (~3600 sqft) and I have had quite a few 'dark spots' that I wanted to cover.

The entire setup took less than 10 minutes - yes, it's THAT simple.
- Unpack
- Connect your base to your LAN/Router/Modem
- Download and install the app
- Scan the QR code on the bottom of your base to connect to the MeshForce's setup WiFi
- Setup your "dots" in 'strategic' places
- Setup your network/SSID/Options
- Done

I honestly believe that this is even simpler than setting up an EERO system, because the dots come 'pre-married' to your base station so all you have to do is just plug them in - genius! You also save time since you can use your google account to sign onto the App.

I was really impressed by this system, the app is simple yet it does not lack any of the vital features. What I loved:
- Setting up and sharing a 'guest' WiFi takes just 2 seconds.
- Port forwarding couldn't be easier.
- Multiple options to setup your mesh, including bridge mode! <3
- The speed of the station (and the bases)
- The dots have a LAN port which you can use to bridge!
- The dots also don't hog the entire wall plug (on a double) so you can still use the 2nd plug :)

I have a gigabit fiber connection at home, and with my former system (Ubiquiti) I was pretty happy with the throughput (around 200Mbps).
The base (and the dots) delivered almost twice that (400Mbps on the base, ~160Mbps on the first dot and ~100Mbps on the 2nd dot) - Keep in mind that if you set this up as a mesh, that's what you'd expect to see, each 'extender' will have half the connection speed as the previous 'hop'.

Overall, this system is impressive for the money. I was a bit skeptical at first but it definitely delivers a great experience for an almost unbeatable price!

title: I'm a Logitech fanboy and still think this is an excellent webcam
text:
I admit that I am a Logitech fanboy.

I use a Logitech C920 webcam and am delighted with it and will continue to use it most of the time.

However, the publisher of one of the programs I use urged checking this camera out for particular uses, namely with stop motion video production.

So I figured I would try it – and it simply blew my socks off.

The Microsoft LifeCam Studio 1080p HD Webcam is simply excellent. If I were given to hyperbole, I’d call it “fantastic” – and mean it. I’m glad I have the Logitech C920 for comparison.

And I can sum up the differences between the two easily enough: there aren’t any significant differences in image or audio quality.

I like the mount on the Microsoft unit much better because it is more flexible. I can bend the mount and the use the Microsoft webcam on a table for my stop motion work or mount it on a standard tripod screw.

You have to download controller software form the Microsoft site (“Microsoft LifeCam Dashboard”). It is less complex and offers fewer controls than the Logitech software, which many people may find more comfortable.

I tried it as the input device on several video programs and, for the most part, had no problems. A couple did refuse to acknowledge it as a 1080p device, but others did. I have to do more checking on the problem here.

Overall, I wouldn't think twice about recommending the Microsoft LifeCam Studio 1080p HD Webcam, even though I am a Logitech fanboy.

Jerry

title: A lot of Features Packed into a Pretty Box
text:
My Cambridge Soundworks radio with iPod dock finally gave out, so the search began. With my old Classic, I shuffled through 10,000 songs at my bedside every night. Waking up to my own music was also a bonus. I also enjoy listening to ball games and local radio. I knew I would not be able to find a comparable dock at this point, so I began my search for a new "clock radio". After reading all the reviews and contacting Como directly with a couple questions, I pulled the trigger on the Walnut Solo. The biggest surprise has been the Internet radio. Living in rural Vermont, I am thrilled to program 6 stations in the region, no antenna necessary. My wife is thrilled to be listening to WDEV again-she missed the Trading Post. These are my initial thoughts:

Positive:
Great size for bedside tables
USB works well. A loaded 128 GB drive will give me plenty of shuffling. Plays FLAC files.
Once I figured out the alarms, they work well. I have two different early morning alarms; it is easy to toggle between the two.
Bluetooth works well, enabling me to listen to stuff from my phone or iPad
The "analog" clock is really nice

Drawbacks
The knobs are as small and awkwardly placed as others have mentioned (thankfully the remote works well)
USB music is not an option for the alarms
The dimming feature could use a setting just a bit dimmer
For some thing I will use every night, using the sleep setting is a bit of a chore
There are other clunky processes, but much like everything else, I will get used to it

The sound quality will be rightfully debated: Solo Vs. Tivoli, stereo vs. mono. As mentioned, I replaced a CSW stereo unit. I also have a Tivoli radio. As a bedside radio, the Solo will not be used as a room filling boomer. The mono speakers don't bother me as the sound is coming from my left anyway. So.. how does it soumd? Hmm... Working through all the different inputs (USB, Internet, Bluetooth and FM), the sound is good, not great, particularly compared with the CSW. Ultimately, I think this is a good tradeoff with all the capabilities the Solo packs into a pretty nifty package.

title: First one died within 6 months, the second one in less than 2.
text:
I have used Ubiquiti's products in the home for years. The UniFi APs are much better than any consumer based products, the 8-Port Router works flawlessly, and an airMAX Bullet AC sat atop the mast of my sailboat for years of uninterrupted service (until I sold the boat).

So, when I needed a POE switch with a small form-factor for the lake house we had just purchased, it was a no-brainer. Or so I thought.

The first switch made an obvious exit within six months (completely dead). The second switch chose a less revealing failure by pretending to be functional (lights were on) but would not switch traffic (nobody home). It only lasted about two months.

When I received notifications that the various smart-home hubs/devices were offline and was unable to access anything remotely, I had my suspicions and ordered another switch; this time a managed TP-Link for about $40 less. This latest switch runs significantly cooler than the UniFi switch. Surprisingly cooler. The point I'm trying to make is that the UniFi switch ran hot. Way too hot, based on my experiences as a data-comm engineer..

For the record, the equipment is in an environmentally controlled room (temperature and humidity) with surge protected, pure sign-wave battery backups providing conditioned power for everything. Other equipment sharing this space includes a router, Access Point, various smart-home hubs/controllers, and a Synology NAS, all of which have performed flawlessly.

I hope this helps. I wasted over $220 on what ended up being a 100% unreliable device, twice. This experience has not sullied my opinion of Ubiquiti, only a segment of their product line. Time will tell if the $75 TP-Link proves to be a winner. We'll see.

title: The Good and the Bad
text:
I've own the PD-931NB for approx 3 weeks. Out of the box, I was more than happy to see all the things that came with it. TV tuner, remote, IPOD Cable, av cable harness, faceplates and different receiver enclosure mounts, also a cloth and pouch for carrying the screen.

This UNFORTUNATELY required modification to the radio bezel for my 2007 dodge ram 1500 quad cab. Yes that's right, I had to grind down the cutout for the factory radio so that the PD-931NB would actually open and function correctly. Installation took well over 4 hours (the wiring part was fine).

Once hooked up, it's quite nice to play around with. It's a different feel (mac gui adopted) with the drag down selection, but it has many options and room for expansion.

Music/Audio wise - Sounds pretty good, I removed all factory speakers and replaced with JBLs and then added a kenwood 12" sub in a sealed enclosure and a matching kenwood 5ch amp. Now my nitpicking starts to come in when I realize the equalizer only consists of bass and treble...
The audio interface is decent, I like the fact that I was able to play music and still have up the playlist on the left side of the screen, but every time I start my vehicle I have to manually unplug the ipod cord and plug it back in to get any volume (this is the only unit I've had this problem with)

The video I only used once, but it sounds great and looks pretty good too clarity-wise and there are a few adjustments you can make to fine tune it. Now I guess I would be a lil happier if the actual screen was more of a solid glass or something more touch sensitive, you literally have to exert force to get the screen to respond. Someone else on here suggested putting a protective screen on top of this so that there won't be finger prints and prolong the screen life (but to me that doubles how hard you have to press down) The actual display is rather thick in size, I imagine you could call it durable but my guess is they took older hardware to put inside to keep the cost down rather than going with slimmer more advanced hardware. Then there is definitely some lag when you do (lag from switching screen to screen, lag in the remote to receiver, and lag starting up) BUT my backup camera works like a charm and seems to have no problem with lag or delivering video.

Bottom line for me this comes right down the middle, it delivers some good options and room for expansion, it has the BASICS anyone looking to upgrade their factory radio would be happy with. To me it just doesn't add up (currently have a pioneer video unit in my other car yes it cost more but only by 60 bucks) I would have liked to see a better more responsive user interface, a real equalizer, a slimmer and more touch sensitive screen, and ipod software that doesn't require a manual pull. Also I was originally was wowwed at the 9.3in screen but with the thickness I think it's just calling to break the motor in a few weeks or months.

Recommend for the basic easy to please users, not sound enthusiasts

title: VESA bolts fit two of three Samsung TVs.
text: I live in earthquake country and have been fortunate not to suffer damage from the occasional shakers. So far. So, I decided to quit rolling the dice on this and bought a total of 3 of these Sanus Systems ELM701B1 anti-tip straps to secure three flat screen Samsung TVs. The strap is designed to secure the TV to the cabinet/stand and then to a wall stud - a 3-point installation. The enclosed instructions also give directions to secure the TV to the stand without securing it to the wall, and directions to secure the TV to the wall stud without attaching the strap to the stand. Because of the locations of my TVs, I was not able to use the 3-point method; either the stand was not sturdy enough to accept screws to secure the strap, or the distance to the wall from the stand was too long for the strap to reach. I secured one TV to just the cabinet/stand, and secured the two other TVs directly to wall studs. All applications seem secure. The Y-strap design allows me to pivot the TV screen for optimal viewing even after installation to accommodate changing viewing requirements. The TV remains secure. This is my primary reason for choosing this design over the 2-strap design. Installation was easy with two caveats: finding the center of wall studs (even with a stud finder) can be challenging; and the included VESA bolts did not work for one of the three Samsung TVs. The included bolts that fit that model were too long without the spacer and too short with the spacer. Hence, the deduction of one star. Fortunately, I had leftover VESA bolts that I could use from an earlier installation of a two-strap design on a fourth TV. (Yah, it's embarrassing: we have 4 TVs.) Don't wait for an earthquake! Get these and install them now!

the camera has a very easy setup. the software it comes with allows you to get full functionality for whatever your needs are. i use it for still pictures and skype. i can conference with colleagues very easily with this web cam, but it does require some adjusting to get the picture where you want it. first, don't use the auto tracking feature if it's just you talking in the video, it will not focus properly and continually auto corrects which is annoying. so turn the tracking off. then you can manually adjust resolution as well as the camera angle. once you first activate the video for chatting, it will auto focus, so be still, it takes a second or two. once it is focused, you're set, it won't auto correct again until you turn it off and use it again later. the software is easy to use and intuitive but does require a little practice. i use this camera virtually everyday and have not had a single problem, very high quality, which is usually the exception, not the rule for HP, though they make the best darn laser printers. if you are looking for a sophisticated web cam that is fully HD capable, pick this up.

title: Soon to be a great Legacy camera, making it a great value toaday!
text:
Hello to all. I'll try not to duplicate what everyone covered excellently already.

This cameras days I suspect are numbered making a terrific buy today. With the D5100 and the D7000, around both outstanding camera values. Even saw a 2 lens D5100 bundle at SAMs Club for only $899.00! I think the is a better buy today.

Ok, then why did I go with the D90 then instead of the cameras mentioned above? The Legacy in the title says it. my older Nikon lenses have the requirement of the body autofocus lens drive. Meaning the lens itself does not have a motor in it at all. My prime f1.8 50mm for instance, and my 70-300mm. I don't want to buy newer glass. So with the D90, I can have my cake and eat it too.

I wanted to get in on the CMOS imager here, my D200 and D40 which I love in direct sun and plentiful indoor light is a chromatic noise festival in lower light! It kept driving me nuts. Using noise reduction programs and losing detail. The D90 just doesn't have that problem. I agree with another reviewer here about usable images to 1600 ISO no problem at all. My D200 is way noisier at this range, my D40 a little better than my D200.

Another big benefit is battery life. Outstanding battery life. After a full day of shooting, the battery was only a quarter used. I am wondering if the battery grip I ordered is really needed since the battery performance so outstanding. My D200 in contrast with battery grip would almost consumed both batteries! CMOS is so much more efficient than CCD. My D40 is better than my D200, but still really lags behind the D90 in battery life. It doesn't sound like a big deal, but having juice for that one shot, it is confidence inspiring knowing you'll get shot no problem.

I am also a white balance and color nut. Most cameras have so so performance in this area around specific light like incandescent or fluorescent lighting. The D90 isn't perfect, but it pulls ahead of my D200 and D40 in accuracy. My long time favorite was my Olympus E10. Pitiful in just about anything vs. today, it just gets the color and white balnce so right. If I can take my sweet time, I still love using this old classic. The D90 is close, but I find a bit of tuning here and there with the comprehensively easy white balance setup along with bracketing, and I am a happy camper.

It is in the everyday life this camera will supplant my other cameras. The polycarbonate body fits my hand and is well balanced. The controls so logical, I am at home really being already a Nikon fan since my first D70s. My brother uses that camera now and loves it.

The D90 reminds me so much what I love about photography. Being there for the moment. Set it to auto, or program and compose and compose for that perfect image. Or go at it full manual. The command and sub command dials like my D70 make it just so easy. Shutter and aperture at your finger tips right now. Would have liked to have instant ISO control like my D200, but that Is no big deal. This camera is small enough almost like my D70 and D40, and light, unlike my D200, I can carry it all day with or without the battery grip with confidence.

Outdoor shots in my woody environs or taking pictures of the balloons that fly by my place help me realize the relaxed and beautiful place I live and the D90 makes it so fun to share. everything about the D90 even the quirky movie mode is fine with me. I even had some fun with the rolling shutter malady and made my scary lousy short feature in HD. Making lemonade out of lemons I say.

I do believe the D90 is a long term keeper for me. All the right metrics are here.

1. Ease of use due to control layout and intuitive menus.
2. Lens motor drive in body for your favorite non motor nikkor lenses.
3. Low light performance is the best I have had ever with usable images to 1600 or more ISO.
3. Light polycarbonate body is mostly all I need in day to day shooting. My Hee Man D200 soldiers on for more inclement conditions
4.battery life is outstanding. A full day shooting no problem with the D90 with a single stock battery.
5. Overall image quality and balance is great. I find myself more involved in composition than worrying about the D90 unlike my other Nikons. My Olympus E10 though a relic today, still gives me that confidence as long as I am not in a hurry.

So overall the D90 delivers much, while sold at low prices today. If you have a need for a Nikon body that can do it all with built in lens drive for your non motor nikkor glass, the D90 will please no end and will meet or exceed your expectations. It did for me.
Thank you your time. P.s. I realize that my review, more commentary is lacking the comprehensiveness of others. I just don' t want to cover again what already has been done so well. Though I did want to share because there are users that may have a similar situation and find the D7000 too dear, and the D5100 not an option. The D90 is the only new Nikon you can buy that for a short time I suspect meets those gates and much more. V.C.

title: Kindle - first impressions
text:
The first thing I did last Monday morning - even before having breakfast - was to order myself a Kindle ebook reader. I had seen a prototype some months ago, and I knew I was going to want one. At the same time, I ordered a 2GB SD card; I figure that should hold me forever. While waiting for delivery, I read the various "reviews" and blog comments, most of which seemed to be written by people who had never seen a Kindle, and who kept repeating the same rhetorical questions which they could probably have answered very easily if they'd bothered to think.

Also while I was waiting, I arranged for some downloads to be in the queue when I powered up the device for the first time. I bought one book ("[[ASIN:0312347294 The World Without Us]]" by Alan Weisman), and ordered previews of two others ("[[ASIN:0316118044 Takeover: The Return of the Imperial Presidency and the Subversion of American Democracy]]" by Charlie Savage, and "[[ASIN:B000W93DEO Arsenals of Folly]]" by Richard Rhodes). I also practiced transcoding a couple of files into Kindle format using the free non-wireless approach.

At 5:45pm today it finally arrived. (Yes, I was like a little kid waiting for Santa.) I opened it up, turned it on, and found myself reading the pre-loaded user guide. By the time I located the "Home" key, the content I had pre-ordered was already installed. Then I turned it off, removed the back panel, and plugged in the SD card. At this point, I encountered the only glitch so far: when I turned it back on, I couldn't get a wireless signal. I checked the various menus to see if I could see any wireless settings, spotted a "Restart" option, clicked it, and the Kindle came right back up with an 80% signal. Not a big deal.

Reading on the Kindle just feels right. There are six font sizes, and I picked the smallest, which works for me. People have described the design as "bland", but for me that's actually the point. After using the Kindle for a few minutes, you don't notice it any more, which is as it should be. Intrusive, edgy styling would be exactly wrong for this kind of device. The controls work well, and I especially like the "silver strip" cursor.

I started reading "Arsenals of Folly", and kept reading until I reached the end of the preview chapter... And that's when it became expensively seductive. Because there's a link there inviting you to buy the full book, and one click, $9.99, and 30 seconds later you've done exactly that. My advice: choose those previews with care, because it's far too easy to buy. (Or perhaps I should just say that it's a very compelling user experience!)

This is easily the best ebook solution I've encountered. I've tried reading ebooks on my PC or Mac - wrong, wrong, wrong: reading a book is a "sitting back" activity, while using a PC is a "sitting forward" thing. (That's a fundamental dichotomy, which is why you can comfortably watch a DVD on a laptop but not a desktop.) I've tried various PDAs, but the screens are too small and the fonts are always ugly. I've never tried a tablet PC, but that seems far too heavy and bulky. The Kindle just works. The size and weight are appropriate, I find the fonts "comfortably satisfying", if that makes any sense, and the e-paper screen is unobtrusive, the way that the page of a book is supposed to be.

Things to try tomorrow: the New York Times, the dictionary, the web browser, and loading up Gibbon's "Decline and Fall...". Oh yes, and reading some more of "The World Without Us". Because that's what this is all about.

title: Superb microphone for the price.
text:
I was in the market for a decent Podcasting microphone that was small enough to travel with, yet still have decent sound reception and clarity. I am not in the position to spend hundreds (or thousands) of dollars for our small company Podcasts but still needed something up to the task. This has been a great purchase since it checked all the boxes for what I was looking for.

Initial setup was easy, attached the included cable and tripod and was pleased to find the adjustment screw sets tight and stays that way. (I have had another brand where the tripod screw didn't lock in place). Microphone feels solid and not plasticy, the controls feel good quality and don't pop/buzz like some other brands when adjusting them. And I am happy with getting an actual usable cable length! Plenty of slack to place the microphone where I want it on whatever work space we are working from.

The plug and play works great, didn't have to fiddle with any drivers or updates. Every time I move locations or plug/unplug the mic, it's been no problem. The quality of sound has been crystal clear, I haven't had to do any post-production EQ or other processing. I was concerned about one session due to some background noise I could not control, but the pickup pattern on this mic is close enough in that the background noise wasn't a factor.

So far I have used this mic for three different Podcasts (and lots of playing around testing) over the last two weeks and it has performed flawlessly. I wouldn't hesitate to buy again, a lot of bang for the buck if you're just getting into Podcasting or just on a budget but don't want to sacrifice quality.

While I think this reader maybe a little over priced, I really like it. The writing experience is perfect. I thought it would be thin and spotty. It's so much like pen and paper. I bought the premium pen and the eraser alone is worth the $30 upgrade. I know folks are upset about not being able to search notes but I'm ok with that. I will use it just like a notepad ... and I will search through just like i do pen and paper notes. I went through a cookbook tonight and planned out meals for the week. I put simple sticky notes by each meal that just had the day of the week I will need the recipe. Now I can click the notes button and see my note and the page it is on. Thursday, I'll go to page 71. Wednesday - page 73. I'm just deciding how I will use it and I am super happy so far. As for the reading experience... anybody researching this will already know that it is a Kindle and hard to beat. One more thing, if you are like me and have many kindle readers, hit the trade in button. I got a $25 gift card and 20% off 32 GB Scribe for my paperweight from 2018!!!
P.S. I saw a review that said the eraser required alot of pressure. That is not the case with mine. I flip the pen over and apply the slightest pressure and the writing fades first. Then I can watch it kind of jolt clear. I have a right hand injury and I am OCD about screen's and such. I know it sounds silly but I would not keep it if it didn't erase smooth with little pressure. I think the premium pen is my favorite part.

title: A Very Good Camera For The ProAm Photographer
text:
Having owned this camera for a while now, I feel much more qualified to judge its advantages and drawbacks. This camera for me followed a full-fledged SLR, including a 75-300mm zoom lens that weighed a ton and was very bulky to boot. The total kit cost me over $900 to put together, and was very unwieldy, especially when you were trying to switch between close-up and long-range shots, and had to keep switching out lenses. For professional photogs who may be used to that, and maybe even prefer it, that's fine. But for me, who prefers ease of use to tons of extraneous equipment, it was difficult at best. This was my first replacement, an all-in-one unit.

First, the advantages. 1) It's all-in-one, so no switching between lenses all the time, which saves time, effort (and money). 2) The cost is less than half of the equivalent SLR. 3) The full digital zoom is the equivalent of a 900mm lens, which is three times the zoom of the 75-300mm zoom lens I had with my SLR. Where others can zoom in on the moon, let's say, and make it fill approximately half the frame, I can zoom in to where the moon more than fills the frame at full zoom. I recently used this with the 2017 total solar eclipse. 4) The flash is programmable for strength, and in Manual mode, you can program the ISO level from 80-1600, which is handy in full light vs. low light situations. 5) You can easily add multiple Canon-compatible lenses, such as solar, color lenses, and the like. It also has several color features included, such as B&W, sepia, mono-color (meaning you can pick one color to appear in the photo, while everything not of that color is B&W), and many others. This is one of the most versatile cameras I've ever owned, and even after years of owning it, I'm still learning about it.

Now, the disadvantages. 1) The color balance is not as great as some higher-end cameras, such as certain SLR's or Nikons that I've seen photos from. In actuality, my cell phone camera has better color balance than this camera (I took several photos on a recent trip with both cameras for comparison). I will say that for the price, I wasn't expecting top-of-the-line photos--I was expecting ease of use more than anything, and I did get that. 2) This camera does not do well in low-temp conditions. Earlier this year, I took it to an event in February that was outside, and after a short time in low temperatures (near freezing), the gears started locking up, and things like zoom and opening and closing the shutter were labored and very noisy. So if you're planning on doing stuff outdoors, make sure it's nowhere near freezing when you do. 3) Although the light balance is OK, it's limited. If you're shooting a shot that involves varying levels of light in the subject (let's say some semi-dark mountains with a bright cloudy sky above them, for instance), it is very difficult to get a balance in the light levels so that the mountains don't appear completely dark, or the sky overly bright and washed out. But again, this is a matter of price--if you're willing to pay $1,200--$2,000 for a camera, you're likely going to get better shots as a result.

Overall, this is a very good camera for someone who either may not be professional (or need the accompanying level of equipment), or who may not want to spend thousands of dollars on equipment for whatever reason. I am a high-level amateur with a lot of experience, but not a lot of money. So for me, spending $2,000 or more on camera equipment is not an option, nor would I have the requisite expertise to use it properly if I did. For a rank amateur who is more on the selfie level, or takes a lot of on-the-fly photos at parties or in bars, this may be a bit on the high side, and a simple point-and-shoot camera might be more your style. But for someone who loves taking decent photos, and who wants a higher-quality camera without paying exorbitant prices for it, this is a nice balance between both worlds. It also gives you more versatility and ease-of-use than a full-fledged SLR would, without having to lug around a ton of equipment.

So overall, this is a competent camera for the higher-level amateur, and one that won't break the bank buying it either.

title: Couldn't have ended better!
text:
I just finished the trilogy and WOW. Reading books 1 & 2 I just could not put it down, I had it on my mind all of the events transpiring and what will happened next. The ending was perfect and I felt completely content in my heart and happy for them. I laughed, cried a little, blushed at times, cheered for them and even learned from them. Christian and Ana weathered the storm and I could not have imagined a better ending. Heck, he even cries a little! The Epilogue was even better. The bonus chapters brought us into Christian's mind and we can see from the very beginning as much as he tried, he never truly saw Ana as another sub. I honestly don't want more, it's perfect that way it is and they are at peace with their lives and that makes me completely satisfied with this trilogy. I have NEVER said that about a book before because I have never become emotionally attached to characters like this. We learn that unconditional love can be tried and tested and in the end, it will win. We see a very dark soul become free and embrace the fact his wife genuinely loves him, Fifty Shades and all.
When it was all said and done --I missed so much what we had in the beginning. It reminded me that relationships are hard, but if I want to be happy... really happy... then it takes work. I learned to feel more comfortable in my sensuality, to not be afraid to ask for what I want and need from him. Life is so hard and if we can find our way back to even a little bit of the jealousy, the great sex, and being so into each other we can't stand it then maybe, just maybe, we won't end up on the down side of the statistics.
