title: A Thorough Review of this Amazing Speaker.
text:
DENON HEOS 7

Be careful with Denon HEOS 7 reviews. Most of the professional bloggers and the general public post reviews after minimal listening time and with and limited depth of usage. I’ve had mine for two weeks and after daily listening I can confirm that it takes time for these monsters to break in and a little time for the user to get things configured for optimal use. Not only that, the system offers an impressive number of connectivity options and I haven’t found a single reviewer that has actually used all of the available options and explained the pros and cons of each. I’m going to try.

Here are the topics I’ll cover in the review of the Denon HEOS 7:
Set up and home network.
The speakers: build and sound quality.
The App.
How I get music to the speakers with lackluster Apple Music support.
How to turn the HEOS wireless speakers into Bluetooth speakers.
Other connectivity options: older iPod, music servers.
What I think after living with them for a while?
Would I buy them again?

Quick background. I love high quality audio. I’m so picky that I seem to never stop tweaking my home theater or listening area speakers to the point that it drives my wife nuts. Also, I don’t mind spending money to get good sound. I have a pair Beats Studio Wireless and a pair of Bose QC25 headphones. My home theater has three full-range Definitive Technologies BPs and four surrounds while my listening area has two DefTec BPs and ProCinema surrounds. We recently noticed a couple of cracks in our sheet rock. Our repair guy called them stress fractures. I think I created them from music and movie volume.

That being said, I wanted great sound in my living room, master bedroom and other places in the house without bulky speakers. My original mission was to buy a SONOS system but thanks to a really helpful sales guy at Best Buy I landed on the Denon’s. We started with the canned “push-to-play” music that’s integrated into the display but I wasn’t satisfied. Most of of that stuff is over equalized by the manufacturer (Bose started that trend) so that it showcases the strengths and hides the weaknesses of the featured speakers. So, the guy got out a 3.5mm cord and we plugged my iPhone into the B&W Zeppelin, the Polks, the Denon’s and the SONOS. I got to test the speakers with the music that I like. After an hour of this, the choice was obvious, the Denon HEOS System. I was surprised and had to pause a moment to consider if I was making the right choice walking away from my intended target, SONOS. In the end, I went HEOS and…well, read on and you’ll see how I feel about my purchase.

I truly appreciate a sales person that goes to extremes to satisfy a customer so I bought two white HEOS 7s from him and a black HEOS 7 and 5 from Amazon.

SET UP:'Super easy. Download the HEOS app then using the included 3.5mm cord, just plug your phone or tablet into the headphone jack and follow the directions. Once set up, the app will automatically prompt you to update the firmware. If you have multiple speakers like I do, you’ll need to repeat for each speaker which can take a while. A batch update would be nice but in the big scheme of things, it’s a necessity of technology that I’m glad Denon makes easy.

The one bad thing is that Denon uses a flat 3.5mm plug. Without the notched plug, that so may manufacturers make, you have to take the case off of your smartphone to plug it in. This is such and easy fix that I’d hope that Denon get’s with it and fixed this soon.

Next, I clicked the gear (settings), selected “My Devices” and gave my speakers custom names. You have to select a canned name then tap it and rename it to something you like. For example, I named the living room speakers “Living Room L” and “Living Room R,” the bedroom speaker “Bedroom” and then named the HEOS 5 “Floater” since I move it around the house.

I’ve read some reviews where the reviewer says that set up was not straight forward or easy. Well, that person must be technically challenged or their home wireless network is weak. For me, it was quick and very easy.

IMPORTANT about your HOME NETWORK: I have known people that have multi-floor or large homes in which they have a single poorly placed wireless router. To solve this, they install a second wireless router up stairs or on the other side of the house but they don’t set the second access point to bridge mode. Instead, they set it up as it’s own network with it’s own SSID (network name). This will cause you a problem using whole home systems not to mention that you are always having to go into your device settings and change networks. These days Apple, Asus, Netgear, et al., make it SO easy to bridge their wireless routers so that they extend the a single network through a large space (Denon makes a HEOS extender too). Either way, it’s a good practice to use a single network that covers your entire living area, inside and out. And for those that want your kids to be on a separate, regulated network, just create a separate SSID with it’s own rules, or quality of service, but keep it on the same master network. The HEOS System will recognize that second SSID. If you do this, setting up a SONOS or HEOS system will be a breeze, and so will a lot of other wireless tasks you’ll be faced with (like wireless printing) as Wi-Fi becomes more and more integral to our digital lives. On to the review.

Setup: 8/10

THE SPEAKERS:
Denon is an audio company. I have owned a string of Denon receivers (I still use an old AVR-4800 in my listening area) and currently own a Marantz in my media room. They know how to create great sound at consumer price points and that’s a good start. I like music delivered with volume, not ear bursting, but what I call “full sound.” As long as they have appropriate power behind them speakers played at higher volumes show you what they are made of. Some get harsh, some distort, some get boomy, some fade in a certain range, but the good ones stay strong and smooth until the power runs out. Strong and smooth is what I’m looking for and I’m amazed at how strong and smooth the HEOS 7s are. As it hits the 90% mark, the amps begin to struggle and you start to hearing the strain. But, 90% on the HEOS is not like 90% on a Bose Soundlink. The HEOS 7 can get crazy LOUD. Two speakers turned up to 80% are insanely loud. This tells me that the speakers have ample power to back up the five active radiators without appreciable distortion.

My living room is set up with two white HEOS 7s in bookcases that flank a fireplace. Not ideal as the recessed bookcase shelf adds a throaty sound (that you’ll read more about in this section) and a little boominess to the bass. It’s not horrible but I notice it. The problem is that there are not many other options for me without the speakers being physically obtrusive. I wanted them to blend into their environment so white speakers in white built-in bookcases in the living room and black on a dark wood chest-on-chest in the bedroom.

I started with the speakers on the lowest bookcase shelf then moved them up one and I like better up there, about five feet off of the floor. We have a opened floorpan and as I move around the living room, kitchen and dining room, they sound better with a little bit of elevation.

Some reviewers write that the mids are weak, I’d kind of agree but I’d call it mildly weak and it’s easy to solve the issue with the EQ built into the app. Drop the bass one notch and increase treble one notch (my current set up) and it seems to help the mids. Luckily, the bass is so heavy (and in bookcases even heavier), you won’t miss the notch of bass. In very specific ranges, the mids can project a throaty sound that I find odd but not offensive. It’s a little worse with the speaker in a bookcase. The Lone Bellow sing “Then Came the Morning.” It’s a very mid-heavy song and certain words can sound like they are being sung unto a bowl. Same thing for Diana Krall’s “Feels Like Home.” At times, her alto voice resonates oddly. You hear it immediately in the first line. I’ll underline the words that the speaker makes sound throaty. “Something in your eyes, makes me want to lose myself. Makes me want to lose myself…in your arms.” It’s a certain frequency at a certain pitch. It’s small but noticeable if you listen for it. On my full-range DefTec’s or my Beats Wireless Headphones, I don’t hear it. Other than that, the sound of the HEOS 7 is as close to perfect as one can ask of a compact speaker.

The HEOS 7 do such a great job producing bass that there is absolutely no need for a sub. Nice, since a sub in a living room can be an eyesore. To be clear, these little speakers do not replicate the bass power of the powered subs in my DefTecs but they will shake things off of shelves and effectively project really deep frequencies that will confuse your house guests. Most will start looking for the hidden sub.

Speaking of bass, Little Big Town’s “Girl Crush” should be one of your go-to speaker tests. Right out of the gate, the picking of the electric guitar followed by Karen Fairchild’s voice are immediate, forward, distinct and clear. It’s an experience that great speakers enhance and lesser speakers destroy. Close your eyes and let it flow into your ears for a little over a minute then get ready. At 1:20, the bass guitar gently lights up the little internal sub. The HEOS 7 allow the bass to roll in smoothly and showcase the gentle warmness without any induced boominess. This is a huge accomplishment for a speaker that’s only 8-inches tall and 6.5-inches deep. It’s a simple song but each instrument is distinct and present and the vocals are so clear that with your eyes closed you’ll think you are listening to much bigger speakers or a live, private performance. The tightly plucked guitar strings, the smooth rolling bass, the subtle Hammond organ and the occasional rhythm guitar strum, it’s all there even when listening to one HEOS 7. Try two of them paired in stereo mode and you’ll hear things that you can’t hear in your car or cheap iPod headphones.

All this goodness in a small package has it’s limits. Listening to “2 Man Show” by Timbaland is just too much for the HEOS 7s. My DefTecs and my Beats Wireless handle the song with ease but the ultra low notes severely roll off (rolling off is better than distortion though). The song still sounds good but if you are accustomed to the song on bass capable systems, you’ll notice the missing pieces. This is not a slam, that song stresses all but the best speakers and I can count the songs that I own on one hand that over stress the HEOS 7s. Kid Ink’s “No Miracles” and Sam Hunt’s “Breaking Up In A Small Town” are also on that short list, but I can live with that.

Here’s good song to test how the speakers handle great vocal performances. Download “Opportunity” from the Annie Soundtrack sung by Sia. Yeah, I know “Annie.” Trust me. Let it play and at 0:52 onward, you’ll see what I mean. Sia sings with strong passion and emotion and behind her is a huge symphony. The HEOS shine. Then at 2:22, tell me this song won’t make your “most played” list. It concludes with a huge crescendo and the HEOS don’t hide a thing, the highs, mids and lows are all there. Chase that with Elton John’s “Tinderbox” with it’s immediate piano and heavy bass…crystal clear. Then enter Sir Elton’s distinct vocals and you’ll know you are on the right track with the HEOS 7s.

If you’re still not sold, queue up Adele’s “Hello.” The song on it’s own isn’t overly taxing on a better than average speaker but in this case, it’s all about the voice. The HEOS 7 showcases their vocal clarity with exceptional accuracy. When the song explodes with Adele’s vocal power, the speakers don’t fail to keep up. I have listened to that same song on a lesser Bose SoundLink II and I found myself disappointed in it’s inability to deliver the song that way it was intended. The HEOS 7 does the reigning queen of the power ballad justice at extreme volume levels.

Compared to the old SONOS Play:5, it’s no contest. The older model lacked tonal warmth and had weak sloppy bass. Probably the reason SONOS offers a separate powered sub. In contrast, the new, late 2015, Play:5 speaker are much, much better. The bass is smooth and the treble is clear. Like the HEOS 7, Mid-tones are are a little weak but I have to admit, the new Play:5 sounds amazing. Listen to the HEOS 7 and new Play:5 side-by-side and you’d be hard pressed to pick on sound alone. That being said, I found the Denon system as a whole a lot better. I wanted to mix large and mid-sized speakers and the HEOS 5 blows the PLAY:3 away. If you have Play:3s you will be forced to add a $600 subwoofer to get full-ranged sound out of them. The HEOS 5 are smaller versions of the 7s with ample bass for mid-sized rooms or even large rooms with low ceilings.

As I write this review, the new Play:5 was available for a live audition but not available for delivery and Denon was running a sale where I got the HEOS 7 for $350 and the HEOS 5 for $250 ($50 more than the HEOS 1 and $50 less than the HEOS 3, crazy right?). So, with the performance, price and availability as it was, the decision scales were definitely tipped to Denon.

As for build quality, these things look and feel great. At nine pounds, the HEOS 7s are well-made speakers (I do wish that Denon has put a handle on the back of the sevens like they did on the fives as it would make moving a nine-pound, teardrop-shaped speaker easier). Their shape is irregular and will be seen as sexy to some and ugly to others. I like the flowing lines of the teardrop shape and the gentle glow of the adjustable (brightness) blue LED feedback light. I like the fabric covers but over time, I think the fabric on the white ones might get a little dingy but the black ones should wear well.

ONE eight-inch tall speaker has two tweeters, two mid-range drivers and a powered sub backed up with two passive radiators for depth and resonance. To put this into perspective, my DefTech BPs have two tweeters, four mids, a powered sub and two passive radiators but that’s all in a three-and-a-half-foot tall, 12-inch deep box. The HEOS 7 is built solid like a tank with the technology of a $1,000 speaker.

Sound: 9/10
Build Quality: 9/10

THE APP
The sales guy warned me that the app for the SONOS was better than the HEOS. From what I’ve experienced so far, he’s right. Set up was easy but dang, everything else is pretty confusing. After hours of tinkering, I learned that the app is very powerful and offers a wealth of adjustments, inputs and information. I had to work to figure things out and I’m good as stuff like this. Denon has a YouTube channel that helps you rename speakers, adjust the limited EQ, creating stereo pairs and such. I’d suggest that you check it out if you buy the system. It’ll save you a lot of frustration.

To make things worse, finding good documentation for the app is pretty hard. That’s bad Denon! The app should have a great support/help button that takes you right to the videos and gives great online documentation.

Here are a few things that might take you a while to figure out:
Tap the GEAR on the main page then tap MUSIC SOURCES to hide unused services to declutter your screen. This alone creates a better user experience.
Tap the GEAR to hide unused INPUTS on each speaker so you only see the AUX In or USB inputs that have audio sources behind them.
Click the PENCIL on the ROOMS screen, then tap the red arrow next to the speaker to rename or modify the speaker group. Also, you can adjust EQ or Balance. IMPORTANT!!! If you use two speakers in one room, select STEREO PAIR. If you don’t, things don’t sound right with two mono/pseudo-stereo speaks in one room. Once they are in Stereo Mode, they deliver correct L/R balance, harmonics and separation. I did not have this set up correctly and it took me a bit to figure it out.
If you use an AUX input source be aware that you have two volume sources. For example, the App has volume and the device (iPhone, Android, iPod, etc) does too. You can easily blow your eardrums out if they are both set to 100% OR you’ll wonder why there is no sound as you have your iPod volume up but the app is at zero (or vice versa). NOTE: even with direct AUX IN, there is no getting away from interacting with the app.
If you have a group of people at your house and they all have the HEOS app and are on your home network, they can insert music into your music queue. It’s actually pretty cool. Say your buddy says, “Hey, have you heard ‘How Could You Babe’ by Tobias Jesso, Jr?” He can call it up, add it as PLAY NEXT or PLAY NOW or ADD TO END OF LIST. The song will stream from his music source then the speakers go back to your playlist. Pretty neat, huh?
To get audio out of a specific speaker, go to ROOMS, highlight a speaker then leave ROOMS and select the source. Repeat and you have different audio in different rooms (this was confusing to me at first).
To get speakers to play the same thing, go to ROOMS, press and hold then drag them together. Drag them apart to separate sound sources. Very slick and very easy.
Configuring the speaker so you have Spotify playing in the bedroom, your iPhone streaming to the living room and Pandora in your craft room takes some figuring out. It’s not difficult, it’s just not intuitive.
Like I said, the app isn’t horrible but I wasn’t buying an app, I was buying sound. Great sound. Nevertheless, with these Wi-Fi, whole home systems the app makes them work.

Here’s the good news, Denon uses DLNA (Digital Living Network Alliance) so they work with a lot of hardware and music sources (or servers) that embrace that universal technology. SONOS uses a proprietary system that is closed. Very close. Apple closed. I don’t like that.

Bad news too is that, as of this writing, the app does not support the new Apple Music, nor Google Play, nor Amazon Music. What the heck Denon? I emailed them and this their reply.

“Thank You for contacting HEOS support. Amazon and Apple Music services are not currently integrated on 3rd party audio devices such as HEOS.  For many years Denon has enjoyed a healthy partnership with Apple and we expect this to continue, however at this time we cannot provide detail about Amazon or Apple Music.  We are aware of the consumer interest and thank you for your inquiry.
 
Until then, you can use the AUX input to play directly from any device’s headphone connection. Or if you have a HEOS 1, you can use the Go Pack to add Bluetooth and stream Amazon or Apple Music that way. You can also buy a standard Bluetooth 4.0 USB adapter. All HEOS speakers are capable of using a Bluetooth adapter. We have tested and recommend the Plugable USB adapter at the following link:

http://www.amazon.com/Plugable-Bluetooth-Adapter-Raspberry-Compatible/dp/B009ZIILLI/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1445523910&sr=8-2&keywords=plugable+usb+4.0”

What? I have to plug my iPhone into the 3.5mm headphones port in the back of the…no way. Since I use Apple Music and most of my songs are cloud-based, that’s a deal breaker for me!

App usability: 5/10
App features: 8/10
Connectivity: 8/10

HERE IS HOW I GET APPLE MUSIC TO PLAY NICE WITH THE HEOS
If you use one of the integrated services (Pandora, Spotify, music that lives on your smartphone, etc., you are set with both Android and Apple devices. They work great. Before I move on, here’s something I discovered about the integrated services. I used the app to stream Mike and Mike on ESPN Radio through Tunein Radio. Once the show was playing, I accidentally closed the HEOS add but the show kept playing. I believe the app creates a handshake between the service and the speaker and wirelessly hands the audio off then goes into standby mode until needed again. But if you want to use the new Apple Music service or Amazon Music, things don’t work that way.

This is where things get a bit technical but it’s worth reading. The good news is that I’ve done a lot of the research for you.

As I was deciding to buy three HEOS 7s and a 5, I had to solve the Apple Music thing. You CAN listen to music that resides on your iPhone or iPad, but NOT using cloud-based music streamed through the Apple/Amazon/Google Music apps. How is this possible when I can stream Pandora, Spotify, iHeart, SeriousXM, TIDAL, Rhapsody, et al? How do the big three get left out? It’s a mind-boggling thing for sure but it’s true. SONOS claims to have a solution for the Apple Music puzzle by the end of 2015. So should Denon.

Well, I happened to have an old Apple Airport Express. As I considered the HEOS, I thought about it sitting in my retired technology box and knew that I could link it to my home network then plug it to the 3.5mm port. BAM! I’m now able to stream anything I want. I knew it’d work so I bought the speakers. When they arrived, I hooked it up and the system worked exactly as I had imagined that it would save one thing. The sound quality of audio coming from Apple Music that’s piped through AUX IN does not sound quite as good as music that lives on my iPhone that streams through the app. I’d wager that it would be hard for some people to tell but I did exhaustive A-B testing with the same song and there is no denying it.

NOTE: audio quality is definitely effected by the source. Tunein Radio sounds like a good radio but not audiophile quality. Pandora, iHeart and SiriusXM sound overly compressed and terrible. Spotify sounds great. Those, and my own content, are the only ones that I tested.

Additionally, since the system is linked to your home network, you can roam throughout your house and the music keeps playing without the 30-foot Bluetooth limitation. With BT, step away from your speaker, or BT hub, and the music stops. Wi-Fi speakers don’t have that issue. Even with the Express plugged into one speaker, I can stream to all four speakers or just the one using the Apple Music app. You end up managing the speakers with the HEOS app while you manage the audio from whatever app you want. It functions very well and it’s worth the small effort it takes to make it all work.

So, here’s a little known fact. SONOS and HEOS cannot stream ANY audio through (and because of) the app. So, if you want to watch VEVO videos on your iPad with the audio coming out of your speakers, you can’t. If you want to stream a Netflix movie or YouTube video with the audio booming through the speakers…you can’t. Unless you use the Express or Bluetooth. You can only stream what the app allows you to stream from the sources it allows. Crazy, right? But, with the Airport Express, I can stream anything I want. Audio from a movie on my computer or YouTube off of an iPad or Apple Music from the cloud, you name it. One reason you won’t though is that there is a 1.5-2 second lag creating what looks like a of of those old Kung-Fu movies where the fighters lips move then a second later the English translation comes out. This is true for both the Airport Express and Bluetooth. If you plug you iPad directly into the 3.5mm port, the delay is only .5 seconds but but’s not completely gone. Not that you’d do that but I thought I’d test it anyway. This is all too bad because I’d love to stream audio to the speakers from YouTube videos watched on my iPad while sitting on my sofa.

AUX In: 10/10.

BLUETOOTH
As you saw in the reply from Denon, you can make the speakers work via Bluetooth with a $12 dongle (link in email above) from Amazon. I tried it and it works but I don’t like it as much as I like the Airport Express. Compared to Wi-Fi connectivity, the 30-foot limitation is well, limiting. I like to keep my phone in my pocket then pull it out to skip/repeat a song from anywhere in the house. But, I bought the dongle and tested it and for those that want or need to use Bluetooth, here’s how you make it work.

The instructions don’t tell you this but if you search on Denon’s website you’ll be instructed to insert the Bluetooth dongle into the USB port in the back of one of the speakers, then open the Bluetooth settings on your mobile device then press and hold the CONNECT button on the back of the speaker for for three seconds. The light on the bottom of the HEOS 7 will start to blink and the name of the speaker that has the dongle in it will appear as a BT device on your phone. In my case, “BEDROOM.” Tap on “Bedroom” and it will Bluetooth connect.

Seems stupid that they just didn’t make the HEOS Bluetooth ready out of the box, but whatever.

Bluetooth: 3/10 since you have to buy a dongle to make it work but unlike SONOS, it does work.

IPOD INPUT
An older iPod works only if plugged into the 3.5mm headphone port. I could not get mine to act as a music server when plugged into the USB port on the back of the speaker. This is something we know works because it’s how the old Bose Sound Docks worked. It seems to me that it should have been something that Denon thought to do but they didn’t. Too bad because if it worked, you’d have a portable music server that you could control and navigate from the app.

USB and MUSIC SERVERS
DLNA makes this super easy. I have an ASUS AC1900 and I have a hard drive plugged into the wireless router with some music on it and when you use the HEOS app and selected Music Server, I was able to quickly, and easily, access the music and stream directly off of the drive without doing anything special. The app automatically sorts the metadata so I could search the server by artist or song. Pretty neat.

I was able to get music to play off of USB thumb drive and a powered hard drive plugged into the USB port on the back of the speaker but I could not get a USB powered hard drive to work. It appears that the 5V/1A port does not provide enough power for that option.

Music Servers: 10/10. DLNA is a great addition. SONOS does not offer this kind of flexibility.

MUSIC/RADIO SERVICES
This is another short entry. If you use the canned app services like Rdio, Pandora, Spotify, Tunein, etc., it just works. Period. A huge benefit of using a supported service is that you don’t need any additional connectivity methods/devices. No need for Apple Airport Express or Bluetooth. It’s the way to go and if Denon will get their act together and get Apple, Google and Amazon services added, the HEOS system would be nearly perfect.

Integrated Services: 4/10 only since the big players are not supported.

WHAT DO I THINK OF THE SYSTEM AFTER LIVING WITH IT FOR A WHILE?
I love the sound. If you are comparing them to full-sized powered speakers, you’ll have things to complain about but if you compare them to any and all compact wireless speakers on the market, you’ll find nothing but small things to nit-pick. Side-by-side with the SONOS Play:5, the app breaks the tie but the rest of the SONOS line is so weak that I was not willing to sacrifice the whole home system for a better app.

Something I did’t see coming was how much I love moving from room-to-room with music seamlessly playing around the house. Today, my wife was making curtains in her craft/sewing room so we moved the HEOS 5 up there. I just plugged it and and it synced up and played.

INTERESTING FACT: If you have the system playing and you unplug a speaker, relocate it and plug it back in again, as the speaker begins scanning for the network, all speakers momentarily stop playing. Once the speaker is back on net, the music comes back. Interesting.

Also, understand that the speakers get better with time. I’ve let them run at high volume levels while at work for several days and it has really helped (as it does with most speakers and headphones). The bass has gotten smoother and the mids have gotten warmer but I can’t tell much difference on the high end. The throatiness that I mentioned earlier is still there but I think it’s has to more to do with placement than the speakers.

WOULD I BUY THEM AGAIN?
Yes. Actually, heck yes! The Denon HEOS system is really good and the HEOS 7 sound amazing with huge, full sound that’s smooth, balanced but a little bass heavy, which I like. You can tone them down with the EQ and personally I’d rather have to much bass that I have the option of toning down rather than thin bass that can’t be adjusted to taste.

I found the confusing app to be full featured and to work well once you get accustomed to it. I found set up to be extremely easy. I love having music throughout the house and I really like that I added the HEOS 5 as a floater that can easily be move into any room. All Denon needs to do is solve the music streaming issues with the big three, improve the app and they have a product that many of you should really consider when shopping for SONOS.

As I said, I’m picky about audio and I’m very content with my purchase of the Denon HEOS 7s and if you can live with the app, I believe you will love them too.

Nora said that if I could find a micro fuse adapter, Redtiger would reimburse me. So, I found the micro fuse adapter at my local Auto zone store. Through all of this, I had sent email questios and had immediate responses from Nora and her team. The customer service is very good! One of my questions was how to tell whether parking mode was working. Nora and her team took the time to go out in the shop and capture the process on video and then emailed me the video which was very informative.

I provided some photos. I show what the front camera view and what the rear camera views. I also included a photo of where the rear camera is mounted.

I highly recommend this dash cam!

title: Have had laptop {AERO 15 OLED XD) for couple of weeks. Lets call it a 4.5 star
text:
I've had the laptop {AERO 15 OLED XD-73US624SP version) for a couple of weeks now.
OVERALL
Despite, missed opportunities in design and implementation, overall I am happy I got the laptop. I seriously love the OLED screen; cpu performance is right where it needs to be. I am happy with the 16 GB of ram and the 1 TB gen 4 SSD. For others who need more storage, the presence of the 2nd gen 3 SSD slot is a big plus. I expect this laptop to serve me well for long time. I guess I can love and still be aware of misses. As of this moment, I am still flipping on giving a 4 or 5 rating. A 4.5 would be comfortable for me to give. But then again my perfect laptop would have to be 6 stars. LOL.
I decided to move this support warning from the bottom of the text to the top, because it really bothers that I cannot register the laptop
SUPPORT
I am perplexed. I have been trying to register the laptop for weeks now. Every link I have tried fails with most common error being 502 Bad Gateway. Does not matter which browser I try and have tried from multiple desktops and laptops. I have bought motherboards and graphics cards from them in the past. So I am surprised and disappointed that they no longer FULLY support their products. These are their own links imbedded in their own web pages. Yeah I expect they are going to reply, Don’t worry, we cover it etc. …… I understand that with Gigabyte being hacked, the company may be distracted from maintaining the business. It reflects badly upon the company.
SCREEN
I love the 4k screen with its high resolution so I can have plenty of open windows and because of the crisp text I can still clearly read data. Basically I can lay panels out on the 15 inch screen like I would for my 27 inch monitor and still read just as well. Most people won’t care but data hogs will be happy. (if you are one, you will know what I am talking about.) Being a 4K screen, Windows will be “suggesting” a 250% scaling which I have dialed back so I can fit more on the display. I have not found any flaws in my display such as dead pixels or backlight issues or bleed. Movies are gorgeous, crisp and bright BUT there is a but.. see section on speakers.
KEYBOARD
Very Decent. A bit of concave shaping helps center fingers. The little locator bars on the J & F help touch typing and a light bit of bounce and key travel helps. Better than keyboard on my old asus . About equal to my old old Toshiba but not quite as nice of the feel of my Lenovo TabX1. A Plus for the AERO, there a real 10 key pad (sadly lacking on the TabX1 due to size). The backlighting is a BIG plus. I have used the control center to zone the colors and brightness for alphanumeric, function keys, control keys and the ten keys. Whoever decided to NOT include the shifted characters for the backlight needs to be wacked up the side of the head. Duh… Guess I will have to keep a flashlight with me at night.
SPEAKERS
Bluntly barely adequate. The listening environment has to be totally quiet. If there is noise such as a fan in the room then the Volume on every setting from Windows, to the player or video application has to be at maximum. I tried to watch a movie and had to turn off a room fan (it’s August). While I could hear strongly spoken dialogue, anything whispered was totally lost and I had no idea of what was said. Gigabyte brags “DTS:X Ultra Immerse yourself In Cinema Grade Sound” So external speakers or headphones are going to be needed. Hooking up a good Bluetooth speaker solved the problem for the movie.
DOCUMENTATION
Not as good as my prior Gigabyte experiences. When I found the manual on the hard drive I thought I was in good shape. Nope, it was just a soft copy of the 2 page quick start guide. So online you will go hunting. Some specifications are there on the sales portion of the Gigabyte site. I am making a offline copy of the Gigabyte info, just in case they delete the info. Then there are a few third party review sites that cover technical data for the laptop.
NOSE CAM
If you have already read or watched the reviews available, you already know the camera placement and quality are such a mess that Gigabyte could have and should have done better right at the beginning of the design and layout planning. I knew about it before I ordered and I will never ever use it. A total waste.

title: Despite some fairly strong poor reviews I bit and am pleasantly surprised, and quite content.
text:
Knowing this isn't an amp from the old MB Quart of the heydays of car audio I am happy with this amp. I'm running it in my truck with a component set of 6.5's and 2 pairs of tweeters for the upper range and a 10" sub.

It's clean, loud and pretty musical if a bit dry and sometimes hard on the high end. The bass seems solid and has some heft and clarity that's nice, satisfying and agreeable. It's got the usual adjustments and crossover functions so set up is easy. On the other end, the speaker and power connections seem robust and secure. I've only had it for a short time and it's not fully tuned in yet but so far I'm pleased. It's a great buy and looks clean.

Update 1 month later: my previous system in another rig, I needed a 2FD cap to avoid voltage drop out to the sound system and dimming head lights. With this amp in this system I'm running a more powerful amp and without a cap I have zero issues with drop out or dimming. Running at full song, it's way too loud to listen inside the cab, but it's still clean if a bit harsh and dry. The amp runs cool and is effectively noiseless. The first week I did have some alternator whine but it disappeared so I didn't investigate further. I keep looking for bits to find fault with but so far it's been a champ.

Update - 2 months later, all is well. Been doing more fine tuning and my over all feelings haven't changed much. The amp is an excellent buy. When driven past half volume to hard levels It gets very dry, thin and sharp. For me at these volumes it's a bit much to listen to but the sonic characteristics of my system change significantly at this point and it's not so good sounding. Below around half volume it's darn good. Amp still runs cool but when pushed hard it gets quit warm but not hot, still in the 40's so that could change come summer. So far it's a keeper.

Update - 1 year later: Still going strong! Playing around with settings on my deck, and filter settings on the amp and various tuning, my system sounds pretty good now. I even added a second 10” sub in parallel and this amp runs fine...that’s a 2 ohm load on this 5 channel amp! On bass heavy music and high at volumes, I can get it pretty hot, but at normal volumes it is merely warm.

2nd update - 2 years later: amp is still going strong! I added a stiffening cap and replaced my door speakers and this amp keeps rocking away. I guess. Got the opposite of a lemon! I do see that there is a different amp now that replaces this amp and the whole line now. Hopefully that will eliminate some of the issues others have reported.

title: An amazing camera for wedding photography
text:
I have been using this camera for almost 5 years now mostly for wedding photography, and it is so wonderful that I am about to replace it with the exact same model.

This one is coming up to the end of it's shutter-life because I have used it so much and incase you don't know: cameras have life expectancies kinda like a car's mileage. The shutter-expectancy for this one is about 200,000 shutters I believe, and I've started having some issues with it (freezing, stalling, strange lines and things on images here and there) now that I've gotten to about 180,000 shutters, but I also am very often having to subject my camera to hours in direct sun in 100º+ weather so I kind of expect it to poop out on me a little early. That is still a good life for most cameras though, and it has been extremely reliable before now.

The lenses you use are extremely important, the difference in image quality between one of $150 lenses and and my favorite 50mm sigma lens (I think it was about $600-$700) is massive, despite being the same camera. The photos in this review are using the sigma lens.

Other points of awesomeness:

The speed in low-light situations is unmatched by any camera any of my photography friends have, and being able to bump that ISO way up is amazing, especially for sparkler send-offs if you want to keep the ambiance and not use a flash. With my flash on I can freeze motion easily without having to bring the ISO higher than 800-1000 and I love that it keeps the golden tones of background lights unlike some Canon's that I've seen.

The quiet mode is really nice when shooting a wedding that is very ..quiet. Sometimes a church will have a lot of echo, and while the quiet mode doesn't make it silent it does slow down the sound and take the edge off which helps a lot with reducing how much attention it draws.

The megapixels.. I can shoot a wedding ceremony entirely on a 50mm from far-ish away if I want to and then just zoom in and crop some of them to have close-ups. Shoot on f/2 and they'll be sharp as a tack.

title: Good overall DVD player, some problems
text:
I have a very good experience with my old Pioneer DVD player, that's why I decided to purchase Pioneer again. The color and audio reproduction is very good for the price range. You also get top notch USB and DivX support. It's not free of faults, however. Let's go over the Pros and Cons:

Pros:
1. Excellent color reproduction (Sony DVP-NS77H has more vivid color however, but Pioneer's is by no mean less admirable)
2. Excellent audio output for its class
3. Well-designed remote
4. User setup is very comprehensive for its class
5. USB port (your flash drive must be formated in FAT file system)
6. Plays a very impressive numbers of video/audio formats (DivX, MP3, WMA, burned DVDs/CDs etc)
6. Excellent value
7. Automatically switch to proper screen size (DVDs)
8. Energy Star compliant

Cons:
1. No Toslink S/PDIF (Digital optical sound)
2. Low-quality optical drive
3. Has problem reading scratched/warped VCD/DVD
4. No LED power-on indicator near power button

That last problem can be annoying. It doesn't read anything more than a minor scratch. I would think it's due to the cheap optical drive it uses. I tried Sony DVP-NS77H, and it was no better, however. Only the expensive Toshiba HD-XA2 was able to read my Contact DVD reasonably. It's not the only DVD that gave me the problem.

Since nowadays DVD players (HD and newer SD models) have long boot up time, and it takes about 10-second to boot up this one, having no power on indicator is a problem. You can see Pioneer's logo on the TV screen, but no LED lights or display on the console itself to tell the user it's on.

Remote is excellent. I wish it's slightly heavier, instead of light-plasticky, but it's very well designed. Everything the user would use frequently is right there near the middle where your hand is locked in by the notch in the back. You don't see good remotes nowadays that come with cheap DVD-players often. No backlight, however, but it's intuitive enough.

It has no Toslink (Optical audio cable), but the Coaxial audio (the one that looks like RCA) is excellent. It's the best audio quality I've heard from a DVD player that costs only $99.

The setup screen gives you everything you need to tweak. It's comparable to my Toshiba XA2, but that one is a top-of-the-line HD-DVD player!!! You can select upscale resolution as well as more advanced stuff like picture colors. I disagree with people who think the menu is difficult to use. It's no harder than most newer DVD players. It has a lot of features that can overwhelm users however, but that's what manual is for (it's not an excellent manual, but one can get most information out of it).

I upscaled my regular DVDs, and the output is amazing! You don't even have to touch the DVD player's color/hue settings (and it's advised you should always change those with your TV's controls with a color tuning DVD, such as Avia or Digital Video Essentials). The SD DVDs' output is almost as good as HD DVDs'.

All upconverted video signal does not allow the pass through of CC signals (the TV close caption, not the DVD subtitle). If you need that, you'd have problem. I suggest you connect both component video cables (at 480i) as well as HDMI (at upconverted resolution of your HDTV monitor), so if you need CC, then use component video output and that should solve the problem (though of course, you'd see the video at a lower resolution).

I have a Sony 50A3000 SXRD HDTV, and if you have something similar, I suggest you turn off all the motion enhancement features (there are three of them hiding in Video Options). If you don't, upconverted video signal compounded with motion enhancements will cause some funny distortion near the edges of display (look like fishbowl effect).

My Toshiba XA2 for some odd reason, does not adjust screen size automatically so the entire picture will fill up the 16:9 screen. This much cheaper model does! You don't know how much time you can save with such convenient feature, you literally don't feel it (until you are deprived of it, of course).

Overall, I believe it's the best upconverting DVD player you can buy for under $100.

title: I'm hooked
text:
After reading about Tivo and personal digital recorders in magazine reviews and here, I decided I would take the plunge. I thought hard about getting the Phillips 60 hour version, but at twice the cost and because I hadn't even tried the concept out, I decided to settle for the Phillips 30 hour unit. After an easy, but time consuming setup (best if you do it right before bedtime), I quickly realized how cool and useful this thing is. The video quality is fine, decent even at the "lesser" levels (movie credits do get blurry and difficult to read), although true videophiles may find it unexceptional. I would have to say the most pleasing aspect of this is that I am now getting the most out of my premium cable movie channels. I am now catching a lot of movies I routinely missed because I was not vigilant enough to find out when they might be on so that I could set my VCR to tape them. Now, the "Network Showcase" feature alerts me to all of the channels' current and upcoming flicks and all I have to do is to say "yea" or "nay" to recording them. Even if I don't check ahead, the thing records movies it thinks I might like based upon preferences I have expressed for other features and shows. Awesome. Also, skipping commercials is an easy and pleasurable feature. By the way, any football (or other live action sports) enthusiast easily will see the usefulness of such a device.
One thing that disturbs me about the Tivo phenomena is that I fear that it may be rendered obsolete quickly because of how rapidly technology is evolving. I purchased the lifetime service option and I will be downright bummed if something else comes along to supplant it before I get my money's worth and I wind up having to buy into something else!

title: Work with my Cochlear Implant Processors
text:
I am completely deaf. I use 2 cochlear implants (CI). I set both CI processors to receive input from the CI processors' "microphones". I put the H390 on my head, covering my ears and the processors. I am able to hear the sound coming from the H390 headset speakers. I next set both CI processors to "Telecoil". With this setting I cannot anything through the CI microphones as the CI microphones are turned OFF. Playing test sounds, I can hear the test sounds and I hear the left and right test sounds separately.
Even though the H390 is not advertised as Hearing-Aid Compatible (HAC) the magnetic coils within the speakers act as telecoils.
For best listening, I set my CI processors to "Microphone + Telecoil" to receive sound from both the H390 headset speakers and the Telecoil.
I am happy with my purchase.

title: Good for having fun.
text:
I wrote a super long review, but it felt rambly, so I'm going to just list points that I like and don't like.

The good:
- Very immersive and fun. Sound stage isn't too large which I like, as I prefer more intimate IEMs (not without detail though).
- Good low end, if a bit simple.
- Great imaging.
- A tad warm.
- Distinctively different sound to what I'm used to. Mentioned as a pro, but also as a con.
- Very easy to put on and they almost always have a good fit.
- Sounds smoother than my other IEMs (only have $50 IEMS atm though), which I like.
- Did I mention fun? They bring a lot of life to some music, notably stuff with a decent bit of low end.

The bad:
- Low end does sometimes seep into mids and drown out some detail.
- Doesn't feel very open on the top end - a bit closed off.
- Distinctively different sound to what I'm used to. I was quite put out by it initially. Things don't sound like they do on a more neutral IEM, especially vocals/mids. But not a dealbreaker.
- Vocals are subdued a bit. Some tracks can sound less emotional because of it.

These have become my main IEMs over my other IEMs, namely old Sennheiser CX 300s, Tin T2s, and Blon BL-03s. I really think there's little risk in picking these up. But I would urge you to check out the ZS ZSX, as it's purportedly a direct upgrade over the ZS 10 Pro.

Update: After getting some other IEMs (Fa7, and OH10), I've gained some more respect for these. Honestly, if you get these, you won't be missing out until you get way higher in price. Great value.

Update 2: left IEM failed after a few months of usage (3 months ago or so). It still make sound but whichever driver was working for the low end gave up, so its just harsh trebly sound. I thought it was my tips or ear shape causing the issue due to them working previously, but after trying everything, I realise its the IEM itself. I tried other cables as well (after it started failing). Review set to 1 start due to this. I've not been rough with these, or using them excessively, so there's no excuse.

title: Excellent Handheld Illuminance Spectrometer (Spectrophotometer), aka Illumination Spectroradiometer!
text:
Excellent device! I feel that it is by far the best in its class, and also the least expensive in its class for the features that if offers.

Let me tell you up front that while the primary target market for this product is folks in the world of photography, set lighting, filmmaking and videography, none of those are my fields. Rather, I am a scientist and an engineer, and I have, for the past two years, been considering purchasing a really good handheld illuminance spectrophotometer (aka illuminance spectrometer) for use in my work with probiotic photosynthetic microbes and in evaluating the LED and other lights used to illuminate them during their fermentation. So, I did a lot of research online, looking at each of the brands/models available, including products primarily intended for the photography/filmmaking/set lighting world, and the products intended for use in the scientific, commercial/industrial, architecture and agricultural realms, and I finally settled on this device as the one offering by far the best quality, best design, and best features for the price.

I can say without reservation that I love this handheld illuminance spectrometer! I feel that the design and craftmanship are both excellent, and it works well. Best yet, it has saved me a tremendous amount of time in evaluating the effects of different wavelengths of light on the photosynthetic probiotic microbes that I work with, and it has saved me a ton of time and headaches in quickly and effortlessly evaluating the real-world illumination performance (versus the wild and often very-inaccurate claims made by vendors) of various models/brands of LED, fluorescent, and incandescent grow lights, including specialty single-color lamps.

This is an odd tool to own, because it is somewhat addictive and habit forming: much to my surprise, every day I find new uses for it, both in my research work and around the house and yard, and in a greenhouse that we have on the property for growing veggies and berries almost year-round, and I have even found myself using it in the poultry pen, and the henhouse!

BTW, both the update software and the utility software for downloading jpg spectral chart files (or other files) from the handheld device are problem-free and work well. I download at least six jpg spectral chart files, along with their associated data files (i.e., csv-delineated files for import into a spreadsheet or database, data files, etc.) to my PC every day, and the task never takes more than a minute or two. The only firmware update that I have performed using the update software went quickly and easily.

BTW, in case I forgot to mention it earlier, this device works excellently in evaluating LED lights, both so-called white light types, and single-color and multi-color types!

I will also note that the manufacturer cautions that a few dead pixels (due to dead 1 nm pixels in the CMOS light sensor, which covers 380 nm to 780 nm in 1`nm increments) may be found in the spectral charts displayed by the device, and that this is normal, that is, something to be expected. My particular device, as I examine it after about 40 hours of use, has exactly three dead pixels (one in the blue range, and two in the red to NIR (near infrared) range; each dead zone is only 1 nm in width, and the dead pixels do not affect the quality or the readability of the display charts at all.

Excellent device, and it is a joy to use! My only warning is that it is addictive! You will keep finding new uses for it!

title: Disaster avoided
text:
Most reviews had issues with the wrong version being shipped. I took a chance with it because I could always use a back up for additional prototyping. The latest version is the R3 and that is what I received. WOOT I can safely assume that after Arduino started manufacturing the R3, sellers like this was stuck with a previous version and unloaded them on unexpected buyers with the hopes we wouldn't notice. But now that the R3 is pretty standard on shelves it should always come with this. I will continue to check in and if anyone else receives less than the R3 I will change my review to reflect 1 star. I am giving them 4 star because of the history as I believe this is not a proper way of doing business.

///////If you are new to Arduino and want to know what the big difference is between the models I highly recommend going to that really popular video site and searching "What's new in the new Arduino Uno" Adafruit has seen to it that a chic explains it nicely./////////

Oddly enough there was a review that said it had a staunch smell of smoke. It in fact does have this smell. It is not from a smoker though. I recognized it immediately as foundry slag. This smell originates from the jumper wires and is very powerful and just picking up the wires and setting them down transfers this to your hand.

Gasoline/Charred Gear Cutting Oil, LMFAO

The jumper wires are coated in silicone (not plastic) so this is somewhat expected. There is a chemical bath the manufacturer can put them thru but it greatly increases the cost.

This kit was $5 less than the one exactly like it from another seller, the only difference is this one was not very clear that it comes with the holder for both the Arduino and breadboard. It was not until after I ordered it that I realized that it was included as per the description but was not in the product image. BONUS!!!.

title: Low profile is great
text:
Long time mechanical keyboard user for a decade now. I wanted to try a low profile version for work to see if it could make typing a little easier on my wrists and I'm happy to report it's really comfortable. The switches used are Kailh chocs and they are very nice to type on. Kailh has come a long way since their cherry clone days and I feel they make some of the better switches out now.

Aesthetics are the first thing that drew me to this board. I really like the way it looks. I bought 2 mini versions of this board in clicky and tactile. The clicky version has a very crispy click and I find this to be one of my favorite blue-type mechanicals I've ever used. Really helps me crank out the sentences for work. Really frees up desk space with the mini design too.

I also got a tactile version for my gaming setup. The new bolt dongle has very low latency ~14ish ms. I cannot tell the difference between this and my wired keyboards, so for me, it's great for gaming. I know logitech makes gaming focused versions with lower latency, but I don't think anyone would be able to tell the difference between this board and a gaming variant in a blind trial - gaming while blind, I know ;)

The only real disappointment is the price in my book. I think these are way overpriced. They should retail for about 80-100 bucks max, especially considering the keycaps are ABS. Other than that, they are really great keyboards. The lighting is nice and battery life has been great.

title: Not perfect but overall... a damn fine television!
text:
For the record I will state that I am a long time Toshiba tv buyer. I have reviewed the last two lcd models that I have owned. I just got this today and have really just started messing around with it.

APPEARANCE: This is one sexy television. The frame blends into the tv under a single pane of glass. Thin, thin, thin! It is up there with the Samsungs as far as looks are concerned. Even the stand looks awesome. On the negative side... the glass is very shiny and shows every reflection that it can find! The crystal clear coat that is supposed to diffuse these reflections must not have been applied here. I have noticed that just about everyone but Vizio is going to shiny screens... it's a shame!

SOUND: Surprisingly strong! My last Toshiba had horrible out of the box sound that really needed tweaking to sound good. Not this one... I am not claiming that it is home theater quality but it's clear and has some depth to it. Good job Toshiba.

PICTURE: This is really what it's all about and the tv does not disappoint. SD picture quality is as good as any display that I have seen. HD picture quality is easily as good as the Samsungs and better than Sony, LG etc. Even the out of the box picture mode, movie 2, is awesome. I used full calibration settings and I think movie 2 is just as good. Colors are rich and really pop and images are clear and smooth. You definitely want to set stabilization to standard! On to the negatives... black is not anywhere near as dark as my last Toshiba. I will say that that last lcd was as good as any plasma that I have seen! The blacks are surely not the worst but also not the best. I will have to see what I think of this when I watch more movies. Next... the dreaded clouding issue. The clouds are there! I have not yet been able to see them when there is actually something on the tv. When watching a letterbox film there was only flashlighting in one corner as opposed to the two on my last set. I plan to attach usb fans to the back of the tv to get rid of this but I haven't gotten them yet. I will update on how they work. So far I must say that the clouding issue seems not to be that bad on my tv. I have not tested 3D as I could care less about it.

CONCLUSION: Overall I have to say that this tv at Amazon's price with free shipping is the best value on the market. This is a great tv with a few flaws but I could not be happier so far. If anything changes I will update the review but as of now I would recommend this set to anyone who cannot afford to spend hundreds or even a thousand more and still wants a top notch set!

UPDATE 5/12/2011: Still thrilled with the overall picture quality. Equal to any other set that I have seen. I am also still not entirely thrilled with the black level. It's not terrible but it just isn't as dark as my last Toshiba set. Only seems to be an issue when watching letterbox movies for the most part but watching Machete blu-ray I could definitely notice the less than stellar blacks... still working on this one! I attached 2 small USB fans to the back of the tv that I purchased for $13 on Amazon, plugged them into the USB port on the tv and NO MORE CLOUDING... GONE! Best of all, you don't need a fan controller, they go on when the tv goes on.

UPDATE 5/19/2011: I have finally gotten a respectable black level on bluray! I activated the auto brightness setting while in movie 2 settings. The auto setting was horrible when i tried it on cable but on bluray it looks great. At this point it seems that I have a top of the line picture with actual black in it! Very happy that I took the chance on this television.

title: Legacy compatibility issues
text:
The good: The product arrived as scheduled. It was functional immediately. I upgraded to Windows 8 Pro to get the functionality of Windows Media Center. Price was great. Product is well engineered by HP.

Application Plan: My plan was to port the extra things I had added to a Windows 7 32 bit computer to the new computer with better performance and storage upgrade. This computer is a media center for the whole house residing in the kitchen where family members can easily access it for web surfing and where it manages DVR functionality for the whole house (including commercial stripping of recordings), video calling (Skype) and landline telephone communications (TapiRex), and a whole house music system (Pandora). It has media extenders connected and drives four other screens in the house. I replaced the existing computer because it was slow responding and the hard drive was getting flakey.

Issues: Several of the problems I have run into are legacy issues for which I cannot fault the new computer -- but I list them so as to be aware before you undertake such a changeout.

1. Legacy Plugins - Two of the addons in my old computer were PCI bus (telephone modem, hauppage TV tuner. The new computer only has PCIe slots. :(
2. Digital Cable Tuner issues - I currently utilize the 3 tuner HDHomeRun digital cable tuner to record TV in Windows Media Center. Initially the new W8 Media Center configured as expected -- but after a day it stopped working (complaining about having a cable card for each tuner). Seems to be a compatibility issue between W8 and the HDHomeRun tuner. It works fine with the W7 machines I have. :(
3. Legacy Extenders don't work -- W8 only supports XBox extenders and Microsoft configured the interface so that legacy extenders do not work any more :(
4. Touch Screen doesn't function as expected -- Because the screen has a bezel surrounding it (Acer 230H), I can't access the all important corners to activate the W8 start screen and tools with my fat finger. :(

I solved most of these problems by going back to Windows 7 and spending $ for upgraded plugins.

title: Wonderful as extension cord for your OTA antenna
text:
My Over The Air signal (free!) TV antenna (inexpensive!) was working fine until recently. I could not pull in all the channels I used to be able to see. I moved the antenna from spot to spot but the moment I sat down or changed the channel, it was all over. I was about to buy a powered antenna as a last resort when I had the AHA! moment to buy this cord. I am SO glad I did! It's long enough to run almost the entire length of the house. Now my antenna can sit in the garage where I get a great signal and the TV is way over on the other end somewhere.
One thing I had to have explained to me is that for cords like this, you must buy a female to female extension coupler (and they're very inexpensive too). For some reason, all these cords are male to male. I kept looking for female to male, right? Plug the male end of the antenna into the female end (marked "input" or "antenna") of the TV (or DVD player, or blu ray player ....). And BTW, I think we used to call the ends RCA plugs - but the actual name is, F-type?
This cable must truly be shielded as they claim. It runs right past the kitchen (and microwave which seems to interfer with the digital signal) and runs behind lamps, down inside walls, and behind the tv where there are all sorts of other electrics and cables. The picture on my 55" TV couldn't be better. I do not have cable or satellite TV, but the TV is not so old that I have to use an analog to digital signal converter box either. I would highly recommend trying this if you are having trouble bringing in an over the air (digital) signal. Sometimes there's interference between you and the TV station and this just might be a really inexpensive fix. (Also look at antennaWeb.org to find out where your tv signals are coming from.) It is not a miracle cure, but if you are able to experiment with the placement, directional facing and height of the antenna, you might think it is! I am just that impressed! And SO lucky I thought of this.
